The spring's inner end hooks onto the central arbor, which winding turns, and its outer end presses against the drum wall, so the drum is pulled round as the spring lets go. In an automatic, the outer end is a sliding bridle that slips when fully wound, so the rotor can never overwind it.
keyNumbers: Power reserve: about 48 hours
Diameter: roughly 10 mm
Parts: drum, lid, arbor and spring
details.madeOf: Brass or a copper-beryllium alloy for the drum and lid, with a hardened steel arbor running through the middle.

parts.name: Mainspring barrel

parts.description: Half a metre of coiled alloy ribbon; its slow unwinding powers everything.

details.didYouKnow: Taken out of its barrel, a modern mainspring relaxes into a curled S shape rather than a flat spiral, a form chosen to give more even force.
details.howItWorks: The mainspring stores the energy that runs the watch. Winding coils it tightly around the barrel arbor, and it slowly uncoils towards the barrel wall, turning the barrel as it goes. Its shape is designed so the force it gives stays fairly even over most of its run, which helps the watch keep steady time.
keyNumbers: Length: about 0.5 m
Thickness: roughly 0.1 mm
Height: about 1 mm
details.madeOf: Modern springs use a cobalt-nickel alloy such as Nivaflex, which does not rust, resists fatigue and is almost unbreakable. Older ones were blued carbon steel and could snap.

parts.name: Mainspring

parts.description: Turns once an hour; its arbor carries the minute hand up through the dial.

details.didYouKnow: The 60 to 1 step from the centre wheel to the seconds wheel is split across two gear meshes, because one gear 60 times bigger than its pinion would never fit in a watch.
details.howItWorks: The centre wheel is driven by the barrel and turns exactly once an hour. Its arbor pokes up through the dial, where the cannon pinion and minute hand sit on it. It also drives the third wheel, passing power on towards the escapement.
keyNumbers: Speed: 1 turn per hour
Ratio to fourth wheel: 60 to 1
Pinion leaves: typically 6 to 12
details.madeOf: A brass or copper alloy wheel riveted to a hardened steel pinion, a pairing that wears well because the soft wheel and hard pinion do not gall.

parts.name: Centre wheel

parts.description: Steps the speed up between the centre wheel and the seconds wheel.

details.didYouKnow: Watch wheels are spoked, often with fancy shapes, not just for looks: less mass means less energy wasted in starting and stopping 8 times a second.
details.howItWorks: The third wheel sits between the centre wheel and the fourth wheel. It shares out the 60 to 1 speed-up between two smaller steps, turning faster than the centre wheel but slower than the seconds wheel. Its pivots run in jewels in the main plate and train bridge.
keyNumbers: Speed: roughly once every 7 to 8 minutes
Speed-up per step: about 7 to 8 times
Wheel thickness: a few tenths of a millimetre
details.madeOf: A thin brass wheel with spokes cut away to save weight, riveted onto a polished, hardened steel pinion.

parts.name: Third wheel

parts.description: Turns once a minute; the seconds hand rides on it.

details.didYouKnow: In many watches the seconds hand sits off in a small sub-dial, because putting the fourth wheel at the centre of the movement takes extra gears.
details.howItWorks: The fourth wheel turns once a minute, so its arbor is the natural place for the seconds hand. It drives the escape wheel pinion, which runs much faster still. Every tick of the escapement lets it move forward a tiny step, which is why the seconds hand creeps round in small jumps.
keyNumbers: Speed: 1 turn per minute
Ratio to escape wheel: about 16 to 1 at 4 Hz
Steps per turn: 480
details.madeOf: Brass wheel on a hardened steel pinion, with a long, slender arbor when it has to reach up through the dial to carry the seconds hand.

parts.name: Fourth (seconds) wheel

parts.description: Hook-toothed wheel that the pallet fork catches and releases, one tooth per tick.

details.didYouKnow: In a Swiss lever escapement the teeth have a club-shaped tip, shaped so the impulse is shared between the tooth and the pallet stone.
details.howItWorks: The escape wheel is the last wheel of the train, always being pushed round by the mainspring's force. The pallet fork lets it advance just a little at each swing of the balance, and as each tooth slides off a pallet stone it pushes back, giving the balance a small kick. In this way it both counts the swings and keeps the balance going.
keyNumbers: Teeth: typically 15
Speed: about 16 turns per minute at 4 Hz
Teeth released: about 4 per second
details.madeOf: Hardened and polished steel, because its teeth rub against ruby pallets thousands of times a minute. Some modern watches use etched silicon, which needs no oil.

parts.name: Escape wheel

parts.description: Rocking lever with two ruby pallets; it locks the escape wheel and gives the balance a nudge each swing. This is the tick.

details.didYouKnow: The lever escapement was invented by the English watchmaker Thomas Mudge in the 1750s, and almost every mechanical watch made today still uses a version of it.
details.howItWorks: The pallet fork rocks to and fro on its own pivot. As the balance swings past, a ruby pin on it knocks the fork over, which unlocks the escape wheel for an instant; the wheel's tooth then slides across a pallet stone and pushes the fork, which passes that push back to the balance. The other pallet then locks the next tooth, and the sound of each lock is the tick you hear.
keyNumbers: Ticks per second: 8
Ticks per day: about 691,200
Pallet stones: 2
details.madeOf: Hardened steel body with two synthetic ruby pallet stones set into it, because the stones must be harder and slicker than the steel escape wheel teeth.

parts.name: Pallet fork

parts.description: The timekeeper: swings back and forth four times a second, like a tiny pendulum.

details.didYouKnow: A watch that is 10 seconds a day out is accurate to about one part in ten thousand, all thanks to a wheel smaller than a fingernail.
details.howItWorks: The balance wheel swings one way, is pulled back by the hairspring, then swings the other way, at a steady rate set by its weight and the spring's stiffness. Each swing lets the pallet fork release the escape wheel once, so the balance decides how fast the whole gear train is allowed to run. A good balance swings through most of a full circle each way.
keyNumbers: Frequency: 4 Hz (28,800 vibrations per hour)
Swing: typically about 270 to 310 degrees
Diameter: roughly 9 to 10 mm
details.madeOf: Usually Glucydur, a beryllium-copper alloy that is hard, non-magnetic and changes size very little with temperature, so the rate stays stable.

parts.name: Balance wheel

parts.description: Arms joining the rim to the balance staff.

details.didYouKnow: The balance staff pivots are so thin that a hard knock could snap them, which is why most watches mount the balance jewels in spring-loaded shock settings.
details.howItWorks: The spokes link the balance rim to its staff, the axle at the centre. Keeping them thin puts most of the mass at the rim, where it gives the most inertia for the least weight. The staff carries the hairspring collet above and the roller with its impulse jewel below.
keyNumbers: Arms: typically 2 to 4
Staff pivots: roughly a tenth of a millimetre across
Arm thickness: a few tenths of a millimetre
details.madeOf: Cut from the same piece of Glucydur as the rim, so rim and arms stay perfectly true, with a hardened steel staff riveted through the centre.

parts.name: Balance spokes

parts.description: Spiral spring finer than a hair; its stiffness sets how fast the balance swings, and so the watch's rate.

details.didYouKnow: The name Nivarox comes from French for neither variable nor oxidising. The balance spring itself was introduced by Christiaan Huygens in 1675 and made pocket watches accurate for the first time.
details.howItWorks: The hairspring's inner end is fixed to the balance staff and its outer end to a stud on the balance cock. As the balance turns, the spring winds or unwinds and pulls it back, so the pair swing like a pendulum. Change the spring's working length or stiffness and the watch runs faster or slower.
keyNumbers: Thickness: a few hundredths of a millimetre
Coils: typically about 12 to 14
Rate error to keep: usually within about 10 seconds a day
details.madeOf: A special iron-nickel alloy such as Nivarox, which keeps nearly the same stiffness as temperature changes and resists magnetism. Some modern watches use silicon instead.

parts.name: Hairspring

parts.description: Plate that holds the barrel and centre wheel in place from below.

details.didYouKnow: The decoration on bridges is often hidden under the dial or rotor, yet makers still finish it carefully, partly as a mark of quality.
details.howItWorks: The barrel bridge holds the barrel arbor in place, closing the sandwich between it and the main plate. It often carries the winding wheels that take power from the crown and rotor down to the barrel. Steel dowel pins locate it so it goes back in exactly the same spot after every service.
keyNumbers: Thickness: roughly 1 to 2 mm
Locating pins: usually 2
Screws: typically 2 or 3
details.madeOf: Real movements usually use brass plated with rhodium or nickel, often decorated with stripes called Côtes de Genève. Plating keeps the brass from tarnishing.

parts.name: Barrel bridge

parts.description: Bridge carrying the lower jewels of the third, fourth and escape wheels.

details.didYouKnow: Jewels are pressed into bridges with a special tool that sets their height to within a few thousandths of a millimetre, which is how endshake is adjusted.
details.howItWorks: The train bridge holds the other end of the third, fourth and escape wheel pivots, each in its own jewel. The gap between bridge and plate is set so each wheel has a tiny amount of up-and-down play, called endshake, letting it spin freely with oil in place. Too little play and the wheels bind; too much and they wobble.
keyNumbers: Wheels held: 3
Endshake per wheel: a few hundredths of a millimetre
Jewels set into it: typically 3 or more
details.madeOf: Plated brass, machined flat and true, with jewels pressed into reamed holes to a precise depth.

parts.name: Train bridge

parts.description: Single-armed bridge over the balance; it carries the regulator used to adjust the rate.

details.didYouKnow: Old pocket watch cocks were often hand-engraved with flowers and scrolls, because the balance was the one part owners loved to look at.
details.howItWorks: The balance cock is a bridge held at only one end, so the balance can be fitted and adjusted easily. It carries the upper balance jewel, the stud that holds the hairspring's outer end, and the regulator. Moving the regulator slides two tiny pins along the hairspring, changing its effective length and so the rate.
keyNumbers: Fixing screws: usually 1
Regulator adjustment: a few seconds a day per small nudge
Jewels: usually 2, a hole jewel and a cap jewel
details.madeOf: Plated brass, often with extra decoration since it is the most visible bridge through a display back. The shock setting in it uses a small steel spring.

parts.name: Balance cock

parts.description: Heat-blued steel screw.

details.didYouKnow: Watchmakers judge bluing by eye, watching the steel run from straw to brown to purple to blue and stopping at exactly the right moment.
details.howItWorks: Bridge screws clamp the bridges down onto the main plate, holding every wheel at the right height. They thread into the plate and seat firmly on the bridge surface. They must be tight enough to stay put but not so tight that the soft brass threads strip.
keyNumbers: Bluing temperature: roughly 290 to 300 °C
Thread size: often around 1 mm or less
Count here: 5
details.madeOf: Steel, heated until a thin oxide layer forms on the surface and gives it a deep blue colour. The colour comes from that film, not from paint.

parts.name: Bridge screw

parts.description: Ball bearing the rotor spins on.

details.didYouKnow: A worn rotor bearing lets the rotor tilt and scrape the inside of the case back, and the scratching sound is a common sign a watch needs a service.
details.howItWorks: The rotor bearing lets the heavy rotor spin with very little friction in either direction. It is a tiny ring of balls running between an inner and outer race, fixed to the centre of the movement. A winding wheel underneath picks up the rotor's motion and sends it down to the barrel through reverser wheels.
keyNumbers: Ball diameter: roughly half a millimetre
Balls: typically around 7 to 10
Rotation: free in both directions
details.madeOf: Hardened steel races and balls, or sometimes ceramic balls, which are lighter and need no oil. Some makers use a ruby jewel bearing instead.

parts.name: Rotor bearing

parts.description: Heavy half-disc that swings with every move of your wrist and winds the mainspring.

details.didYouKnow: If you sit very still all day, an automatic can slowly run down. Most need several hours of normal wear a day to stay fully wound.
details.howItWorks: The rotor is an off-centre weight that gravity keeps pointing downwards, so every move of your wrist makes the movement turn around it. That swinging is geared down heavily and used to wind the mainspring a little at a time. Reverser wheels let it wind whichever way it spins.
keyNumbers: Swing: free through a full 360 degrees
Gear reduction to barrel: very high, often over 100 to 1
Weight: a few grams
details.madeOf: Steel or brass, often with a heavy rim of tungsten alloy, which is very dense and so packs more swing into a small space. Luxury watches sometimes use solid gold.

parts.name: Winding rotor

summary: An automatic wristwatch with no battery: a coiled mainspring, wound by the swinging rotor as you move, drives a train of gears that the balance wheel releases one tick at a time, about eight ticks a second.

name: Jet Engine
overview:
A jet engine makes thrust by throwing a huge amount of air backwards. This one is a high-bypass turbofan, the type on almost every airliner. It does four things in order: suck, squeeze, bang, blow.

At the front, the big fan pulls in air. Most of that air (here about ten times as much as goes through the middle) bypasses the core and is simply pushed out the back by the fan. That cool, slow bypass stream makes most of the thrust, quietly and efficiently. The rest enters the core, where the compressor's rows of spinning blades squeeze it to about thirty times atmospheric pressure.

In the combustor, fuel is sprayed into that compressed air and burned continuously. The hot, expanding gas rushes out through the turbines and spins them. The high-pressure turbine drives the compressor through one shaft, and the low-pressure turbine drives the fan through a second shaft running inside the first. Whatever energy is left leaves through the exhaust nozzle. Around it all, the nacelle smooths the airflow, and its reverser cowls can redirect the fan air forward to slow the aircraft after landing.

parts.description: Rounded lip that feeds smooth air to the fan at every flight angle; hot air piped inside keeps ice off it.

details.didYouKnow: On some low-slung airliners the bottom of the inlet is visibly flattened, a trick used to fit a big fan under the wing while keeping enough clearance above the runway.
details.howItWorks: The inlet slows the incoming air slightly and spreads it evenly across the whole fan face, whether the aircraft is parked, climbing steeply or flying in a crosswind. Its thick, rounded lip stops the airflow tearing away when air is sucked in sideways at low speed. Inside, honeycomb acoustic panels soak up much of the fan's noise before it can escape forwards, and hot air bled from the compressor is piped round the lip to stop ice forming.
keyNumbers: About 2 m across at the lip on an engine of this size
Anti-icing air typically arrives at roughly 200 °C
Air reaches the fan at roughly half the speed of sound at take-off
details.madeOf: The lip is usually aluminium, which conducts the anti-icing heat well and can be formed into a smooth curve; the barrel behind it is often carbon-fibre composite with a perforated honeycomb lining for noise absorption.

parts.name: Inlet cowl

parts.description: Hinged door around the fan case; mechanics swing both halves up to reach the accessories.

details.didYouKnow: Cowl doors left unlatched after maintenance have occasionally torn off during take-off, which is why newer designs make an open latch hard to miss, with flags or latches that hang down visibly.
details.howItWorks: The two fan cowl doors form the smooth outer skin around the fan case and core accessories, so air flows cleanly past the outside of the engine. They are hinged at the top and latched together along the bottom; on the ground mechanics release the latches and prop the halves open with hold-open rods. That gives direct access to the accessory gearbox, generator, fuel pump, oil tank and engine computer mounted on the fan case.
keyNumbers: 2 halves per engine, hinged along the top
Each door is typically a couple of metres long
Usually 3 or 4 latches along the bottom joint
details.madeOf: Typically carbon-fibre or glass-fibre composite panels with metal hinges and latches, because the doors are large and need to be light enough for a mechanic to lift while still stiff enough to keep their shape at airspeed.

parts.name: Fan cowl door

parts.description: Rear half of the nacelle. On landing it slides back and blocker doors turn the fan air forward to help brake.

details.didYouKnow: On a dry runway, certified landing distances usually assume no reverse thrust at all, so the reversers act as a safety margin and a way to save brake wear.
details.howItWorks: In normal flight these cowls form the rear of the bypass duct, guiding the fan air out the back. After touchdown the pilot pulls the reverse levers, hydraulic or electric actuators slide the outer sleeve rearwards, and blocker doors fold into the bypass duct. The fan air is forced outwards through cascades of curved vanes that angle it forwards, pushing against the aircraft's motion. Locks and interlocks stop the system deploying in flight.
keyNumbers: 2 halves per engine, split so they can open for maintenance
Typically deployed for about 10 to 20 seconds per landing
Usually stowed again below roughly 110 km/h to avoid ingesting debris
details.madeOf: Mostly carbon-fibre composite skins over honeycomb for low weight, with metal cascades, actuators and lock mechanisms where loads are concentrated.

parts.name: Thrust reverser cowl

parts.description: Nose cone that splits the incoming air smoothly onto the fan blades.

details.didYouKnow: Many spinners have a white spiral painted on them so ground crew can see at a glance whether the fan is still turning and dangerous to approach.
details.howItWorks: The spinner covers the bolts and hub of the fan disc and turns with the fan. Its smooth cone guides air outwards onto the roots of the fan blades, where the blade is thick and the air would otherwise stumble. Its shape is also chosen to shed ice and to deflect hail and small debris outwards into the bypass stream rather than into the core.
keyNumbers: Turns at fan speed, typically about 4,000 to 5,000 rpm at take-off
Roughly half a metre across at its base
Typically 1 piece bolted to the front of the fan disc
details.madeOf: Usually aluminium or a glass or carbon composite, sometimes with a rubber tip, because it needs to be light, smooth and able to flex slightly rather than shatter if hit by ice.

parts.name: Spinner

parts.description: Wide-chord titanium blade. Together the fan blades move over 300 kg of air a second and make about four-fifths of the thrust.

details.didYouKnow: The buzz-saw noise you hear from the front of an airliner at take-off comes from shock waves at the supersonic fan blade tips.
details.howItWorks: Each blade is a twisted wing: at the root it is steeply angled and at the tip almost flat, because the tip travels much faster than the root. The blades push a huge mass of air backwards, and most of it skips the core entirely and leaves through the bypass duct. The inner part of each blade also feeds air into the booster. Their roots slide into dovetail slots in the fan disc, and under load the blades untwist slightly, which the designers allow for.
keyNumbers: Tip speed roughly 400 to 450 m/s at take-off, faster than sound
Each blade is typically about 0.6 to 0.8 m long
A full fan of 18 to 36 blades is typical in this class
details.madeOf: Wide-chord blades like these are often hollow titanium alloy, strong and tough enough to survive bird strikes; many newer engines use carbon-fibre composite blades with a titanium leading edge to save weight.

parts.name: Fan blade

parts.description: Forged titanium hub with dovetail slots that hold each blade against about 50 tonnes of centrifugal pull.

details.didYouKnow: A fan disc that broke in 1989 because of a tiny defect in its titanium led to new melting methods that make aerospace titanium far cleaner.
details.howItWorks: The fan disc is the hub that every fan blade locks into, and it bolts to the front of the long low-pressure shaft. As the fan spins, each blade tries to fly outwards with a force of many tonnes, and the disc's thick rim and dovetail slots resist all of it at once. It also passes the turning effort from the low-pressure turbine, via the shaft, into the blades.
keyNumbers: Around 50 tonnes of pull per blade at full speed
Typically retired after roughly 20,000 to 30,000 flights
Spins at roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm at take-off
details.madeOf: Forged titanium alloy, usually Ti-6Al-4V, because it combines high strength with low weight and resists fatigue; the forging is ultrasonically inspected for hidden flaws.

parts.name: Fan disc

parts.description: Ring wrapped in Kevlar, built to contain a blade if one ever breaks off.

details.didYouKnow: To be certified, an engine must pass a blade-off test in which a fan blade is deliberately blown off with a small explosive charge at full power, and the case has to contain it.
details.howItWorks: The fan case forms the tight outer wall of the fan duct, with a soft abradable lining that the blade tips can lightly rub to keep the gap small. Its other job is safety: if a blade ever breaks off at full speed, the case must catch it and keep it inside the engine. Layers of Kevlar wrapped around the outside stretch and absorb the impact energy like a net. The case also carries the outlet guide vanes, the nacelle doors and many accessories.
keyNumbers: About 2 m in diameter
Tip gap to the fan blades typically just a few millimetres
Built in 2 halves in this model, joined into a full ring
details.madeOf: Traditionally an aluminium or titanium ring wrapped in Kevlar fabric; several newer engines use a woven carbon-fibre composite case, which is lighter and can absorb the impact itself.

parts.name: Fan containment case

parts.description: Fixed vane that straightens the swirling fan air and ties the fan case to the core.

details.didYouKnow: Engineers set the number of guide vanes to a carefully chosen ratio with the number of fan blades, because the right mismatch cancels out some of the fan's tonal noise.
details.howItWorks: Air leaves the fan swirling round in the direction of rotation, and that swirl is wasted energy. The outlet guide vanes are curved to catch the swirling flow and turn it straight backwards, which raises its pressure slightly and adds thrust. Because they span the bypass duct, they also act as spokes, carrying loads between the outer fan case and the core structure.
keyNumbers: Typically several dozen vanes in a ring
Straightening the swirl recovers a few per cent of thrust
Each vane is roughly 0.5 m long
details.madeOf: Usually aluminium or titanium alloy, and in some newer engines carbon composite, chosen for light weight and enough stiffness to double as structural struts.

parts.name: Outlet guide vane

parts.description: Central structure carrying the front bearings; the engine's forward mount bolts to it.

details.didYouKnow: An airliner is not pulled by its fan blades directly: the push ends up passing through a few large bolts in the engine mounts.
details.howItWorks: The fan frame is the engine's front backbone. Its hub holds the front bearings for the low-pressure shaft, and struts connect it outwards to the fan case. The engine's forward mount bolts to it, so most of the thrust that pushes the aircraft passes through here into the pylon and wing. Its hollow struts also carry oil and air pipes and the drive shaft that runs out to the accessory gearbox.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 100 to 150 kN of take-off thrust
The whole engine typically weighs about 2.5 to 3 tonnes
Usually supports 2 bearings at the front of the engine
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy or high-strength steel castings and forgings, because the frame must be stiff and strong enough to carry the whole engine's thrust while staying as light as possible.

parts.name: Fan frame hub

parts.description: Low-pressure compressor disc, turning with the fan.

details.didYouKnow: Booster stages are bolted to the fan, so if you could turn the fan by hand on the ground, the booster would turn with it.
details.howItWorks: This first booster disc sits just behind the fan and is bolted to it, so it turns at fan speed on the low-pressure shaft. It holds the first row of booster blades and passes the low-pressure turbine's turning effort into them. Because the fan turns relatively slowly, the booster disc sees modest stresses compared with the high-pressure discs further back.
keyNumbers: Turns at fan speed, roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Air entering it is close to outside temperature
Typically about 0.5 m in diameter
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, light and strong at the near-ambient temperatures at the front of the core; in many engines the booster stages are joined into one drum-shaped spool.

parts.name: Booster stage 1 disc

parts.description: Booster blades give the core air its first squeeze.

details.didYouKnow: Any hail or ice that gets into the core meets these blades first, and spin flings much of it outwards to be dumped overboard.
details.howItWorks: These blades take the air that the inner part of the fan has pushed into the core and give it the first proper squeeze. Like all compressor blades they act like tiny wings, speeding the air up; fixed stator vanes behind them then slow it down again, turning speed into pressure. They are short and turn relatively slowly, so each row adds only a modest rise.
keyNumbers: Air leaves this row at roughly 1.6 times atmospheric pressure
Air temperature roughly 50 °C at take-off on a mild day
Blades typically about 10 cm tall
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, which stays strong at these mild temperatures and is light enough to keep the spinning mass down.

parts.name: Booster stage 1 blades

parts.description: Low-pressure compressor disc, turning with the fan.

details.didYouKnow: Real engines of this size have anywhere from about 2 to 4 booster stages, depending on how much of the squeeze the designers give to the faster high-pressure compressor.
details.howItWorks: The second booster disc carries the middle row of booster blades and is joined to its neighbours to form a single rotating drum on the low-pressure shaft. It turns at the same speed as the fan and the first booster disc. Between it and its neighbours sit fixed stator vanes from the compressor case.
keyNumbers: Turns at roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Air around it is roughly 75 °C at take-off
Typically about 0.5 m in diameter
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, chosen for its strength-to-weight ratio in the cool front section of the core.

parts.name: Booster stage 2 disc

parts.description: Booster blades give the core air its first squeeze.

details.didYouKnow: Even a thin layer of dirt on compressor blades costs fuel, so airlines regularly wash engines with water or foam to restore lost efficiency.
details.howItWorks: The second row of booster blades adds another step of pressure to the air already squeezed by stage 1. As the air gets denser it takes up less room, so the flow passage narrows slightly and these blades are a little shorter than the row in front. The stators behind them straighten the flow ready for the last booster row.
keyNumbers: Air leaves at roughly 2 times atmospheric pressure
Air temperature roughly 75 °C at take-off
Blades a little shorter than stage 1, typically under 10 cm
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, forged and machined to an exact airfoil shape and finished smooth so the air flows cleanly over it.

parts.name: Booster stage 2 blades

parts.description: Low-pressure compressor disc, turning with the fan.

details.didYouKnow: The bleed valves behind the booster open at low power to stop the compressor stalling, and they also throw out rain and ice before they reach the core.
details.howItWorks: The last booster disc holds the final low-pressure compressor row and closes the back of the booster drum. Behind it, the air is handed over to the high-pressure compressor, which turns about three times faster on a separate shaft. Bleed valves around this region can open to dump air into the bypass duct when the core cannot swallow it all.
keyNumbers: Turns at roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Air around it roughly 100 °C at take-off
Sits just ahead of the switch to the faster HP shaft
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, light and strong; booster temperatures never get high enough to need heavier nickel alloys.

parts.name: Booster stage 3 disc

parts.description: Booster blades give the core air its first squeeze.

details.didYouKnow: By this point the air has gained only a small fraction of its final pressure; the high-pressure compressor still has to squeeze it about another twelve-fold.
details.howItWorks: These are the last blades turning at fan speed. They bring the core air to its highest pressure from the low-pressure system and pass it, through a curved transition duct, inwards and down to the smaller-diameter high-pressure compressor. Matching the flow here between two shafts spinning at very different speeds is one of the trickiest parts of engine design.
keyNumbers: Air leaves at roughly 2.5 times atmospheric pressure
Air temperature roughly 100 °C at take-off
Blades typically just a few centimetres to 10 cm tall
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, the same as the other booster blades, because temperatures are still mild enough for it.

parts.name: Booster stage 3 blades

parts.description: High-pressure compressor disc, spinning at around 15,000 rpm on the outer shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Real engines of this class have about 9 or 10 HP compressor stages; this model shows 6 to keep things readable.
details.howItWorks: This is the first disc on the high-pressure spool, driven by the high-pressure turbine through the hollow outer shaft. It spins about three times faster than the fan, which lets its blades do much more work on the air. The discs in this spool are bolted or welded together into a stiff drum so they turn as one.
keyNumbers: Spins at around 15,000 rpm
Air around it roughly 100 to 150 °C at take-off
Typically about 0.5 m in diameter
details.madeOf: Forged titanium alloy, which is strong and light at the moderate temperatures at the front of the HP compressor; some modern engines machine disc and blades from one piece, called a blisk.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 1 disc

parts.description: Each row squeezes the air further; by the last row it is about 30 times atmospheric pressure and over 500 °C.

details.didYouKnow: A compressor surge sounds like a loud bang and can send a puff of flame from the exhaust, but it is usually brief and the engine recovers on its own.
details.howItWorks: These are the tallest blades in the HP compressor and they meet the air first. Ahead of them and behind the first few rows sit variable stator vanes, whose angle the engine computer adjusts so the air hits these blades at the right angle at every speed. Get it wrong and the blades stall like a wing, causing a surge.
keyNumbers: Air leaves at roughly 4 times atmospheric pressure
Air temperature roughly 150 °C at take-off
Tip speed roughly 400 m/s
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, light enough to keep spinning loads down at 15,000 rpm and still comfortable at these temperatures.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 1 blades

parts.description: High-pressure compressor disc, spinning at around 15,000 rpm on the outer shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Rotating discs are life-limited: each one has a logbook, and it is scrapped after a set number of take-offs whether or not it looks worn.
details.howItWorks: The second HP disc carries the next row of blades and joins its neighbours in the rotating drum. Each disc is shaped thick at the bore and thinner towards the rim, so that the metal is used where the spinning stresses are highest. Seals between discs stop high-pressure air leaking back to the lower-pressure front.
keyNumbers: Spins at around 15,000 rpm
Air around it roughly 150 to 200 °C at take-off
Typically retired after a fixed life of many thousands of flights
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, forged close to shape and then precisely machined, for the best strength for its weight.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 2 disc

parts.description: Each row squeezes the air further; by the last row it is about 30 times atmospheric pressure and over 500 °C.

details.didYouKnow: Small amounts of erosion on these blade edges, from years of sand and dust, measurably increase an engine's fuel burn.
details.howItWorks: The second row keeps raising the pressure, with the variable stators around it still adjusting to the engine's speed. Since the air is now denser, the gas path has narrowed and these blades are shorter than stage 1. Each row of blades and the stator row behind it together form one stage.
keyNumbers: Air leaves at roughly 6 times atmospheric pressure
Air temperature roughly 210 °C at take-off
Blades typically a few centimetres tall
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy airfoils, often with a hard coating on the leading edge to resist erosion from dust and sand.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 2 blades

parts.description: High-pressure compressor disc, spinning at around 15,000 rpm on the outer shaft.

details.didYouKnow: The air you breathe in the cabin in flight was usually squeezed by the engine compressor first, then cooled by the aircraft's air-conditioning packs.
details.howItWorks: The third HP disc sits in the middle of the spool. Around this region, air is often tapped off through holes in the casing to supply the aircraft, for example for cabin pressurisation, and to cool parts further back in the engine. The disc keeps turning as part of the drum driven by the HP turbine.
keyNumbers: Spins at around 15,000 rpm
Air around it roughly 200 to 280 °C at take-off
Typically about 0.4 to 0.5 m in diameter
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, still within its comfortable temperature range here, though the front-to-back temperature rise is starting to make that limit matter.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 3 disc

parts.description: Each row squeezes the air further; by the last row it is about 30 times atmospheric pressure and over 500 °C.

details.didYouKnow: Engineers check these hidden blades with a borescope, a thin camera slid in through small ports in the casing, so the engine need not be taken apart.
details.howItWorks: By the middle row the air has been squeezed several times over, so these blades are short and work in dense, warm air. They keep adding energy, which the stators behind convert into pressure. Clearance between the blade tips and the casing matters a lot here, since any air leaking over the tips is wasted work.
keyNumbers: Air leaves at roughly 9 times atmospheric pressure
Air temperature roughly 280 °C at take-off
Tip gap typically under a millimetre
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy, light and strong, but titanium can burn if rubbed hard at high temperature, so designers stop using it as the air gets hotter further back.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 3 blades

parts.description: High-pressure compressor disc, spinning at around 15,000 rpm on the outer shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Titanium is avoided in the hottest rear stages partly because a hard rub there could start a titanium fire, which burns fiercely once lit.
details.howItWorks: The fourth disc marks the start of the hotter rear compressor. Here the temperature of the air is high enough that titanium would lose strength, so the material changes. The disc is still part of the same high-pressure drum, driven by the turbine through the outer shaft.
keyNumbers: Spins at around 15,000 rpm
Air around it roughly 300 to 350 °C at take-off
Nickel alloys are almost twice as dense as titanium
details.madeOf: A nickel-based superalloy or heat-resistant steel, which keeps its strength at higher temperatures than titanium and does not risk catching fire.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 4 disc

parts.description: Each row squeezes the air further; by the last row it is about 30 times atmospheric pressure and over 500 °C.

details.didYouKnow: The air at this point is already hotter than a domestic oven at full blast, purely from being squeezed, with no fuel burned yet.
details.howItWorks: These short blades work in air that is now hot and dense, adding another step of pressure. Because the air is so compressed, a small blade can still do a lot of work. The stators between these rear stages are usually fixed rather than variable, since the flow here behaves more predictably.
keyNumbers: Air leaves at roughly 13 times atmospheric pressure
Air temperature roughly 360 °C at take-off
Blades typically only 2 to 3 cm tall
details.madeOf: Heat-resistant nickel alloy or steel, chosen because the air is too hot for titanium to keep its strength for thousands of hours.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 4 blades

parts.description: High-pressure compressor disc, spinning at around 15,000 rpm on the outer shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Every flight's warm-up and cool-down counts towards a disc's life, so a short-haul aircraft uses up its engine discs much faster than a long-haul one.
details.howItWorks: The fifth disc carries the next-to-last compressor row. It runs hot and has to cope with the temperature difference between its warm rim and cooler bore, which creates extra thermal stress on every flight. Air is often bled off near the rear stages to cool the turbine, which needs high-pressure air to force through its blades.
keyNumbers: Spins at around 15,000 rpm
Air around it roughly 400 to 450 °C at take-off
Rim speed roughly 300 m/s
details.madeOf: Nickel-based superalloy, forged and heat-treated for strength and fatigue resistance at high temperature.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 5 disc

parts.description: Each row squeezes the air further; by the last row it is about 30 times atmospheric pressure and over 500 °C.

details.didYouKnow: These blades are so small you could hold one between finger and thumb, yet they spin around 15,000 times a minute.
details.howItWorks: The second-to-last row keeps raising the pressure in a very small passage. The blades are only a few centimetres tall, so even tiny tip gaps are a large fraction of the blade and matter for efficiency. Some engines blow cooling air on the outside of this part of the casing to keep the gaps tight.
keyNumbers: Air leaves at roughly 20 times atmospheric pressure
Air temperature roughly 450 °C at take-off
Blades typically about 2 cm tall
details.madeOf: Nickel alloy or heat-resistant steel, needed for strength in air this hot.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 5 blades

parts.description: High-pressure compressor disc, spinning at around 15,000 rpm on the outer shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Air leaving the compressor is well above the temperature at which kerosene can ignite by itself, one reason fuel and air are only mixed inside the combustor.
details.howItWorks: The last compressor disc holds the final row and connects at the back to the hollow shaft leading to the HP turbine. It sees the hottest compressor air in the engine and also sits right next to the combustor, so its rear face is shielded and cooled. Behind it, a diffuser slows the air before it enters the combustion chamber.
keyNumbers: Spins at around 15,000 rpm
Air around it roughly 500 to 550 °C at take-off
Joins directly to the high-pressure shaft
details.madeOf: Nickel-based superalloy, often made by powder metallurgy for very even, flaw-free structure.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 6 disc

parts.description: Each row squeezes the air further; by the last row it is about 30 times atmospheric pressure and over 500 °C.

details.didYouKnow: Across the whole compressor, the air's pressure rises about thirty-fold in well under a metre of engine length.
details.howItWorks: This final row brings the air to the engine's peak pressure before it enters the combustor. Its outlet guide vanes then remove the swirl so the air enters the diffuser flowing straight. These are the smallest rotating blades in the engine, working in air that is both the densest and hottest of the compressor.
keyNumbers: Air leaves at roughly 30 times atmospheric pressure
Air temperature over 500 °C at take-off
Blades typically under 2 cm tall
details.madeOf: Nickel-based superalloy, the only practical choice for blades at these temperatures and stresses.

parts.name: HP compressor stage 6 blades

parts.description: Split casing around the compressor; rows of fixed stator vanes line its inner wall.

details.didYouKnow: The variable stator vanes on the front of the compressor are moved by actuators that use pressurised fuel as their hydraulic fluid.
details.howItWorks: The compressor case forms the outer wall of the core's gas path and holds the fixed stator rows that sit between each spinning blade row. On the outside, rings and levers link the variable stator vanes so actuators can turn them all together. The case also has bleed ports, sensor bosses and small borescope holes. It is split in two halves so the compressor can be inspected and repaired.
keyNumbers: Holds pressures up to roughly 30 times atmospheric
Usually split into 2 halves along its length
Inner wall runs within a fraction of a millimetre of the blade tips
details.madeOf: Titanium alloy at the cooler front and usually steel or nickel alloy at the hot rear, with abradable linings where blade tips run.

parts.name: Compressor case

parts.description: Ring-shaped chamber where fuel burns at about 2,000 °C; thousands of small holes feed a film of cooler air along its walls.

details.didYouKnow: Modern combustors burn much of the fuel lean, with extra air, which lowers peak temperature and cuts the nitrogen oxides that form in very hot flames.
details.howItWorks: The liner is a ring-shaped chamber where fuel and compressed air burn continuously. Only part of the air enters at the front to burn with the fuel; the rest flows around the outside and is fed in through rows of holes, first to finish burning and then to dilute and cool the gas before it reaches the turbine. A film of cooler air along the inside wall keeps the metal from melting.
keyNumbers: Flame temperature about 2,000 °C
Liner wall typically kept below about 900 °C
Gas spends only a few milliseconds inside
Typically well under half a metre long
details.madeOf: Nickel or cobalt superalloy sheet with a ceramic thermal barrier coating, because the walls must survive flame temperatures far above their melting point for thousands of hours.

parts.name: Combustion chamber liner

parts.description: Sprays kerosene as a fine mist into the front of the combustion chamber.

details.didYouKnow: One well-known modern fuel nozzle is 3D-printed in a single piece that replaced around 20 separate parts and lasts about five times longer.
details.howItWorks: Each nozzle sprays fuel as a fine cone of droplets into the front of the combustor, where swirling air from vanes around the tip mixes it in quickly. Fine droplets evaporate fast, burn completely and make less smoke. Many nozzles have two fuel circuits: a small one for starting and idle and a larger one that opens at higher power.
keyNumbers: Typically about 18 to 24 nozzles around the ring
Fuel flow for the whole engine roughly 1 kg/s at take-off
Roughly 0.3 kg/s at cruise
details.madeOf: Heat-resistant stainless steel or cobalt and nickel alloys, because the tip sits right next to the flame; some recent designs are 3D-printed as a single piece.

parts.name: Fuel nozzle

parts.description: Spark plug used only to light the engine; after that the flame keeps itself going.

details.didYouKnow: Each igniter usually sparks only on starts and in bad weather, so it may fire for just a few minutes in a whole flight.
details.howItWorks: During start, an exciter box charges a capacitor and dumps it through the igniter, making a powerful spark at the combustor wall several times a second. Once the fuel-air mix lights and the flame spreads round the whole ring, the igniters are switched off and the flame sustains itself. Pilots can switch them on continuously in heavy rain, icing or turbulence as a precaution against flame-out.
keyNumbers: 2 igniters per engine, often used alternately
Spark typically several thousand volts
Fires roughly 1 to 3 times a second during start
details.madeOf: Nickel alloy shell with a ceramic insulator and a hard-wearing electrode tip, built to survive repeated sparks at the edge of the flame.

parts.name: Igniter plug

parts.description: Pressure vessel around the combustion chamber; it holds the highest pressure in the engine.

details.didYouKnow: The combustor case sits next to some of the hottest parts but never sees the flame itself, because a blanket of compressor air flows between it and the liner.
details.howItWorks: This casing surrounds the combustion chamber and contains the full compressor delivery pressure, the highest pressure anywhere in the engine. Air from the compressor fills the space between the case and the liner before entering the liner's holes. The case also carries the fuel nozzles and igniters, which pass through it into the chamber, and links the compressor case to the turbine case structurally.
keyNumbers: Holds roughly 30 bar of pressure at take-off
Air inside over 500 °C
Typically about 0.6 to 0.8 m in diameter
details.madeOf: In real engines usually a nickel-based alloy or heat-resistant steel, because the compressed air around it is over 500 °C; it is sized like a pressure vessel with thick flanges.

parts.name: Combustor case

parts.description: Nickel-alloy disc that drives the high-pressure compressor through the outer shaft.

details.didYouKnow: A burst turbine disc cannot be contained by the casing, so these discs are given strictly limited lives and inspected with great care.
details.howItWorks: The HP turbine disc holds the blades that take power out of the hottest gas in the engine. It is bolted to the back of the hollow high-pressure shaft, so all the power it collects goes straight forwards to drive the compressor. Cooling air is fed through passages in the disc to its rim and up into the blades. Many engines of this size have one HP turbine stage like this model; some have two.
keyNumbers: Spins at around 15,000 rpm
Rim typically about 650 to 700 °C
Delivers roughly 20 MW to the compressor at take-off
details.madeOf: Powder-metallurgy nickel superalloy, because the disc must stay extremely strong at hot rim temperatures under huge spinning loads.

parts.name: HP turbine disc

parts.description: Single-crystal blades running in gas hotter than their melting point, kept alive by cooling air blown through internal passages.

details.didYouKnow: Each blade is grown as a single metal crystal, cast through a spiral-shaped grain selector that lets only one crystal grow up into the blade.
details.howItWorks: Gas leaving the combustor is aimed by fixed nozzle vanes onto these blades, which turn its energy into rotation. The gas is hotter than the metal can stand, so cool air from the compressor is pushed up through winding passages inside each blade and out of hundreds of tiny holes, forming a protective film over the surface. A ceramic coating adds further insulation.
keyNumbers: Gas temperature roughly 1,400 to 1,600 °C
Nickel alloy melts at about 1,300 °C
Each blade pulls outwards with several tonnes of force
Typically about 5 cm tall
details.madeOf: Single-crystal nickel superalloy, grown as one crystal with no grain boundaries so it resists creep, coated with a ceramic thermal barrier layer.

parts.name: HP turbine blades

parts.description: Low-pressure turbine disc; these stages drive the fan through the long inner shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Exhaust gas temperature, usually measured near the front of the low-pressure turbine, is one of the main numbers pilots and engineers use to judge engine health.
details.howItWorks: The first LP turbine disc sits right behind the HP turbine and receives the hottest gas of the low-pressure system. It is bolted to the other LP turbine discs to form a drum, which connects through a cone to the rear of the long inner shaft. The turning effort it collects travels forwards along that shaft to the fan.
keyNumbers: Turns at fan speed, roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Gas around it roughly 850 to 950 °C at take-off
Real engines of this class have about 4 to 7 LP turbine stages
details.madeOf: Nickel-based superalloy, such as an Inconel-type alloy, which keeps its strength at the high temperatures still present here.

parts.name: LP turbine stage 1 disc

parts.description: Long blades that take the remaining energy out of the gas to turn the fan.

details.didYouKnow: As an engine ages its turbine gets less efficient and runs hotter, and the shrinking gap to the temperature limit is a major reason engines go in for overhaul.
details.howItWorks: These blades take the first share of the energy left in the gas after the HP turbine. Fixed vanes in front of them steer the gas onto the blades at the right angle. Because the LP turbine turns slowly, it needs long blades and several stages to extract enough power to drive the big fan. Their tips carry small shrouds that lock together into a ring, damping vibration and sealing against leakage.
keyNumbers: Gas falls from roughly 900 °C to about 820 °C across this row
Pressure falls from roughly 5 to 3.5 times atmospheric
Blades typically about 10 cm long
details.madeOf: Cast nickel superalloy; at this hot front stage they may still have some internal cooling, though most LP turbine blades are uncooled.

parts.name: LP turbine stage 1 blades

parts.description: Low-pressure turbine disc; these stages drive the fan through the long inner shaft.

details.didYouKnow: The LP turbine gets steadily wider towards the back, which is why the rear of the engine core flares out in a cone.
details.howItWorks: The second LP turbine disc carries a slightly larger row of blades, because the gas expands as it loses pressure and needs a bigger passage. It is bolted into the LP turbine drum with its neighbours, all turning together with the fan via the inner shaft.
keyNumbers: Turns at roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Gas around it roughly 750 to 820 °C at take-off
Typically about 0.7 m in diameter at the blade tips
details.madeOf: Nickel-based superalloy, still needed for strength at these temperatures.

parts.name: LP turbine stage 2 disc

parts.description: Long blades that take the remaining energy out of the gas to turn the fan.

details.didYouKnow: LP turbine blades are long and thin, so engineers worry less about heat here and more about vibration and flutter.
details.howItWorks: This row continues to draw energy from the expanding gas. Each stage takes a similar slice of work, so the gas cools and drops in pressure a step at a time. These blades are longer than stage 1 to match the growing gas passage, and they are not cooled, since the gas is now cool enough for the metal to cope.
keyNumbers: Gas falls from roughly 820 °C to about 740 °C
Pressure falls to roughly 2.5 times atmospheric
Blades typically about 12 to 15 cm long
details.madeOf: Cast nickel superalloy, uncooled, with interlocking tip shrouds to damp vibration.

parts.name: LP turbine stage 2 blades

parts.description: Low-pressure turbine disc; these stages drive the fan through the long inner shaft.

details.didYouKnow: The low-pressure turbine is one of the heaviest modules in the engine, because it needs so many large stages to drive the fan.
details.howItWorks: The third LP disc holds the next-to-last turbine row and is part of the same slow-turning drum. Temperatures here are lower, so the disc can be a bit lighter for its size. Sealing rings between discs stop gas bypassing the blades through the gaps.
keyNumbers: Turns at roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Gas around it roughly 650 to 740 °C at take-off
Typically about 0.75 m in diameter at the blade tips
details.madeOf: Nickel-based superalloy; the stress and temperature are lower here, but nickel is still needed for long life.

parts.name: LP turbine stage 3 disc

parts.description: Long blades that take the remaining energy out of the gas to turn the fan.

details.didYouKnow: Titanium aluminide is a heat-resistant intermetallic about half as heavy as nickel alloy, and it has started to replace nickel in rear turbine blades.
details.howItWorks: Longer still, these blades work in cooler, lower-pressure gas, extracting their share of power for the fan. Because the gas is thinner, the blades need more area to do the same work. Their tip shrouds run inside honeycomb seals on the casing, which they lightly cut into to form a tight seal.
keyNumbers: Gas falls from roughly 740 °C to about 660 °C
Pressure falls to roughly 1.8 times atmospheric
Blades typically about 15 to 20 cm long
details.madeOf: Cast nickel superalloy; some newer engines use lighter titanium aluminide in their rearmost stages.

parts.name: LP turbine stage 3 blades

parts.description: Low-pressure turbine disc; these stages drive the fan through the long inner shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Because the whole LP turbine turns at fan speed, it has to be made big to compensate; geared turbofans add a gearbox so the turbine can spin faster and be smaller.
details.howItWorks: The last LP turbine disc sits at the very back of the drum, next to the rear bearing that supports the end of the low-pressure shaft. It carries the longest turbine blades in the engine. Behind it, the gas passes through a rear frame and into the exhaust.
keyNumbers: Turns at roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Gas around it roughly 600 to 650 °C at take-off
Typically about 0.8 m in diameter at the blade tips
details.madeOf: Nickel-based superalloy, giving long fatigue life at moderate temperature.

parts.name: LP turbine stage 4 disc

parts.description: Long blades that take the remaining energy out of the gas to turn the fan.

details.didYouKnow: Even at idle the exhaust behind an engine is hot and fast enough to be dangerous, which is why ground crews keep well clear of the area behind a running engine.
details.howItWorks: The last row of turbine blades squeezes the remaining useful energy out of the gas before it leaves. The gas is now only a little above outside pressure, so these blades need to be the longest of all. Exit guide vanes behind them remove swirl so the exhaust leaves straight backwards for the most thrust.
keyNumbers: Gas leaves at roughly 600 °C at take-off
Pressure falls to roughly 1.3 times atmospheric
Blades typically about 20 cm long
details.madeOf: Cast nickel superalloy or, in some newer engines, titanium aluminide, which saves weight in these long blades.

parts.name: LP turbine stage 4 blades

parts.description: Casing around the turbines; cool air is blown on its outside to shrink it and tighten the gap to the blade tips.

details.didYouKnow: Shrinking the turbine case with cool air is called active clearance control, and closing the tip gap by even a few tenths of a millimetre saves noticeable fuel.
details.howItWorks: The turbine case forms the outer wall around the HP and LP turbines and holds the fixed nozzle vanes between each row of blades. It has to stay round and stable while its inside faces gas hundreds of degrees hotter than its outside. In cruise, the engine computer blows cool fan air through pipes onto the outside of the case, shrinking it slightly so the blade tip gaps close up and less gas leaks past.
keyNumbers: Inside faces gas of roughly 600 to 1,500 °C
Tip gaps are kept to a fraction of a millimetre
Built in 2 halves in this model
details.madeOf: In real engines a nickel-based superalloy, which keeps its strength and shape at high temperature; the inner shroud segments may be ceramic composite in newer designs.

parts.name: Turbine case

parts.description: Hollow outer shaft joining the HP turbine to the HP compressor.

details.didYouKnow: The two shafts in a turbofan are not connected at all: one spins inside the other at a completely different speed.
details.howItWorks: The HP shaft is a short, stiff hollow tube connecting the HP turbine at the back to the HP compressor in front. Every bit of power the turbine collects goes forwards through it to drive the compressor. Near the front, a bevel gear on this shaft drives a tower shaft down to the accessory gearbox, which is how the starter spins the engine and how the pumps and generator are powered.
keyNumbers: Spins at around 15,000 rpm
Transmits roughly 20 MW at take-off
Typically about 1 m long
details.madeOf: High-strength steel or nickel alloy, chosen for stiffness and strength in a hot environment at very high speed.

parts.name: High-pressure shaft

parts.description: Long inner shaft running through the hollow HP shaft, from the LP turbine forward to the fan.

details.didYouKnow: The LP shaft carries tens of megawatts, enough to power a small town, through a tube slim enough to fit inside the hollow HP shaft.
details.howItWorks: The LP shaft is the engine's long inner backbone, running from the LP turbine at the back, through the hollow HP shaft, to the fan at the front. It carries a huge twisting load from turbine to fan while spinning relatively slowly. It must also be stiff enough to avoid whipping like a skipping rope at certain speeds, which is controlled by bearing placement and careful balancing.
keyNumbers: Turns at roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Carries roughly 15 to 25 MW to the fan at take-off
Typically about 2 m long
Twisting load around 40,000 newton-metres
details.madeOf: Very high-strength steel or nickel alloy, because it must carry enormous torque in a thin tube that fits inside the HP shaft.

parts.name: Low-pressure shaft

parts.description: Ball bearing that carries the fan's forward pull into the engine frame.

details.didYouKnow: Engine bearings are monitored with magnetic plugs in the oil system that catch tiny metal flakes, giving early warning long before a bearing fails.
details.howItWorks: This ball bearing locates the low-pressure rotor along its length. The fan pulls forwards while the LP turbine is pushed backwards, and the bearing carries the difference into the fan frame. Jets of oil spray directly into it to lubricate and carry away heat, and air-pressurised seals around its chamber stop the oil leaking out into the gas path.
keyNumbers: Turns at roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Carries a net axial load of several tonnes
Oil typically runs at roughly 100 to 150 °C
details.madeOf: Ultra-clean bearing steel such as M50, sometimes with ceramic silicon nitride balls, because it must run at high speed and load for tens of thousands of hours.

parts.name: Fan thrust bearing

parts.description: Roller bearing supporting the back end of the LP shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Pilots usually let engines idle for a few minutes before shutdown, partly so the oil around hot rear bearings does not cook into carbon once the cooling flow stops.
details.howItWorks: This roller bearing holds up the back of the LP shaft inside the rear turbine frame. Unlike a ball bearing, its cylindrical rollers let the shaft slide slightly forwards and back, which is essential because the shaft grows in length as it heats up. Oil is fed in under pressure and scavenge pumps suck it back out to the tank.
keyNumbers: Turns at roughly 4,000 to 5,000 rpm
Lets the shaft grow a few millimetres as it heats
Sits close to gas at roughly 600 °C
details.madeOf: High-grade bearing steel rollers and races in a cooled, sealed chamber, because it lives in the hottest region any bearing in the engine has to endure.

parts.name: Rear roller bearing

parts.description: Tapering duct that speeds up the hot core exhaust.

details.didYouKnow: Some nozzles have a sawtooth trailing edge called chevrons, which mix the hot and cold streams more gently and make the jet noticeably quieter.
details.howItWorks: The core nozzle narrows towards the back, which speeds up the hot gas leaving the LP turbine and turns its remaining pressure into thrust. The core stream exits faster and hotter than the surrounding bypass air, and the two streams mix behind the engine. The shape of the nozzle exit strongly affects jet noise.
keyNumbers: Gives roughly a fifth or less of total thrust
Core exhaust typically leaves at about 300 to 400 m/s
Exhaust roughly 500 to 600 °C at take-off
details.madeOf: Nickel alloy or titanium sheet, able to withstand the hot exhaust while staying light.

parts.name: Core exhaust nozzle

parts.description: Cone in the middle of the nozzle that shapes the exhaust flow.

details.didYouKnow: The exhaust plug does not spin, even though it sits right behind turbines turning thousands of times a minute.
details.howItWorks: The exhaust plug fills the centre of the core nozzle and, together with the nozzle wall, forms a ring-shaped exit for the hot gas. Its tapering shape lets the flow join smoothly behind the engine instead of breaking up into turbulent eddies. It also covers the back of the rear turbine frame and provides a vent for air from the oil system.
keyNumbers: Exhaust around it roughly 500 to 600 °C at take-off
Typically about 0.5 to 1 m long
Does not rotate
details.madeOf: Usually nickel alloy or titanium sheet; a few recent designs use lighter ceramic composite, which copes better with heat.

parts.name: Exhaust plug

parts.description: Driven by a shaft from the core, it turns the pumps and generator bolted to it.

details.didYouKnow: A hand-cranking pad on the gearbox lets mechanics turn the core slowly during inspections, sometimes with a small socket wrench or drive motor.
details.howItWorks: A tower shaft geared to the HP shaft runs out through a strut to this gearbox, where a train of gears splits the drive to several pads. Each pad turns a different accessory at its own speed: the fuel pump, oil pumps, hydraulic pump and electrical generator. Running the other way, the starter turns the gearbox to spin the HP shaft for engine start.
keyNumbers: Takes its drive from the HP shaft at around 15,000 rpm
Absorbs roughly a few hundred kilowatts
Typically drives 5 to 8 accessories
details.madeOf: Gears and shafts of case-hardened steel; the housing is typically cast aluminium or magnesium alloy, which keeps weight down.

parts.name: Accessory gearbox

parts.description: Air-driven turbine that spins the core up to light-off speed.

details.didYouKnow: Starters have duty-time limits and must cool down between attempts, because they are designed only for short bursts.
details.howItWorks: For start-up, compressed air from the aircraft's auxiliary power unit, a ground cart or another running engine spins a small turbine inside the starter. Through reduction gears and a clutch, it turns the accessory gearbox and so the HP shaft. Once the core reaches about a quarter of its speed, fuel and spark are added; after light-off the starter keeps helping until the engine can accelerate on its own, then the clutch disengages.
keyNumbers: Air supply typically about 2 to 3 bar
Starter turbine spins at tens of thousands of rpm
A typical start takes about 30 to 60 seconds
details.madeOf: Steel gears and turbine wheel in an aluminium housing, chosen to be compact and light while handling a short burst of high power.

parts.name: Air starter

parts.description: Supplies the aircraft's electrical power.

details.didYouKnow: Aircraft use 400 Hz instead of household 50 or 60 Hz because higher frequency allows much smaller, lighter transformers and motors.
details.howItWorks: The generator is driven by the accessory gearbox and supplies the aircraft's main electrical power. Because engine speed varies, many generators in this class include a built-in constant-speed drive that holds the output frequency steady. Each engine usually drives one, with the auxiliary power unit as a backup.
keyNumbers: Typically about 90 kVA per engine in this class
Supplies 115 volts AC at 400 Hz
Typically 1 per engine
details.madeOf: Copper windings and steel laminations inside an aluminium housing, oil-cooled to carry away the heat of high power in a compact unit.

parts.name: Electrical generator

parts.description: Pressurises the fuel and meters exactly how much goes to the nozzles.

details.didYouKnow: In many engines this unit also sends high-pressure fuel to work the actuators that move compressor vanes and valves, using fuel as hydraulic fluid.
details.howItWorks: Fuel arrives from the wing tanks and is pressurised in two stages: a low-pressure centrifugal stage and then a high-pressure gear pump. The metering unit, commanded by the engine computer, precisely sets how much fuel goes to the nozzles and returns the rest. Along the way the fuel passes through a heat exchanger, cooling the engine oil and warming itself to prevent ice.
keyNumbers: Delivers roughly 1 kg/s of fuel at take-off
Raises fuel to up to roughly 70 bar
Driven by the gearbox at several thousand rpm
details.madeOf: Aluminium housings with hardened steel gears and precision valves, chosen for low weight and tight tolerances.

parts.name: Fuel pump & metering unit

parts.description: Holds the oil that lubricates and cools the bearings and gearbox.

details.didYouKnow: Oil levels should be checked soon after shutdown, because oil slowly drains into the gearbox and sumps and an engine sitting overnight can look low.
details.howItWorks: The tank stores the oil for the engine's closed-loop lubrication system. A pump draws oil from it to the bearings and gearbox, then scavenge pumps return it via filters and coolers. The tank also separates air bubbles from returning oil and has a sight gauge and sensors so crews can check its level.
keyNumbers: Holds roughly 15 to 25 litres of oil
Typically uses well under half a litre an hour
Oil runs at roughly 100 to 150 °C
details.madeOf: Aluminium or stainless steel, lightweight yet tough enough to resist vibration and corrosion.

parts.name: Oil tank

parts.description: FADEC: the dual-channel computer that runs the engine, from fuel flow to the variable compressor vanes.

details.didYouKnow: Most FADECs alternate which channel is in charge on each flight, so both stay proven working.
details.howItWorks: FADEC stands for full authority digital engine control. It reads sensors for speeds, temperatures and pressures and adjusts fuel flow, compressor vanes, bleed valves and turbine clearance many times a second. When the pilot moves the thrust lever, the FADEC decides how to deliver that safely, protecting against surge, overspeed and overheat.
keyNumbers: 2 independent channels, each able to run the engine alone
Updates its control outputs many times a second
Reads dozens of sensors around the engine
details.madeOf: Circuit boards inside a sealed, vibration-isolated aluminium box, typically mounted on the fan case where it stays relatively cool.

parts.name: Engine control computer

parts.description: Pipe carrying fuel from the metering unit round to the ring of nozzles.

details.didYouKnow: Uneven fuel flow from a partly blocked nozzle can create a hot streak in the turbine that shows up on inspections long before it causes a failure.
details.howItWorks: The manifold distributes fuel from the metering unit round the outside of the combustor to each nozzle. It must deliver evenly so every nozzle gets the same flow, avoiding hot spots that could damage the turbine. Flexible joints let it move as the hot engine expands and contracts.
keyNumbers: Feeds typically about 18 to 24 nozzles
Carries fuel at up to roughly 70 bar
Encircles a combustor about 0.6 to 0.8 m across
details.madeOf: Stainless steel tubing, often with fire-resistant sleeves, because it carries pressurised fuel very close to hot engine casings.

parts.name: Fuel manifold

summary: A high-bypass turbofan like those on a single-aisle airliner. The big fan at the front gives most of the thrust; behind it a core compresses air about thirty-fold, burns fuel in it, and uses the hot gas to spin the turbines that drive the fan and compressor.

name: Road Bicycle
overview:
A bicycle is a machine for turning pedalling into forward motion as efficiently as possible. Your legs push the pedals round; the cranks turn the chainring, the chain carries that turn back to a sprocket on the rear wheel, and the rear wheel pushes the bike along. The ratio between the chainring and the sprocket you're in sets how far the bike travels per pedal stroke.

The frame is two triangles: the front triangle (top tube, down tube and seat tube) and the rear triangle (seat stays and chain stays). Triangles don't flex easily, so the frame stays stiff while weighing very little. The fork holds the front wheel and turns in the head tube when you steer; its angle and offset make the bike steady enough to ride no-handed.

Each wheel is a tension structure: thin spokes, pulled tight, hang the hub from the rim, so the wheel carries the rider's weight while weighing under a kilogram. Derailleurs shift the chain between sprockets for different gears, and rim brakes squeeze pads onto the wheel rims to stop.

parts.description: 25 mm clincher tyre pumped to around 6 bar; its tread is almost smooth, since road tyres grip through the rubber, not the pattern.

details.didYouKnow: Wider tyres at the same pressure do not have a bigger contact patch, just a shorter, wider one, which is partly why road tyres have crept from 23 mm to 25 mm and beyond.
details.howItWorks: The tyre's two edges, called beads, hook under lips on the rim, and the air in the tube pushes them outwards so they lock in place. Where the tyre meets the road it flattens into a small contact patch, and the rubber there grips by deforming into tiny bumps in the tarmac. The front tyre steers the bike, so a grippy, well-inflated front matters most in corners.
keyNumbers: About 25 mm wide when fitted
Typically 5.5 to 7 bar of pressure
Roughly 200 to 300 g each
Contact patch about the size of a thumbprint
details.madeOf: A woven nylon casing coated in rubber compound, with beads of steel wire or folding aramid fibre. The rubber blend trades grip against wear and rolling resistance.

parts.name: Front tyre

parts.description: Thin butyl tube that holds the air inside the tyre.

details.didYouKnow: Road bikes use slim Presta valves rather than car-style Schrader valves because they need a smaller hole in the narrow rim and seal better at high pressure.
details.howItWorks: The tube is a sealed rubber balloon that sits inside the tyre and is inflated through a valve poking through the rim. It does not carry the load itself: the air pressure stretches the tyre casing tight, and the casing does the work. If the tyre gets cut or pinched against the rim, the tube is what leaks.
keyNumbers: Typically 0.8 to 1 mm wall thickness
About 80 to 110 g
Presta valve about 6 mm across
details.madeOf: Butyl rubber, chosen because it holds air far better than natural rubber. Lighter versions use latex, which rolls more smoothly but loses air within a day or two.

parts.name: Front inner tube

parts.description: Aluminium hoop the tyre hooks onto; its sides double as the braking surface.

details.didYouKnow: Many rim-brake rims have a small wear groove or dot on the braking surface; when it disappears, the wall has grown too thin and the rim should be replaced.
details.howItWorks: The rim is the outer hoop that holds the tyre and anchors the far end of every spoke. Spoke nipples thread through holes in its inner wall, and tightening them pulls the rim true. On this bike its flat sidewalls are also the braking track, so the front brake pads rub directly on them, wearing them very slowly over the years.
keyNumbers: 622 mm bead seat diameter (700c)
About 400 to 500 g
32 spoke holes
Braking track lasts typically many thousands of km
details.madeOf: Extruded aluminium alloy rolled into a hoop and joined by welding or a pinned sleeve. Aluminium is light, stiff and gives a consistent braking surface in the wet.

parts.name: Front rim

parts.description: Stainless spokes laced in a crossing pattern; under tension they hang the hub from the rim.

details.didYouKnow: A wheel does not stand on its bottom spokes; it hangs from the top ones, which is why a thin wire wheel can carry many times its own weight.
details.howItWorks: These 16 spokes run from the left hub flange to the rim and work only in tension, like the strings of a harp. When the wheel is loaded, the spokes at the bottom lose a little tension while the rest hold the hub suspended. On a rim-brake front wheel the hub is symmetrical, so these left spokes carry the same tension as the right ones.
keyNumbers: 16 spokes on this side
About 2 mm thick at the ends
Typically 100 to 120 kgf tension each
Roughly 290 mm long
details.madeOf: Cold-drawn stainless steel wire, often butted thinner in the middle to save weight and add a little stretch. Stainless resists rust and fatigue over millions of turns.

parts.name: Front spokes (left side)

parts.description: Stainless spokes laced in a crossing pattern; under tension they hang the hub from the rim.

details.didYouKnow: A wheel builder often tunes spoke tension by plucking the spokes and listening, since spokes at similar tension ring at a similar pitch.
details.howItWorks: The right-hand set of 16 spokes mirrors the left, crossing each other usually three times on the way to the rim so they can also handle braking forces through the rim. Because there is no chain or cassette at the front, the right side is not truly a drive side here and the two sides are dished evenly. Balancing their tension is what keeps the rim straight and centred.
keyNumbers: 16 spokes on this side
About 100 to 120 kgf each
Typically laced 3-cross
Spoke ends threaded about 2 mm diameter
details.madeOf: Stainless steel with threaded ends that screw into brass or aluminium nipples at the rim. Brass nipples are heavier but less likely to seize or crack.

parts.name: Front spokes (right side)

parts.description: Centre of the wheel: an axle on sealed ball bearings, with flanges the spokes hook into.

details.didYouKnow: The 100 mm front hub width has been the road bike standard for decades, so a front wheel from long ago will often still fit a modern rim-brake fork.
details.howItWorks: The hub body spins around a fixed axle on two sealed cartridge bearings, one near each flange. The quick release passes through the hollow axle and clamps its end caps into the fork dropouts. The front hub only has to support weight and braking loads, so it is simpler and lighter than the rear.
keyNumbers: 100 mm between the fork dropouts
About 100 to 150 g
Two cartridge bearings
Axle typically 9 mm for quick release

parts.name: Front hub

parts.description: Lever-operated skewer that clamps the wheel into the frame, removable without tools.

details.didYouKnow: The quick release was invented by Italian racer Tullio Campagnolo in the 1930s, reportedly after cold fingers stopped him undoing a wing nut during a race.
details.howItWorks: A thin rod runs through the hollow hub axle with a nut on one end and a cam lever on the other. Closing the lever turns the cam, which pulls the rod tight and squeezes the fork dropouts between the hub end caps. Small tabs on the fork ends, called lawyer lips, stop the wheel falling out if the lever is ever left open.
keyNumbers: Rod about 5 mm thick
Roughly 50 to 60 g
Clamping force up to several hundred kgf

parts.name: Front quick release

parts.description: 25 mm clincher tyre pumped to around 6 bar; its tread is almost smooth, since road tyres grip through the rubber, not the pattern.

details.didYouKnow: Riders often swap a worn rear tyre for the front one and fit the new tyre at the front, because a front blowout or slide is the more dangerous one.
details.howItWorks: The rear tyre is built the same way as the front but works harder: it carries more of the rider's weight and transmits all the pedalling force to the road. That extra load and the scrubbing from drive torque make the centre of the tread wear flat much faster. It is usually run slightly firmer than the front for the same reason.
keyNumbers: About 25 mm wide
Carries roughly 55 to 60% of the total weight
Typically lasts about 3,000 to 5,000 km
Often 0.3 to 0.5 bar firmer than the front

parts.name: Rear tyre

parts.description: Thin butyl tube that holds the air inside the tyre.

details.didYouKnow: The two neat holes of a pinch flat are nicknamed a snakebite, because they look like fang marks.
details.howItWorks: Like the front tube, it is a thin balloon that pressurises the tyre so the casing can carry the load. The rear takes the heavier load, so it is the one most likely to get a pinch flat, where hitting an edge squashes the tyre and nips two small holes in the tube against the rim.
keyNumbers: About 80 to 110 g
Loses roughly 0.5 to 1 bar a week
Valve typically 48 to 60 mm long for shallow rims

parts.name: Rear inner tube

parts.description: Aluminium hoop the tyre hooks onto; its sides double as the braking surface.

details.didYouKnow: Rear rims are sometimes drilled off-centre so the spokes sit nearer the drive side, which lets the two sides run closer to equal tension.
details.howItWorks: The rear rim holds the tyre and the outer ends of all 32 spokes, but on the rear wheel the spokes pull it unevenly to make room for the cassette. Its sidewalls are braked on by the rear caliper, which does less of the stopping work than the front, so the rear braking surface usually wears more slowly.
keyNumbers: 622 mm bead seat diameter (700c)
About 400 to 500 g
32 spoke holes
Typically 15 to 19 mm inner width

parts.name: Rear rim

parts.description: Stainless spokes laced in a crossing pattern; under tension they hang the hub from the rim.

details.didYouKnow: The uneven tension between the two sides of a rear wheel is a key reason rear wheels go out of true more often than front wheels.
details.howItWorks: The left, non-drive spokes run at a wider angle to the rim because the rear hub is offset, or dished, to fit the cassette on the right. That wider angle means they need much less tension to balance the steep drive-side spokes. Being looser, they are the ones most likely to slacken or fatigue if the wheel is not well built.
keyNumbers: 16 spokes on this side
Typically 50 to 70% of drive-side tension
About 60 to 80 kgf each
Roughly 290 to 295 mm long
