parts.name: Rear spokes (non-drive side)

parts.description: Stainless spokes laced in a crossing pattern; under tension they hang the hub from the rim.

details.didYouKnow: If you pluck the two sides of a rear wheel, the drive side rings at a noticeably higher pitch because it is so much tighter.
details.howItWorks: The drive-side spokes run almost straight up from the right hub flange, which sits close to the centre to leave room for the cassette. To keep the rim centred they must be pulled much tighter than the left side. They also carry the pedalling torque from the hub out to the rim, which is why they are laced tangentially, crossing each other, rather than radially.

About 110 to 130 kgf each
Highest tension on the bike
Typically laced 2- or 3-cross

parts.name: Rear spokes (drive side)

parts.description: Centre of the wheel: an axle on sealed ball bearings, with flanges the spokes hook into.

details.didYouKnow: A freehub lets you stop pedalling while the wheel spins on; early racing bikes often had a fixed gear, so the pedals turned whenever the wheel did.
details.howItWorks: The rear hub holds the axle bearings and carries a freehub body on the drive side, which the cassette slides onto. Inside the freehub, spring-loaded pawls catch a toothed ring when you pedal, and click past it when you coast, which is the ticking sound of a freewheeling bike. Its flanges are set off-centre to make space for the eleven sprockets.
keyNumbers: 130 mm between the rear dropouts
About 250 to 350 g
Typically 2 to 4 pawls

parts.name: Rear hub

parts.description: Lever-operated skewer that clamps the wheel into the frame, removable without tools.

details.didYouKnow: Shifting onto the smallest sprocket before removing the rear wheel makes it much easier to slip out of the chain and back in again.
details.howItWorks: The rear quick release works like the front one, but it also has to stop the axle being pulled forward in the dropouts by chain tension. Because modern dropouts face downwards, the chain pull mostly pushes the axle up into the slot, and the clamp keeps it there. Removing it lets the wheel drop out once the chain is lifted off the cassette.
keyNumbers: Rod about 5 mm thick
About 165 mm long
Roughly 55 to 65 g
details.madeOf: A steel or titanium skewer rod with an alloy cam lever. The rod is slightly longer than the front one to span the wider rear hub.

parts.name: Rear quick release

parts.description: Stack of eleven sprockets from 11 to 28 teeth on the rear hub; the smaller the sprocket, the higher the gear.

details.didYouKnow: In top gear, 50 teeth to 11, one turn of the pedals turns the rear wheel about four and a half times, carrying the bike nearly 10 m.
details.howItWorks: The eleven sprockets slide onto splines on the freehub and are held by a threaded lockring. The rear derailleur moves the chain sideways from one to the next, and ramps and shaped teeth on each sprocket help the chain climb or drop at the right spot. Combined with the two chainrings, it gives 22 gear combinations, though several overlap.
keyNumbers: 11 to 28 teeth
About 250 to 300 g

Lasts about 2 to 3 chains
details.madeOf: Hardened steel sprockets for wear resistance, often with the largest ones on an aluminium or plastic carrier to save weight. Steel teeth last much longer than alloy ones under chain wear.

parts.name: Cassette

parts.description: Joins the seat tube to the head tube along the top of the front triangle.

details.didYouKnow: Frame sizes are often quoted from the top tube or seat tube, but two bikes with the same number can fit very differently because of their angles.
details.howItWorks: The top tube closes the front triangle and largely sets the bike's reach, how far forward you stretch to the bars. It carries mostly bending and compression loads between the head tube and seat tube, so it can be thinner than the down tube. On this bike the rear brake cable runs along it.
keyNumbers: About 540 to 560 mm long on a medium frame
Roughly 30 to 35 mm diameter
Wall thickness under 1 mm in the middle

parts.name: Top tube

parts.description: The frame's biggest tube, from the bottom bracket up to the head tube; it resists the twisting of hard pedalling.

details.didYouKnow: Doubling a tube's diameter at the same wall thickness makes it about eight times stiffer in bending, which is why aluminium frames use fat tubes.
details.howItWorks: The down tube runs diagonally from the head tube to the bottom bracket and resists both twisting from hard pedalling and the steering and braking loads fed in through the fork. Its large diameter matters because a tube's stiffness rises steeply with its width. It often carries the bottle cage bolts and frame decals.
keyNumbers: Typically 35 to 50 mm across on aluminium
About 620 to 650 mm long
Two bottle cage bolts, typically M5
details.madeOf: Usually the thickest tube of an aluminium or steel frame, often ovalised or shaped where it meets the head tube and bottom bracket. Widening the tube gives stiffness without much extra weight.

parts.name: Down tube

parts.description: Runs from the bottom bracket up to the seat post clamp.

details.didYouKnow: 27.2 mm is one of the most common seat post sizes because it suits the bore of classic round frame tubes.
details.howItWorks: The seat tube connects the bottom bracket to the saddle and anchors the seat stays, top tube and front derailleur. The seat post slides inside and is clamped at the top by a collar, often helped by a slot cut in the tube. Its angle sets how far behind the pedals you sit.
keyNumbers: Seat angle typically 73 to 74 degrees
About 500 to 560 mm long
Inner diameter commonly 27.2 mm
details.madeOf: Round aluminium or steel tubing, machined inside the top end so the seat post fits precisely. The round section is needed for the front derailleur band clamp or braze-on.

parts.name: Seat tube

parts.description: Short tube holding the steering bearings that the fork turns in.

details.didYouKnow: A taller head tube lifts the handlebars, so endurance bikes use longer head tubes than race bikes of the same size.
details.howItWorks: The head tube is a short, stout tube that houses the headset bearings, through which the fork steerer passes. Its angle, together with the fork's offset, sets the trail that makes the bike self-centring and stable. It takes large loads from braking and bumps fed in through the fork.
keyNumbers: Head angle typically 72 to 73.5 degrees
About 130 to 170 mm long
Fits a 1 1/8 inch steerer
details.madeOf: A thick-walled aluminium or steel tube, machined at both ends to press or seat the bearing cups. It has to stay perfectly round so the bearings run smoothly.

parts.name: Head tube

parts.description: Lower arm of the rear triangle, from the bottom bracket to the rear dropout.

details.didYouKnow: Short chainstays make a bike feel snappier when you stand up and sprint, which is why race bikes keep them as short as tyre clearance allows.
details.howItWorks: The left chainstay runs from the bottom bracket back to the left rear dropout and helps hold the rear axle firmly in line. It carries the rider's weight and braking loads, but unlike the right chainstay it does not take the direct pull of the chain, so it is under less tension. Its length helps set how lively or relaxed the bike feels.
keyNumbers: About 405 to 415 mm long
Tapers to roughly 16 to 20 mm at the dropout
Holds the left side of a 130 mm axle
details.madeOf: Aluminium or steel tube, shaped and tapered towards the dropout, then welded and painted. It can be slimmer than the drive side because it is less heavily loaded.

parts.name: Chainstay (non-drive side)

parts.description: Upper arm of the rear triangle, from the top of the seat tube to the rear dropout.

details.didYouKnow: Designers sometimes make seat stays very thin on purpose, so the rear triangle flexes slightly over bumps and takes the sting out of rough roads.
details.howItWorks: The left seat stay links the top of the seat tube to the left rear dropout, completing one side of the rear triangle. It is quite slender because it mostly takes compression from the rider's weight. Near the top it joins the brake bridge that the rear caliper bolts to, so braking forces pass through it too.
keyNumbers: About 500 to 550 mm long
Typically 14 to 18 mm diameter
Joined to the right stay by a brake bridge
details.madeOf: A thin aluminium or steel tube, often curved or flattened to allow a little vertical flex for comfort. Lighter tubing is fine because the loads here are modest.

parts.name: Seat stay (non-drive side)

parts.description: Lower arm of the rear triangle, from the bottom bracket to the rear dropout.

details.didYouKnow: When a chain falls off on the inside, it often wedges between the small chainring and this stay, which is why many bikes carry a chain catcher.
details.howItWorks: The drive-side chainstay sits next to the chain and chainrings and takes the full pull of the chain every pedal stroke. It is usually shaped, dented or dropped to clear the big chainring and the tyre, yet still stiff enough not to flex sideways under power. It often carries a small rubber or metal pad to stop the chain chipping the paint when it slaps.
keyNumbers: About 405 to 415 mm long
Chain pull up to roughly 1,000 to 2,000 N in a hard sprint
Clearance for about a 53-tooth ring
details.madeOf: Aluminium or steel tube, often larger or more heavily shaped than the left stay because of the extra chain load. Shaping by hydroforming or crimping makes room for the drivetrain.

parts.name: Chainstay (drive side)

parts.description: Upper arm of the rear triangle, from the top of the seat tube to the rear dropout.

details.didYouKnow: The derailleur hanger is often a separate, softer part designed to bend in a crash, sparing the frame and making a cheap, swappable fix.
details.howItWorks: The right seat stay mirrors the left, running from the seat cluster to the drive-side dropout, which also carries the threaded derailleur hanger. That means it helps hold the rear derailleur in line with the cassette. Together the two stays and the brake bridge keep the rear caliper centred over the rim.

Typically 14 to 18 mm diameter
Derailleur hanger usually bolts on with 1 or 2 screws

parts.name: Seat stay (drive side)

parts.description: Where the frame tubes meet at the bottom; it holds the bearings the cranks spin on.

details.didYouKnow: On an English-threaded bottom bracket, the drive-side cup has a left-hand thread so pedalling does not slowly unscrew it.
details.howItWorks: The bottom bracket shell is where the seat tube, down tube and both chainstays meet, so it is the most heavily loaded junction on the frame. It holds the bottom bracket bearings, either screwed into threads or pressed in, and the crank axle runs through it. Every pedal stroke twists it from side to side.

About 34 to 35 mm inner diameter threaded
Typically 260 to 275 mm above the ground

parts.name: Bottom bracket shell

parts.description: One leg of the carbon fork; its forward curve (rake) helps make the steering stable.

details.didYouKnow: Rake and head angle together create trail, the distance the tyre touches the road behind the steering axis, which helps the wheel straighten itself.
details.howItWorks: The left blade runs from the crown down to the left front dropout, and its forward bend adds offset ahead of the steering axis. With rim brakes, this blade sees fairly even loads, since there is no disc caliper pulling on one side. It flexes slightly front to back over bumps, softening road buzz before it reaches your hands.

Whole fork roughly 350 to 450 g
About 370 mm from axle to crown

parts.name: Fork blade (left)

parts.description: One leg of the carbon fork; its forward curve (rake) helps make the steering stable.

details.didYouKnow: Carbon forks are usually designed to bend slightly before they break and are tested against fatigue for the equivalent of many thousands of kilometres.
details.howItWorks: The right blade mirrors the left, and the two together clamp the front axle in their dropouts. Both blades have to bend and twist identically, or the front wheel would steer slightly on its own under braking. Lawyer lips on the dropout keep the wheel in place if the quick release is loose.

Dropouts about 100 mm apart
Clearance for roughly a 25 to 28 mm tyre

parts.name: Fork blade (right)

parts.description: Joins the two fork blades to the steerer tube.

details.didYouKnow: Braking makes the front of the bike dive, and the fork crown is where that whole bending load concentrates, which is why it is the bulkiest part of the fork.
details.howItWorks: The crown is where the two blades meet the steerer, so it takes the biggest bending loads in the fork when you brake hard. The front brake caliper bolts through a hole in its centre, so braking forces feed straight into it. Its shape also sets the clearance between the tyre and the fork.

Handles braking loads of roughly 1,000 N or more

parts.description: Tube rising from the fork through the head tube; the stem clamps to its top.

details.didYouKnow: Overtightening a stem on a carbon steerer can crush it, so mechanics use a torque wrench and a carbon assembly paste with grit for grip.
details.howItWorks: The steerer is the tube that rises through the head tube, turning in the headset bearings. The stem clamps around its top, and a star nut or expanding plug inside it lets a top cap preload the bearings. Spacers above or below the stem set the bar height before the steerer is cut to length.

Typically 250 to 300 mm long before cutting
Stem bolts usually about 5 Nm

parts.name: Steerer tube

parts.description: Pair of angular-contact bearings in the head tube that let the fork turn smoothly.

details.didYouKnow: A worn headset can develop indexed steering, where the fork tends to click into the straight-ahead position because the balls have dented their races.
details.howItWorks: Two bearings, one at the top and one at the bottom of the head tube, let the fork rotate while keeping it held firmly in line. Their angled contact surfaces take both the side-to-side and up-and-down loads from steering and bumps. Tightening the top cap squeezes the bearings to remove play before the stem bolts lock it in.

About 50 to 100 g

parts.name: Headset bearings

parts.description: Clamps the handlebar to the steerer; its length sets how stretched out you ride.

details.didYouKnow: Flipping a stem upside down changes the bar height by a couple of centimetres without buying any new parts.
details.howItWorks: The stem clamps the steerer at one end and the handlebar at the other, with a faceplate held by four bolts. Its length and angle set how far and how low your hands reach, so swapping stems is the quickest way to change a bike's fit. A shorter stem quickens the steering slightly, a longer one calms it.

Usually about plus or minus 6 degrees

parts.name: Stem

parts.description: Curved bar giving several hand positions, including the low drops for speed.

details.didYouKnow: At racing speeds, air resistance is the main force a rider fights, and dropping onto the drops can cut drag by roughly 10 to 20%.
details.howItWorks: The drop bar gives three main hand positions: on the tops, on the lever hoods, and down in the curved drops. Riding in the drops lowers your upper body and reduces air drag, while the tops are more relaxed for climbing. Bar tape wraps the bar for grip and comfort, hiding the brake and gear cables underneath.

About 125 to 130 mm of drop
31.8 mm clamp diameter
Roughly 250 to 300 g

details.didYouKnow: Integrated brake and gear levers only became standard in the early 1990s; before then road riders shifted with small levers on the down tube.
details.howItWorks: Pulling the left lever back works the front brake through a cable. Pushing the lever sideways pulls the front derailleur cable onto a ratchet to shift to the big ring, while a small inner paddle releases it to drop to the small ring. Its hood also makes the most common place to rest your hands.

details.didYouKnow: Many riders spin the rear derailleur dozens of times more often than the front, so the right lever usually wears out first.

details.didYouKnow: On hard braking, a road bike's limit is often tipping over the front wheel, not skidding, because the bike is short and the rider sits high.

details.didYouKnow: Every post has a minimum insertion mark; at least that much must stay inside the frame or the post and seat tube can crack.

details.didYouKnow: Sit bone width varies a lot between riders, so many bike shops measure it by having you sit on a soft gel pad that records the imprint.

About 250 to 300 g
Rails usually 7 mm round

parts.description: Opposite crank, set 180° round so the pedals alternate.

details.didYouKnow: Many power meters sit only in the non-drive crank and simply double the left leg's figure, which is close but not exact, since most people's legs are slightly uneven.
details.howItWorks: The non-drive crank slides onto splines at the other end of the axle and is clamped by pinch bolts or a self-extracting bolt. Set exactly opposite the drive crank, it puts one pedal down as the other comes up, so your legs take turns. Because it carries no chainrings, it passes its torque through the axle to the drive side.
keyNumbers: 172.5 mm long
Set 180 degrees from the drive side
About 150 to 200 g
Pinch bolts typically about 12 to 14 Nm
details.madeOf: Forged aluminium alloy, matched in length to the drive crank. The same alloy and shape keep both sides equally stiff and strong.

parts.name: Crank arm (non-drive side)

parts.description: Clipless pedal: a cleat on the shoe clicks into it so you can pull up as well as push down.

details.didYouKnow: Clipless pedals are confusingly named: they clip in, but replaced the older toe clips and straps, which is where the name comes from.
details.howItWorks: A spring-loaded clip on the pedal body grabs a plastic or metal cleat bolted to the rider's shoe. A sharp outward twist of the heel releases it. The pedal body spins on bearings around a steel spindle that screws into the crank with a normal right-hand thread.
keyNumbers: About 120 to 160 g each
Cleat float typically 0 to 6 degrees
Spindle thread 9/16 inch
details.madeOf: A composite or carbon-reinforced plastic body with a steel or titanium spindle and steel bearings. The body only needs to be stiff, while the spindle must be very strong.

parts.name: Pedal (drive side)

parts.description: The other clipless pedal.

details.didYouKnow: Precession, the slow rolling movement of the bearing on its thread, would loosen a right-hand-threaded left pedal, which is why left pedals use a reverse thread.
details.howItWorks: The non-drive pedal works the same way as its partner, but its spindle has a left-hand thread so that pedalling forces keep tightening it rather than unscrewing it. Most riders unclip this foot first when stopping, so its release tension is often set a little lighter. It is usually marked with an L on the spindle.
keyNumbers: About 120 to 160 g
Left-hand 9/16 inch thread
Release angle typically about 15 degrees
details.madeOf: The same composite body, steel spindle and sealed bearings as the drive-side pedal. Bearings are sealed to keep out water and road grit.

parts.name: Pedal (non-drive side)

parts.description: Hollow steel axle on two bearings that joins the cranks through the frame.

details.didYouKnow: A creak that seems to come from the pedals, the saddle or the frame very often turns out to be a dry or loose bottom bracket.
details.howItWorks: The axle passes through the bottom bracket shell and turns on two bearings, one on each side of the frame. Both cranks fix to it, so it carries the twisting force from the non-drive side across to the chainrings. Putting the bearings outside the shell lets the axle be wide and hollow, which is both stiff and light.
keyNumbers: Axle typically 24 mm diameter
Bearings about 37 mm outer diameter
Rotates roughly 80 to 100 times a minute
details.madeOf: A hollow steel or aluminium axle with steel cartridge bearings in alloy cups. Steel axles are strong and cheap; the hollow tube saves weight without much loss of stiffness.

parts.name: Bottom bracket & axle

parts.description: Roller chain of about 110 links; it transmits your pedalling to the rear wheel with very little loss.

details.didYouKnow: Chains do not truly stretch; their pins and rollers wear so the pitch grows, and replacing a chain at about 0.5% wear saves the cassette and chainrings.
details.howItWorks: The chain is a loop of pin-joined links, each with a roller that sits between the teeth of the chainring and sprocket. Only the top run carries load as it pulls the cassette round; the bottom run returns through the derailleur. Its narrow, flexible side plates let it bend sideways to reach every sprocket.
keyNumbers: About 110 links
Pitch of 12.7 mm (half an inch)
Around 95 to 98% efficient when clean
About 250 to 270 g
details.madeOf: Hardened steel plates, pins and rollers, often plated or coated against rust. Steel is the only practical material that survives the high contact stresses and constant wear.

parts.name: Chain

parts.description: Spring-loaded arm that guides the chain across the cassette to change gear and keeps the chain tight.

details.didYouKnow: The word derailleur is French for something that derails, which is exactly what it does, deliberately knocking the chain off one sprocket onto the next.
details.howItWorks: The rear derailleur hangs from the frame's dropout and swings on a parallelogram linkage, moving the cage sideways when the cable pulls or a spring pushes back. A second spring rotates the cage backwards to take up slack chain when the chain is on smaller cogs. The limit screws stop it from pushing the chain off either end of the cassette.
keyNumbers: Handles up to about 30 to 32 teeth
Total capacity typically about 33 to 39 teeth
About 200 to 250 g
details.madeOf: Aluminium body and cage plates with steel springs and pivots, sometimes carbon parts on lighter models. Aluminium keeps it light while staying stiff enough to shift accurately.

parts.name: Rear derailleur

parts.description: Two small pulleys in the derailleur cage that steer and tension the chain.

details.didYouKnow: Jockey wheels pick up a crust of oily grit faster than almost anything else on a bike, so scraping them clean is a classic part of a quick tune-up.
details.howItWorks: The upper jockey wheel sits close to the cassette and guides the chain onto each sprocket during a shift. The lower wheel, at the end of the sprung cage, keeps tension in the slack bottom run of chain. Both spin quickly on small bushings or bearings and have shaped teeth to keep the chain aligned.
keyNumbers: Typically 11 teeth each
About 30 to 40 mm across
Spin up to roughly 500 rpm when pedalling hard
details.madeOf: Hard-wearing plastic or ceramic-bearing alloy pulleys. Plastic is quiet, light and gentle on the chain.

parts.name: Jockey wheels

parts.description: Cage on the seat tube that pushes the chain between the two chainrings.

details.didYouKnow: Front shifts work best with light pedal pressure, because the chain must climb or fall between rings that differ by 16 teeth.
details.howItWorks: The front derailleur is a narrow steel cage clamped to the seat tube just above the big chainring. When the cable pulls, a linkage moves the cage outward, and its inner plate pushes the chain sideways until the big ring's pins catch it. Releasing the cable lets a spring move the cage back, and the outer plate nudges the chain onto the small ring.
keyNumbers: Cage typically 1 to 3 mm above the big ring
Clamp diameter commonly 31.8 or 34.9 mm
About 80 to 100 g
details.madeOf: A steel cage, which resists wear from the chain rubbing on it, mounted on an aluminium arm and clamp. Steel inner plates stand up to repeated chain contact.

parts.name: Front derailleur

parts.description: Steel cable in a housing along the top tube, pulled by the lever to close the rear caliper.

details.didYouKnow: Brake housing is a tight steel coil that is strong when bent, while gear housing uses lengthwise strands that barely compress, keeping shifts accurate.
details.howItWorks: A stranded steel inner wire slides inside a protective outer housing. When you squeeze the lever, the wire pulls and the housing pushes back, so the force travels round curves to the rear caliper. Along the top tube the bare wire often runs between housing stops, which reduces friction over the long run.
keyNumbers: Inner wire about 1.5 to 1.6 mm
Housing typically 5 mm across
Total run about 1.5 to 1.8 m
details.madeOf: Stainless steel inner wire inside a plastic-lined, spiral-wound steel housing with a rubber or plastic outer coating. The liner cuts friction and the steel coil resists compression.

parts.name: Rear brake cable

summary: A road bike with a diamond frame, 2×11 derailleur gears and rim brakes: about 8 kg of tubes, wheels and a chain that turn leg power into speed with around 95% efficiency.

name: Family Car
overview:
A car is a self-contained machine for carrying a few people and their luggage in comfort and safety. Its parts fall into a few big systems: a body that protects the people inside, an engine that makes power, a drivetrain that delivers it to the wheels, and the suspension, steering and brakes that keep it under control.

This one has a petrol engine at the front, mounted sideways. Inside, four pistons are pushed down in turn by burning fuel and air, turning the crankshaft. The gearbox beside it picks a ratio, and driveshafts carry the turn out to the front wheels. Exhaust gas leaves through a pipe running under the car to a silencer at the back, and a radiator at the front gets rid of the engine's waste heat.

The body is a single welded steel shell, a monocoque, with bolt-on doors, bonnet, boot lid, wings and bumpers. Its front and rear are built to crumple in a crash, absorbing energy while the stiff passenger cell around the seats stays intact. Each wheel hangs on springs and dampers so the tyres stay in contact with the road over bumps, and each has a disc brake squeezed by hydraulic pressure from the pedal.

parts.description: Hinged steel lid over the engine bay.

details.didYouKnow: Some cars have pop-up bonnets: sensors in the bumper detect a pedestrian strike and small charges lift the rear of the bonnet by several centimetres in a split second.
details.howItWorks: The bonnet pivots on two hinges near the windscreen and is held shut by a latch at the front, with a second safety catch so it cannot fly up if the main latch is released while driving. In a frontal crash it is designed to fold up in the middle rather than slide back into the windscreen. There is also a deliberate gap between it and the hard engine parts below so it can dent and cushion a pedestrian's head.
keyNumbers: Outer skin typically about 0.7 mm thick
Roughly 12 to 18 kg in steel
Often 60 to 100 mm of crush space above the engine
details.madeOf: Two thin pressed steel skins, an outer panel and a ribbed inner frame, glued and hemmed together at the edges. Some cars use aluminium to save weight at the front, where it matters most for handling.

parts.name: Bonnet

parts.description: Pressed steel panel spot-welded to the roof rails.

details.didYouKnow: Many roofs have plastic strips running along each side that hide the joint to the body; laser brazing lets some makers do away with those strips entirely.
details.howItWorks: The roof skin is stretched over transverse steel bows that link the left and right roof rails, so the whole top of the car acts like a stiff box lid. That ties the tops of the A, B and C pillars together, which helps the passenger cell resist twisting and crushing in a rollover. Curtain airbags are folded up in the rails along its edges, hidden behind the headlining.
keyNumbers: About 0.7 mm thick
Roof rack loads typically limited to about 50 to 75 kg
Roughly 1.4 to 1.5 m above the road
details.madeOf: Thin deep-drawn steel sheet, galvanised against rust and joined to the rails by spot welds, adhesive or laser brazing. The panel itself is about appearance and dent resistance; the strength is in the rails and bows underneath.

parts.name: Roof panel

parts.description: Hinged lid over the luggage space.

details.didYouKnow: In the United States every new car's boot must have a glow-in-the-dark release handle inside it, so anyone trapped there can let themselves out.
details.howItWorks: The boot lid swings up on hinges at its front edge, helped by gas struts or torsion bars that balance its weight so it rises on its own once unlatched. The latch at the bottom is usually electrically released from the key fob or a button. It typically carries the number plate lights, a rear camera and sometimes a small spoiler lip that tidies the airflow leaving the roof.
keyNumbers: Boot space typically about 450 to 500 litres
Lid roughly 10 to 14 kg
Opening height typically about 0.7 m off the ground
details.madeOf: Pressed steel outer and inner panels hemmed together, though some makers use aluminium or plastic composite to save weight. Plastic lids also let radio and phone antennas hide inside them.

parts.name: Boot lid

parts.description: Plastic cover over a steel crash beam; it takes low-speed knocks and shapes the airflow.

details.didYouKnow: Plastic bumper covers can often be repaired by plastic welding or heat reshaping rather than replaced, because the material springs back from moderate dents.
details.howItWorks: Behind the painted cover is a steel or aluminium beam bolted to the body rails through crash boxes, small crumple tubes that collapse in a low-speed knock so the expensive rails do not have to. Foam or plastic lattice between the cover and the beam softens contact with a pedestrian's legs. The bumper also hides parking sensors, and on many cars the radar for adaptive cruise control.
keyNumbers: Cover typically about 3 mm thick
Crash boxes designed for knocks up to about 15 km/h
Pedestrian leg tests run at about 40 km/h
details.madeOf: The cover is injection-moulded polypropylene blended with rubber and talc, which flexes and springs back instead of denting. The beam beneath is high-strength steel or extruded aluminium.

parts.name: Front bumper

parts.description: Plastic cover over the rear crash beam.

details.didYouKnow: Parking sensors work like a bat: they send out an ultrasonic click and time the echo, which is why snow or mud over them can trigger false beeps.
details.howItWorks: Like the front, a moulded cover sits over a crash beam fixed to the rear rails through crumple boxes, so parking bumps are absorbed without damaging the body. The rear cover usually carries ultrasonic parking sensors, reflectors and a cut-out for the tailpipe or a hidden exit underneath. It also helps air leave the car cleanly, which trims drag.
keyNumbers: Typically 4 parking sensors
Sensors work at roughly 40 kHz, above human hearing
Cover about 3 to 5 kg
details.madeOf: Polypropylene-based plastic for the cover, chosen because it is light, cheap to mould into complex shapes and shrugs off small knocks. The crash beam is steel or aluminium.

parts.name: Rear bumper

parts.description: Bolt-on panel over the front wheel, easy to replace after a scrape.

details.didYouKnow: The word wing for this panel comes from the days when mudguards stood out separately from the body, curving over the wheels like wings.
details.howItWorks: The wing forms the side of the car from the headlight back to the front door and shapes the arch over the front wheel. It is bolted to the body rails rather than welded, so after a scrape a body shop can unbolt and swap it. On this car the left wing sits on the driver's side, beside the gearbox and battery under the bonnet, with a plastic arch liner keeping wheel spray off the metal.
keyNumbers: About 0.7 mm thick steel
Typically 3 to 5 kg
Held by roughly 8 to 12 bolts
details.madeOf: Pressed steel sheet, galvanised and painted, though some makers use plastic composite for front wings because they carry little load and resist dents.

parts.name: Front wing (left)

parts.description: Steel door shell with a side-impact beam, window mechanism and lock inside.

details.didYouKnow: The satisfying thunk of a closing door is often tuned by acoustic engineers, who adjust the seals, latch and damping material to make the sound feel solid.
details.howItWorks: This is the driver's door. It hangs on two hinges bolted to the A-pillar and latches onto a striker on the B-pillar, while a check strap holds it open at set positions. Inside, a steel beam runs across it to resist intrusion in a side impact, and an electric regulator raises and lowers the window. The driver's door panel usually carries the master switches for all four windows and the mirrors.
keyNumbers: Typically 20 to 30 kg fully fitted
Opens to about 65 to 70 degrees
Impact beam steel up to about 1,500 MPa strength
details.madeOf: A pressed steel outer skin hemmed over a stiffer inner frame, with a high-strength steel tube or channel as the impact beam. Plastic trim, foam and a speaker sit on the cabin side.

parts.name: Front door (left)

parts.description: Rear passenger door, shaped around the rear wheel arch.

details.didYouKnow: Child locks are on the rear doors because that is where young children usually sit; the switch is hidden on the door's edge so it can only be changed with the door open.
details.howItWorks: The rear door hangs from hinges on the B-pillar and latches on the C-pillar, behind the driver. Its back edge is cut around the rear wheel arch, which is why the window often cannot wind fully down and a small fixed glass panel fills the corner. A child lock on its edge stops it being opened from inside; on this side it opens towards passing traffic in countries that drive on the right.
keyNumbers: Typically 18 to 25 kg
Window often lowers only about two thirds
Child lock switch on the door edge
details.madeOf: Pressed steel skins with an internal side-impact beam, like the front door. The inner panel is a single pressing with holes for the window motor and lock, covered by a plastic trim panel.

parts.name: Rear door (left)

parts.description: Welded-on rear side panel around the rear wheel; part of the body shell.

details.didYouKnow: A small arrow beside the fuel gauge on most dashboards points to the side of the car the filler flap is on, handy in a hire car.
details.howItWorks: The rear quarter panel is the outer skin of the body behind the rear door, wrapping over the rear wheel and meeting the boot and rear bumper. Unlike the front wing it is welded to the inner wheel arch and pillars, so it adds stiffness to the shell. On many cars one of the two quarter panels carries the fuel filler flap.
keyNumbers: About 0.7 mm thick
Repair can take several days in a body shop
Fuel filler flap typically about 100 mm across
details.madeOf: Pressed galvanised steel, often formed together with much of the body side in one large stamping. Being part of the shell, it gets the same zinc coating, electro-dip primer and paint as the rest of the structure.

parts.name: Rear quarter panel (left)

parts.description: Heated, electrically adjusted mirror with an indicator repeater.

details.didYouKnow: European rules require door mirrors to swing away if struck, which is why they fold with a firm push rather than breaking off.
details.howItWorks: This is the driver's mirror. Two small electric motors behind the glass tilt it up, down, in and out, a heating pad clears mist and frost, and an LED repeater flashes with the indicators so cars alongside can see them. The housing is mounted so it folds back on impact rather than snapping off. In Europe the driver's mirror often has an aspheric outer edge that bends the view to shrink the blind spot.
keyNumbers: Glass roughly 150 to 200 mm wide
Usually 2 adjuster motors
Mirror unit about 1 to 2 kg
details.madeOf: A painted or black plastic housing over a metal or glass-filled nylon base, with silvered glass bonded to a plastic backing plate. Plastic keeps the weight down on the end of the door.

parts.name: Door mirror (left)

parts.description: Bolt-on panel over the front wheel, easy to replace after a scrape.

details.didYouKnow: Body shops often replace a bolt-on wing in an hour or two, but matching the paint to the rest of the car can take longer than the fitting.
details.howItWorks: The right wing mirrors the left, forming the side of the nose and the arch over the right front wheel. On this left-hand-drive car it is on the kerb side, so it is the wing most likely to pick up scuffs from kerbs, posts and parking. Under the bonnet beside it sits the engine itself, while the long right driveshaft runs out to the wheel it covers.
keyNumbers: About 0.7 mm thick steel
Typically 3 to 5 kg
Wheel arch gap often about 20 to 40 mm above the tyre
details.madeOf: Galvanised pressed steel, bolted on so it can be replaced as a separate part. The plastic wheel arch liner behind it protects the inside from stones and spray.

parts.name: Front wing (right)

parts.description: Steel door shell with a side-impact beam, window mechanism and lock inside.

details.didYouKnow: Doors usually have small drain holes in their bottom edge, because rain runs down past the window seal and needs a way out before it rusts the door.
details.howItWorks: The front passenger door hangs on the right A-pillar and latches on the right B-pillar, with a side-impact beam and electric window inside. On this left-hand-drive car it opens onto the pavement side, so passengers usually step out away from traffic. Its panel usually has just one window switch, and the front passenger side airbag sits in the seat or door beside it.
keyNumbers: Typically 20 to 30 kg fully fitted
Two hinges and one latch
Usually 2 or 3 rubber seal lines
details.madeOf: Steel outer and inner pressings with a high-strength steel impact beam and plastic trim. Door seals of EPDM rubber keep out wind and water.

parts.name: Front door (right)

parts.description: Rear passenger door, shaped around the rear wheel arch.

details.didYouKnow: Road safety advice is to let children out of the kerb-side rear door, which on a left-hand-drive car in right-hand traffic is this one.
details.howItWorks: The right rear door hangs on the right B-pillar and is shaped around the rear wheel arch. On this left-hand-drive car it opens onto the kerb side, which makes it the safer door for children to use. Inside it has a side-impact beam, window mechanism, child lock and often a fixed quarter glass at the back.
keyNumbers: Typically 18 to 25 kg
Window often lowers only about two thirds
Opens to about 70 degrees
details.madeOf: Pressed steel skins hemmed together around an impact beam, with plastic and fabric trim on the inside. Steel is cheap, strong and easy to repair.

parts.name: Rear door (right)

parts.description: Welded-on rear side panel around the rear wheel; part of the body shell.

details.didYouKnow: Repairing a badly damaged quarter panel usually means cutting it out and welding in a new section, which is why the same dent costs far more here than on a door or wing.
details.howItWorks: The right rear quarter panel wraps the right rear wheel and joins the C-pillar, boot opening and rear bumper. Because it is welded into the shell it helps carry loads and keeps the rear of the body stiff. The fuel tank sits under the floor just inboard of the rear wheels, with the filler pipe running up to a flap in one of the quarter panels.
keyNumbers: About 0.7 mm thick
Typically joined by dozens of spot welds
Wheel arch radius roughly 350 to 400 mm
details.madeOf: Galvanised pressed steel welded and bonded to the inner arch and pillars. It is protected by the factory's zinc coating, electro-dip primer and seam sealer.

parts.name: Rear quarter panel (right)

parts.description: Heated, electrically adjusted mirror with an indicator repeater.

details.didYouKnow: The famous warning that objects in the mirror are closer than they appear is a US requirement; European cars use convex mirrors without printing the warning.
details.howItWorks: The passenger-side mirror is further from the driver's eyes, so it is usually convex to show a wider view, which makes cars in it look smaller and further away. Like the left mirror it has two adjuster motors, a heater and an LED indicator repeater. On many cars it can dip automatically when reversing so the driver can see the kerb.
keyNumbers: Typically about 1.2 to 2 m radius of curvature
Glass roughly 150 to 200 mm wide
Unit about 1 to 2 kg
details.madeOf: A moulded plastic shell on a metal or reinforced plastic base, holding curved silvered glass on a plastic carrier. The breakaway joint is spring-loaded so the mirror folds and clicks back.

parts.name: Door mirror (right)

parts.description: Opening that lets cooling air reach the radiator.

details.didYouKnow: Many cars draw most of their cooling air through the lower bumper opening rather than the upper grille, which is partly there for the badge and the look.
details.howItWorks: The grille lets air at speed rush into the nose and through the radiator, while keeping out stones and birds. Behind it, the radiator and air-conditioning condenser sit one in front of the other so the same air cools both. Some cars fit active shutters behind the grille that close when little cooling is needed, cutting drag on the motorway.
keyNumbers: Typically 0.5 to 1 kg
Cooling airflow often adds roughly 5 to 10% of total drag
Car drag coefficient typically about 0.27 to 0.32
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded plastic such as ABS or polypropylene, often painted, chromed or textured. Plastic is light, cheap to shape and gives a little in a pedestrian impact.

parts.name: Radiator grille

parts.description: Laminated glass: two layers bonded to a plastic film so it cracks but doesn't shatter.

details.didYouKnow: Laminated glass traces back to 1903, when French chemist Edouard Benedictus dropped a flask coated in dried celluloid and saw that it cracked but held together.
details.howItWorks: The windscreen is glued into the body with a thick bead of polyurethane adhesive, so it becomes part of the structure, stiffening the roof and giving the passenger airbag something to push against. If a stone hits it, the outer layer cracks but the plastic film holds the pieces together and keeps occupants inside. Wipers, a rain sensor and often a camera for lane-keeping and emergency braking sit at its top.
keyNumbers: Typically about 4.5 to 5 mm thick
PVB film about 0.76 mm
Roughly 12 to 15 kg
UK MOT fails chips over 10 mm in the driver's view zone
details.madeOf: Two sheets of float glass bonded to a sheet of PVB plastic in an autoclave under heat and pressure. Some have a fine heating mesh or an acoustic film to cut wind noise.

parts.name: Windscreen

parts.description: Toughened glass with printed heater wires to clear mist and frost.

details.didYouKnow: Scraping the inside of a heated rear window can break a printed line, leaving a stripe that stays misted; small repair kits can paint the gap back in.
details.howItWorks: A current through the thin printed lines warms the glass enough to clear mist and melt frost, usually switching off on a timer after about a quarter of an hour. On many saloons some of those lines also act as the radio aerial. Because it is toughened, a heavy blow shatters it into small blunt cubes rather than sharp shards.
keyNumbers: About 3.5 to 4 mm thick
Heater typically draws roughly 100 to 200 W
Toughened glass is roughly 4 to 5 times stronger than ordinary glass
details.madeOf: Toughened glass, heated and then quickly cooled with air jets so its surface is locked in compression. The heater lines are a silver-based paste printed on and fired into the glass.

parts.name: Rear window

parts.description: Toughened glass that winds down into the door.

details.didYouKnow: Anti-pinch windows often sense a trapped object by watching for the motor slowing down or drawing extra current, without any separate sensor.
details.howItWorks: This is the driver's window. It runs in rubber-lined channels and is raised and lowered by an electric motor and regulator inside the door. It usually has a one-touch auto up and down, with anti-pinch sensing that reverses the glass if it detects something like a hand in the way.
keyNumbers: About 3.5 to 4 mm thick
Takes roughly 3 to 4 seconds to close
Glass typically 4 to 5 kg
details.madeOf: Toughened glass, which shatters into small blunt pieces if broken. Some cars use laminated side glass for better noise insulation and security.

parts.name: Front side window (left)

parts.description: LED headlight unit with dipped beam, main beam and daytime running light.

details.didYouKnow: Daytime running lights have been required on new car models in the EU since 2011, because cars that are lit up in daylight are easier to spot.
details.howItWorks: Rows of LEDs fire into reflectors or small lenses that shape the light into a sharp-edged dipped beam, which lights the road without dazzling oncoming drivers. Main beam switches on more LEDs to throw light far ahead, while a separate light strip acts as the daytime running light. Because the dipped beam pattern is uneven by design, it suits driving on one side of the road and needs adjusting for the other.
keyNumbers: Dipped beam roughly 15 to 25 W
Light colour about 5,500 to 6,500 K
LEDs typically outlast the car
details.madeOf: A polycarbonate lens with a scratch-resistant hard coat, over a plastic housing with an aluminium heat sink for the LEDs. Polycarbonate is far tougher than glass against stone chips.

parts.name: Headlight (left)

parts.description: Brake light, tail light and indicator in one moulded unit.

details.didYouKnow: The rules on single rear fog lights say they go on the driver's side or the centre, so they sit on opposite sides on left- and right-hand-drive versions of the same car.
details.howItWorks: The unit combines a dim red tail light, a brighter brake light triggered by a switch on the brake pedal, and an amber indicator. On this left-hand-drive car, the left side is the driver's side, which is where a single rear fog light is usually fitted so following drivers see it closest to the centre of the road. LEDs light almost instantly, warning drivers behind a fraction of a second sooner than old filament bulbs.
keyNumbers: LED brake lights light about 0.2 s faster than bulbs
That is roughly 5 m of travel at 100 km/h
Indicators flash about 60 to 120 times a minute
details.madeOf: A red and clear acrylic lens welded to a plastic housing, with LEDs on a circuit board. Acrylic is clear, weatherproof and easy to mould with optical patterns.

parts.name: Tail light (left)

parts.description: Toughened glass that winds down into the door.

details.didYouKnow: Toughened side glass is the easiest window for rescue crews to break, which is why emergency hammers aim for the side windows rather than the laminated windscreen.
details.howItWorks: The passenger's window works like the driver's, running in sealed channels and driven by a motor in the door. It can be operated from its own switch or from the driver's master panel, which can also lock it out. When it is raised, a lip seal at the bottom wipes rain off the glass.
keyNumbers: About 3.5 to 4 mm thick
Glass typically 4 to 5 kg
Motor usually a 12 V DC unit
details.madeOf: Toughened glass, with the edges ground smooth so they can be exposed when the window is partly down.

parts.name: Front side window (right)

parts.description: LED headlight unit with dipped beam, main beam and daytime running light.

details.didYouKnow: When driving a left-hand-drive car in Britain, owners are told to adjust the headlights or fit beam deflectors, because the kick-up would otherwise point at oncoming drivers.
details.howItWorks: This lamp mirrors the left, with dipped, main and daytime running lights. In countries that drive on the right, the dipped beam's sharp cut-off rises on the right-hand side, lighting the kerb, signs and pedestrians while staying low towards oncoming traffic. Automatic levelling tilts both headlights down when the boot is loaded so the beam does not rise into other drivers' eyes.
keyNumbers: Beam reaches roughly 50 to 70 m on dipped
Main beam can reach well over 100 m
Unit typically 2 to 4 kg
details.madeOf: Polycarbonate lens on a plastic housing, with LEDs, optics and electronics sealed inside against moisture. A breathable vent lets pressure equalise without letting water in.

parts.name: Headlight (right)

parts.description: Brake light, tail light and indicator in one moulded unit.

details.didYouKnow: Some modern cars flash their brake lights rapidly during an emergency stop to warn the car behind more urgently.
details.howItWorks: This unit carries the right-side tail, brake and indicator lights. On this left-hand-drive car the right side is the kerb side, which is where a single reversing light is usually placed. A third brake light, mounted high in the middle of the car, works together with both tail units so drivers several cars back can see it.
keyNumbers: Brake light roughly 5 to 10 times brighter than the tail light
Housing typically about 0.5 to 1 kg
LEDs rated for many thousands of hours
details.madeOf: Moulded acrylic lens and plastic housing with LEDs and reflectors inside, sealed with a gasket against spray.

parts.name: Tail light (right)

parts.description: Pressed steel floor of the monocoque; rails underneath carry the suspension and engine.

details.didYouKnow: Car bodies are lowered into a tank of primer and given an electric charge, so the paint is drawn into every hidden cavity, not just the surfaces a sprayer can reach.
details.howItWorks: The floor is the base of the monocoque, the single welded shell that does the job of a separate chassis. A tunnel down the middle and box-section sills along the sides make it stiff, while steel rails underneath carry the engine subframe at the front and the twist-beam axle at the rear. In a crash, the front and rear rails are designed to crumple progressively while the floor around the seats stays intact.
keyNumbers: Body shell roughly 250 to 350 kg
Thousands of spot welds, typically 4,000 or more
Twist stiffness often 20,000 Nm per degree or more
details.madeOf: Galvanised steel pressings of several grades and thicknesses, often laser-welded into tailored blanks before pressing. The whole shell is dipped in an electro-coat primer and sprayed with sealer underneath.

parts.name: Floor pan

parts.description: Steel wall separating the engine bay from the cabin.

details.didYouKnow: Americans often call it the firewall, a term borrowed from early aircraft and from older cars, where it really did keep an engine fire away from the occupants.
details.howItWorks: The bulkhead walls off the engine bay from the cabin, keeping out heat, noise and fumes, and stops the engine and gearbox being pushed into the footwell in a crash. The pedal box hangs from it on the driver's side, with the brake servo and master cylinder bolted to the engine side. The steering column, wiring and heater pipes pass through it in sealed grommets.
keyNumbers: Steel typically 0.8 to 1.2 mm thick
Insulation can be 20 mm thick or more
Roughly 10 kg of steel
details.madeOf: Pressed steel welded into the shell, lined with sound-deadening felt, foam and bitumen pads. Higher-strength steel is used in the lower part where crash loads hit.

parts.name: Bulkhead

parts.description: Front roof pillar framing the windscreen; high-strength steel to protect the cabin in a rollover.

details.didYouKnow: A-pillar blind spots are big enough to hide a cyclist or pedestrian; driving instructors teach a quick lean forward at junctions to look around them.
details.howItWorks: The A-pillar runs from the scuttle up to the roof, framing the windscreen and carrying the front door hinges. In a rollover or offset crash it has to stop the roof and windscreen frame from folding back onto the occupants. On this car the left pillar is right beside the driver, so it is the one that most blocks the view when turning left at junctions.
keyNumbers: Steel strength up to about 1,500 MPa
Typically 60 to 100 mm wide in view
Roof strength tests in the US require about 3 times the car's weight
details.madeOf: Hot-stamped boron steel, heated until red hot, pressed and quenched in the die so it becomes extremely strong. That lets the pillar stay slim enough to see past.

parts.name: A-pillar (left)

parts.description: Centre pillar between the doors; the strongest part of the side structure.

details.didYouKnow: Some cars deliberately make the bottom of the B-pillar softer than the top so it folds in a controlled way and pushes the occupant away from the impact.
details.howItWorks: The B-pillar rises from the sill to the roof between the front and rear doors, taking the front door's latch and the rear door's hinges. In a side impact it is the main barrier between the intruding car and the driver's chest. It also carries the driver's seatbelt upper mounting, often on a height adjuster.
keyNumbers: Up to about 1,500 MPa steel strength
Euro NCAP side barrier about 1,400 kg at 60 km/h
Belt height adjuster typically about 50 to 80 mm of travel
details.madeOf: Hot-stamped boron steel, sometimes tailor-tempered so the top stays very hard while the bottom stays tougher and can bend without cracking. This balance helps it absorb energy instead of snapping.

parts.name: B-pillar (left)

parts.description: Adjustable seat on a steel frame; its head restraint limits whiplash in a rear impact.

details.didYouKnow: The driver's seat usually wears out first, and the outer bolster takes most of the damage because drivers slide over it every time they get in.
details.howItWorks: This is the driver's seat. It slides on rails, rises on a ratchet lever and reclines, so drivers of very different sizes can reach the pedals and see out. Its head restraint is placed close behind the head to stop it snapping back in a rear impact, and many seats have a side airbag in the outer bolster. A seatbelt pretensioner beside it tightens the belt in the first instant of a crash.
keyNumbers: Typically 15 to 25 kg
Fore-aft travel roughly 200 to 250 mm
Height adjustment about 40 to 60 mm
details.madeOf: A welded steel frame with steel springs or straps, shaped polyurethane foam and a woven fabric cover. Foam density varies across the seat to give firm support at the sides and comfort in the middle.

parts.name: Front seat (left)

parts.description: Front roof pillar framing the windscreen; high-strength steel to protect the cabin in a rollover.

details.didYouKnow: Small-overlap crash tests, where only about a quarter of the car's width hits the barrier, forced many makers to strengthen their A-pillars in the 2010s.
details.howItWorks: The right A-pillar frames the passenger side of the windscreen and carries the front passenger door hinges. It is a key load path in a small-overlap crash on the right front corner, where it must stop the wheel and structure being driven into the footwell. The curtain airbag for the right side is anchored at its top, running back along the roof rail.
keyNumbers: Steel strength up to about 1,500 MPa
Curtain airbag inflates in roughly 25 ms
Windscreen bonded to it with about 10 mm of adhesive bead
details.madeOf: Hot-stamped boron steel inside an outer skin, often with a separate reinforcing tube. The heat treatment gives several times the strength of ordinary body steel.

parts.name: A-pillar (right)

parts.description: Centre pillar between the doors; the strongest part of the side structure.

details.didYouKnow: In a pole crash test, the car is slid sideways into a rigid post at an angle, which concentrates the load where it is hardest for the structure to spread it.
details.howItWorks: The right B-pillar ties the floor to the roof between the passenger doors. It carries the front passenger's seatbelt mounting and takes the door latch and hinges, so it holds both right doors in place. In a side pole crash it works with the roof rail, floor cross-members and door beams to spread the load around the cabin.
keyNumbers: Up to about 1,500 MPa steel
Euro NCAP pole test at about 32 km/h
Belt pretensioner acts within roughly 10 to 20 ms
details.madeOf: Hot-stamped high-strength steel under a plastic interior trim, often with a softer lower zone. The outer skin is ordinary body-side steel.

parts.name: B-pillar (right)

parts.description: Adjustable seat on a steel frame; its head restraint limits whiplash in a rear impact.

details.didYouKnow: A rear-facing child seat must never go in front of an active airbag; many cars have a key switch to turn the passenger airbag off for exactly this.
details.howItWorks: The front passenger seat adjusts like the driver's, with sliding rails, a recline and a head restraint. A pressure sensor or occupancy mat in the cushion tells the car whether someone is sitting there, for the seatbelt reminder and, on some cars, to decide whether to fire the passenger airbag. A side airbag is often built into its outer bolster.
keyNumbers: Typically 15 to 25 kg
Side airbag about 10 to 15 litres
Fore-aft travel roughly 200 to 250 mm
details.madeOf: Steel frame, sprung base, moulded polyurethane foam and fabric cover. The covers are often flame-retardant and tested for abrasion over many thousands of cycles.

parts.name: Front seat (right)

parts.description: Bench for three with a split-folding back.

details.didYouKnow: ISOFIX anchor spacing is set by an international standard, which is why the same child seat can click into thousands of different car models.
details.howItWorks: The rear bench seats three, with a seatbelt for each position. Its back is split, typically 60/40, and folds forward so long items can reach through from the boot. The outer two seats usually have ISOFIX anchor bars at the base of the backrest, letting child seats click rigidly onto the body. On this car the fuel tank sits under the cushion.
keyNumbers: Typically 60/40 split
ISOFIX bars 280 mm apart
Usually 3 three-point seatbelts
details.madeOf: Steel tubular frames and wire, polyurethane foam and fabric. The folding backrests need strong steel latches so luggage cannot burst through in a crash.

parts.name: Rear seat

parts.description: Moulded panel holding the instruments, air vents and passenger airbag, over a steel cross-beam.

details.didYouKnow: The airbag lid's tear seam is often cut from behind by a laser to just the right depth, invisible from the front but weak enough to split on demand.
details.howItWorks: The dashboard is a moulded shell hung on a steel cross-car beam that runs between the A-pillars and supports the steering column. It holds the instruments, the infotainment screen and air vents, with the heater and air-conditioning unit hidden behind it. The passenger airbag bursts through a hidden seam on its top, so it has to tear open cleanly in a crash.
keyNumbers: Passenger airbag roughly 100 to 120 litres
Cross beam typically 8 to 12 kg
Wiring in the whole car often totals well over 1 km
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded polypropylene or ABS, often with a soft-touch foamed skin, over a steel or magnesium cross beam. Plastics are light and can be moulded with the clips and ducts built in.

parts.name: Dashboard

parts.description: Turns the front wheels through the steering rack; the driver's airbag sits in its centre.

details.didYouKnow: A driver's airbag inflates faster than you can blink and has already started deflating through vent holes by the time your head reaches it.
details.howItWorks: Turning the wheel twists the steering column, which drives the pinion in the steering rack to swing the front wheels. Electric power steering adds force, so the effort feels light when parking and firmer at speed. A coiled ribbon cable behind the wheel, called a clockspring, keeps the airbag, horn and buttons connected while the wheel turns lock to lock.
keyNumbers: About 370 to 380 mm across
Roughly 2.5 to 3 turns lock to lock
Driver airbag about 40 to 60 litres
Airbag fills in about 30 ms
details.madeOf: A cast magnesium or aluminium skeleton, moulded in polyurethane foam and often wrapped in leather. Magnesium keeps it light and stiff, reducing vibration felt by the driver.

parts.name: Steering wheel

parts.description: Collapsible shaft from the wheel to the rack; it telescopes in a crash.

details.didYouKnow: Before collapsible columns became common in the late 1960s, rigid steering columns were a major cause of chest injuries for drivers in frontal crashes.
details.howItWorks: The column carries the steering wheel's rotation down through the bulkhead to the rack, usually via one or two universal joints that let it bend around the pedals and engine. In a frontal crash it telescopes or slides out of its mountings, so the wheel does not spear back towards the driver. It also carries the ignition lock or steering lock, the stalks for lights and wipers, and adjusters for reach and height.
keyNumbers: Collapse stroke typically about 50 to 100 mm
Reach and height adjustment about 40 to 50 mm each
Usually 1 to 2 universal joints
details.madeOf: Steel tubes and shafts, with collapsible sections that slide together or deform under a set force. On many cars the electric power steering motor is mounted on the column itself.

parts.name: Steering column

parts.description: Lid over the camshafts and valves that keeps the oil in.

details.didYouKnow: An old leaking valve cover gasket is a classic cause of a burning-oil smell, as oil drips onto the hot exhaust manifold below.
details.howItWorks: The valve cover sits on top of the cylinder head and seals in the oil that is constantly sprayed over the camshafts and valve gear. Its gasket stops leaks onto the hot exhaust below. It often contains an oil separator for the crankcase ventilation system, which sends fumes from inside the engine back to the intake to be burnt instead of venting them to the air.
keyNumbers: Typically 1 to 2 kg
Gasket handles up to about 120 degrees C
Oil filler cap usually about 40 mm across
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre reinforced nylon or cast aluminium. Plastic is lighter, cheaper and damps valve-train noise, and it can have the breather passages moulded in.

parts.name: Valve cover

parts.description: Aluminium casting on top of the block with the valves, camshafts, spark plugs and combustion chambers.

details.didYouKnow: At 6,000 rpm each valve opens and closes about 50 times a second, so the springs have to slam it shut accurately billions of times over the engine's life.
details.howItWorks: The head closes off the top of the four cylinders and forms the combustion chambers. Two camshafts, turned by a belt or chain from the crankshaft at half its speed, open the intake and exhaust valves at precisely timed moments, and a spark plug in the middle of each chamber lights the squeezed fuel and air. Coolant flows through passages around the hot chambers and exhaust ports to stop them overheating.
keyNumbers: Typically 16 valves, 4 per cylinder
Camshafts turn at half crankshaft speed
Head roughly 10 to 15 kg
Spark plug gap about 0.7 to 1.1 mm
details.madeOf: Cast aluminium alloy, chosen because it is light and conducts heat away quickly. Hardened steel valve seats and guides are pressed in where the valves hit and slide.

parts.name: Cylinder head

parts.description: Main casting containing the four cylinders, coolant passages and crankshaft bearings.

details.didYouKnow: Mounting the engine sideways, as the 1959 Mini popularised, frees up so much space that almost every small and mid-size family car now does it.
details.howItWorks: The block is the backbone of the engine: it holds the four cylinder bores the pistons slide in, carries the crankshaft in main bearings along its bottom, and has water jackets for coolant around the cylinders. Mounted across the car, it sits with its gearbox to one side and the exhaust facing the bulkhead. Rubber engine mounts connect it to the body so vibration is not passed into the cabin.
keyNumbers: 1.5 litres total, about 375 cc per cylinder
Bore typically about 72 to 78 mm
Block roughly 20 to 30 kg in aluminium
Coolant runs at about 90 degrees C
details.madeOf: Cast aluminium alloy, usually with thin cast-iron liners or a sprayed coating in the bores for wear. Aluminium saves a lot of weight over the cast iron used in older engines.

parts.name: Engine block

parts.description: Slides up and down in its cylinder, pushed down by burning fuel and air.

details.didYouKnow: Because the cylinder numbers usually start at the timing belt or chain end, piston 1 is the one a mechanic finds first when setting the engine's timing.
details.howItWorks: Piston 1 is at one end of the engine and starts the firing order 1-3-4-2, so it fires first in each cycle. It moves in step with piston 4: both reach the top together, but when piston 1 is on its power stroke, piston 4 is on its exhaust stroke. Each piston fires once every two turns of the crankshaft, pushing its connecting rod down to turn the crank.
keyNumbers: About 72 to 78 mm across
Roughly 250 to 350 g with pin
Crown up to about 300 degrees C
Peak gas pressure up to about 60 to 100 bar
details.madeOf: Cast or forged aluminium alloy with silicon for low expansion, with steel rings in grooves near the top to seal against the cylinder wall. Aluminium keeps the moving weight low so the engine can rev freely.

parts.name: Piston 1

parts.description: Slides up and down in its cylinder, pushed down by burning fuel and air.

details.didYouKnow: Inline four-cylinder engines have a leftover shake at twice engine speed, which is why some use a pair of counter-rotating balance shafts to cancel it.
details.howItWorks: Piston 2 fires last in the order 1-3-4-2, one half turn of the crankshaft after piston 4. It moves up and down in step with piston 3, so the two pairs (1 and 4, 2 and 3) balance each other's main up-and-down forces. With the four pistons firing evenly every half turn, the crankshaft gets a power stroke every 180 degrees.
keyNumbers: About 72 to 78 mm across
Stroke typically about 80 to 90 mm
Average piston speed up to about 17 m/s near the redline
details.madeOf: Aluminium-silicon alloy with three rings: two compression rings to seal the gas and an oil ring to scrape excess oil off the bore. The skirt is often coated to reduce friction.

parts.name: Piston 2

parts.description: Slides up and down in its cylinder, pushed down by burning fuel and air.

details.didYouKnow: Piston rings are not closed circles; each has a tiny gap so it can spring outwards against the cylinder wall and expand as it heats up.
details.howItWorks: Piston 3 fires second in the order 1-3-4-2, half a crankshaft turn after piston 1. It shares its crank position with piston 2, but the two are always on different strokes of the four-stroke cycle. Its gudgeon pin links it to a steel connecting rod, which converts its straight-line push into twisting force on the crank.
keyNumbers: About 375 cc swept per cylinder
Compression ratio typically about 10 to 12 to 1
Rings about 1 to 1.5 mm tall
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy, cast or forged, with a hollow underside to save weight and sometimes an oil jet spraying underneath to cool the crown.

parts.name: Piston 3

parts.description: Slides up and down in its cylinder, pushed down by burning fuel and air.

details.didYouKnow: At 6,000 rpm each piston stops and reverses direction 200 times a second, briefly experiencing accelerations of more than a thousand times gravity.
details.howItWorks: Piston 4 is at the gearbox end of the engine and fires third in the order 1-3-4-2. It moves exactly in step with piston 1, so when one is starting its power stroke the other is starting to push exhaust gas out. Spreading the firing across both ends of the engine in this order helps keep the crankshaft loads even.
keyNumbers: About 72 to 78 mm across
Fires once every 720 degrees of crank rotation
Up to roughly 50 power strokes a second at 6,000 rpm
details.madeOf: Aluminium-silicon alloy, with a steel gudgeon pin running through it to the connecting rod. Hard anodising or coatings in the top ring groove help it survive the heat.

parts.name: Piston 4

parts.description: Turns the pistons' up-and-down motion into rotation.

details.didYouKnow: The crankshaft never actually touches its bearings when running; it floats on a thin film of pressurised oil only a few thousandths of a millimetre thick.
details.howItWorks: The crankshaft runs along the bottom of the block on five main bearings, with four offset crank pins that the connecting rods grip. As each piston is pushed down, its rod turns the crank like a cyclist's leg on a pedal. One end drives the camshafts and accessories via a belt or chain, and the other end carries the flywheel and clutch that pass the drive to the gearbox.
keyNumbers: Usually 5 main bearings
Roughly 10 to 15 kg
Idles at about 700 to 800 rpm
Redline typically about 6,000 to 6,500 rpm
details.madeOf: Forged steel or cast nodular iron, with the bearing journals induction-hardened and ground very smooth. Counterweights opposite the crank pins balance the rotating mass.

parts.name: Crankshaft

parts.description: Pan under the engine holding about four litres of oil.

details.didYouKnow: The sump is the lowest point of the engine, which is why grounding a car on a rock or high kerb can crack it and drain the oil in seconds.
details.howItWorks: The sump is the oil reservoir at the bottom of the engine. An oil pump draws oil up through a strainer pickup in its lowest point and pushes it through a filter to the crankshaft bearings, camshafts and pistons, after which it drains back down. A drain plug at the bottom lets the oil be changed, and a dipstick tube reaches into it so the level can be checked.
keyNumbers: Holds about 4 litres
Oil pressure typically up to about 4 to 5 bar
Oil changes roughly every 15,000 to 30,000 km or yearly
details.madeOf: Pressed steel or cast aluminium. Steel is cheap and dents rather than cracks if it hits something; aluminium sumps can also stiffen the bottom of the engine.

parts.name: Oil sump

parts.description: Branches that share incoming air between the four cylinders.

details.didYouKnow: Some engines have intake runners that switch length with a flap, using long paths for low-speed pulling power and short ones for high-rpm power.
details.howItWorks: Air drawn through the filter and the throttle valve enters a central plenum, then splits into four runners, one to each cylinder's intake ports. The runners are shaped and sized to use pressure waves in the air to help fill the cylinders at useful engine speeds. Fuel injectors spray petrol either into the runners or straight into the cylinders, mixed to about 14.7 parts air to one part fuel by weight.
keyNumbers: Four runners
Air-fuel ratio about 14.7 to 1 by weight
Up to roughly 4,000 litres of air a minute at full throttle
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre reinforced nylon, moulded in sections and welded together. Plastic is light, has smooth inner walls for good airflow, and stays cooler than metal so the air stays denser.

parts.name: Intake manifold

parts.description: Collects hot exhaust gas from the four cylinders into one pipe.

details.didYouKnow: Exhaust manifolds can visibly glow red during hard running on a test bench, which is why heat shields around them are essential.
details.howItWorks: Each cylinder pushes out a pulse of hot gas when its exhaust valve opens, and the manifold gathers those pulses into a single outlet. On this car it faces back towards the bulkhead and leads almost straight into the catalytic converter, so the converter heats up quickly after a cold start. A heat shield over it protects nearby wiring and hoses.
keyNumbers: Gas up to about 900 degrees C
Typically 3 to 6 kg
Four inlet ports to one outlet
details.madeOf: Cast iron or welded stainless steel tube, both able to survive red-hot temperatures and constant heating and cooling. Some modern engines cast the manifold into the cylinder head instead.

parts.name: Exhaust manifold

parts.description: Six-speed manual transaxle bolted to the engine, with the differential built in.

details.didYouKnow: Reverse gear on many manual boxes has no synchromesh, which is why it can crunch if you select it before the car has fully stopped.
details.howItWorks: The clutch connects the engine to the gearbox input shaft, and the gear lever slides selector forks to lock different pairs of gears to their shafts. Synchromesh rings match shaft speeds before each gear engages, so changes are smooth. Because this is a transaxle, the output gear drives the differential directly, which splits the torque to the two driveshafts and lets the wheels turn at different speeds in corners.
keyNumbers: 6 forward gears and reverse
First about 3.5 to 4 to 1, sixth about 0.7 to 0.8 to 1
Final drive typically about 3.5 to 4.5 to 1
Roughly 35 to 45 kg with about 2 litres of oil
details.madeOf: A cast aluminium casing with hardened steel gears and shafts, running in gear oil. Aluminium keeps the weight down while the gears need the toughness of case-hardened steel.

parts.name: Gearbox

parts.description: Thin aluminium tubes and fins where coolant sheds the engine's waste heat into the passing air.

details.didYouKnow: Roughly a third of the energy in the fuel leaves as heat in the coolant; the cabin heater simply borrows some of it via a second small radiator.
details.howItWorks: A water pump pushes hot coolant from the engine through the radiator's many thin tubes, while air passing through the fins between them carries the heat away. A thermostat keeps coolant away from the radiator until the engine is warm, and an electric fan behind it pulls air through when the car is crawling in traffic. The system is pressurised, which raises the coolant's boiling point well above 100 degrees C.
keyNumbers: Cooling system holds roughly 5 to 7 litres
Cap pressure about 1.1 to 1.4 bar
Coolant boils at about 120 degrees C under pressure
details.madeOf: Brazed aluminium tubes and fins, with plastic end tanks crimped on. Aluminium conducts heat well, resists corrosion with the right coolant and is light.

parts.name: Radiator

parts.description: Starts the engine and powers the electrics when it isn't running.

details.didYouKnow: Car batteries are among the most recycled products in the world; in Europe nearly all of their lead is recovered and reused.
details.howItWorks: The battery delivers a big burst of current to spin the starter motor, then the engine-driven alternator takes over, recharging it and powering the electrics. Six lead-acid cells in series each give about 2.1 volts. On this car it sits at the front left of the engine bay, near the gearbox and starter, keeping the heavy starter cable short.
keyNumbers: About 12.6 V when fully charged
Typically 45 to 70 Ah capacity
Cold cranking roughly 400 to 650 A
Weighs about 13 to 18 kg
details.madeOf: Lead plates in sulphuric acid inside a polypropylene case. Cars with stop-start often use an absorbent glass mat or enhanced flooded design that copes with frequent restarts.

parts.name: 12-volt battery

parts.description: Carries drive from the gearbox to the left front wheel, with a constant-velocity joint at each end.

details.didYouKnow: A rhythmic clicking when turning sharply on full lock is the classic sign of a worn outer constant-velocity joint, usually after its boot has split and let in grit.
details.howItWorks: On this car the gearbox sits on the left, so the left driveshaft is the short one. A plunging joint at the gearbox end lets the shaft change length as the suspension moves, while the fixed ball-type joint at the wheel end allows the wheel to steer and bounce while still being driven smoothly. Rubber boots filled with grease seal both joints.
keyNumbers: Roughly 0.4 to 0.6 m long
Outer joint works up to about 45 to 50 degrees
Carries up to roughly 1,000 Nm in first gear
details.madeOf: A steel shaft, sometimes hollow, with case-hardened steel joint parts and rubber or thermoplastic boots. Steel copes with the twisting loads from first gear.

parts.name: Driveshaft (left)

parts.description: Carries drive from the gearbox to the right front wheel.

details.didYouKnow: The constant-velocity joint lets the wheel turn at an exactly steady speed even at an angle, something an ordinary universal joint cannot do.
details.howItWorks: Because the gearbox is offset to the left, the right driveshaft has further to go to reach its wheel. Many cars fit an intermediate shaft with a support bearing on the engine so the two driveshafts end up near equal length. If they were very unequal, they would twist by different amounts under hard acceleration and tug the steering, an effect called torque steer.
keyNumbers: Roughly 0.7 to 0.9 m long including any intermediate shaft
Two constant-velocity joints
Turns about 500 times per km
details.madeOf: Steel shafts with hardened steel constant-velocity joints, packed with grease and sealed by rubber boots. Some longer shafts include a rubber damper to absorb vibration.

parts.name: Driveshaft (right)

parts.description: Runs under the floor from the engine to the silencer at the back.

details.didYouKnow: Burning a litre of petrol produces roughly a litre of water as vapour, which is why exhausts drip on cold mornings.
details.howItWorks: The pipe carries exhaust gas from the catalytic converter under the floor to the silencer at the back, routed through a tunnel in the floor pan and kept away from the fuel tank. It hangs on rubber mountings so engine movement and vibration are not passed into the body. A flexible braided section near the front lets the engine rock on its mounts without cracking the pipe.
keyNumbers: Typically about 45 to 55 mm across
Around 3 to 4 m of pipe
Usually 3 to 5 rubber hangers
details.madeOf: Stainless or aluminised steel tube. Stainless resists the acidic water that condenses inside the exhaust on short trips, which is what rusts cheap pipes from the inside out.

parts.name: Exhaust pipe

parts.description: Ceramic honeycomb coated with platinum-group metals that cleans the exhaust.

details.didYouKnow: Because of the valuable metals inside, catalytic converters have become a target for thieves, who can cut one off a car in a couple of minutes.
details.howItWorks: Hot exhaust passes through thousands of tiny channels whose walls are coated in platinum, palladium and rhodium. These metals help three reactions happen at once: carbon monoxide and unburnt fuel are oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, and nitrogen oxides are reduced back to nitrogen. Oxygen sensors before and after it let the engine computer keep the fuel mixture just right so all three work.
keyNumbers: Starts working at roughly 250 to 300 degrees C
Often 400 to 600 cells per square inch
Typically a few grams of precious metals
Cuts harmful emissions by over 90% when hot
details.madeOf: A ceramic honeycomb, usually cordierite, with a thin washcoat holding the precious metals, wrapped in an insulating mat inside a stainless steel shell.

parts.name: Catalytic converter

parts.description: Chambers and baffles that quieten the exhaust note.

details.didYouKnow: Many silencers have a tiny drain hole drilled in their lowest point to let condensed water escape before it rusts through.
details.howItWorks: Exhaust leaves the engine in loud pressure pulses. Inside the silencer, perforated tubes and baffles bounce the sound waves back and forth so they partly cancel each other, while packing material soaks up higher frequencies as heat. Designers must quieten the noise without causing so much back pressure that the engine loses power.
