parts.description: Long strip of hydrophones along each side for passive listening at low frequencies.

details.didYouKnow: Low-frequency sound can travel hundreds of kilometres in the deep sound channel, a layer of the ocean where temperature and pressure bend sound back towards the middle.
details.howItWorks: These long strips of hydrophones listen along each side of the boat, where the hull is quietest and away from the bow's flow noise. Because the array is long, it can pick up the deep, low-frequency hum of distant engines and propellers, which travels much further underwater than high-pitched sound. Comparing when a sound reaches different parts of the array also helps estimate how far away its source is.
keyNumbers: Each roughly 15 to 20 m long
2 arrays, one per side
Tuned to low frequencies, often below about 1 kHz
details.madeOf: Piezoelectric sensors in flat panels of polyurethane or rubber, fixed to the casing over sound-isolating mountings so the boat's own vibration does not reach them.

parts.name: Flank sonar array

parts.description: Slim optical periscope raised just above the waves to take a quick look while staying hidden.

details.didYouKnow: Low power is usually about 1.5x rather than 1x because the image seen down a long tube looks smaller than life, and 1.5x makes things appear their natural size.
details.howItWorks: A series of prisms and lenses carries the image down a long tube to an eyepiece in the control room, where the officer walks it round to scan the horizon. The head is very slim to leave only a tiny wake and to be hard to see. It is raised for only a few seconds at a time, just high enough to clear the waves, then lowered again.
keyNumbers: Head roughly 5 to 10 cm across
Low and high power, often about 1.5x and 6x
Exposed for typically a few seconds
details.madeOf: A stainless or high-strength steel tube that must resist bending in the flow, with precision optical glass inside, often filled with dry nitrogen to stop fogging.

parts.name: Attack periscope

parts.description: Camera mast with daylight and thermal sensors that feeds pictures to screens in the control room.

details.didYouKnow: Because optronic masts do not need to pass through the hull, newer designs have moved the control room away from directly under the sail to wherever it fits best.
details.howItWorks: Instead of a long optical tube, this mast carries cameras in its head: a daylight camera, a thermal imager and often a laser rangefinder. It can take a full 360 degree panorama in a second or two, then lower, letting the crew study the recording on screens without keeping the mast up. Only cables pass through the hull, so the mast does not need to reach down into the control room.
keyNumbers: Full sweep in roughly a second or two
Mast roughly 6 m long
Thermal camera sees warm ships at night
details.madeOf: A steel or composite mast with a sealed sensor head, often shaped and coated to reduce radar reflections.

parts.name: Optronic mast

parts.description: Air pipe raised above the surface so the diesels can breathe while the boat stays submerged.

details.didYouKnow: The snorkel was developed in the Netherlands in the 1930s and widely adopted in the Second World War; sailors still call snorkelling snorting, from the German word Schnorchel.
details.howItWorks: Raised just above the waves at periscope depth, the snorkel draws fresh air down to the diesels while a separate pipe carries the exhaust out, usually below the surface. A float or sensor valve at the top slams shut when a wave washes over it, so the sea cannot get in. The diesels then briefly suck air from inside the boat, causing a sharp pressure drop the crew feel in their ears.
keyNumbers: Air pipe roughly 0.5 m across
Snorkel at about 10 to 15 m keel depth
Typically a few hours a day of snorting
details.madeOf: Steel induction pipe with a head valve, often with a radar-absorbing coating. The exhaust mast must tolerate hot, corrosive gases.

parts.name: Snorkel mast

parts.description: Antenna mast for communications and for detecting enemy radar.

details.didYouKnow: Radar has to travel out and back to see you, while ESM only needs the outgoing pulse, so a well-tuned receiver can hear a radar from several times further away than the radar can detect the boat.
details.howItWorks: This mast is raised at periscope depth so its antennas clear the water, letting the boat send and receive radio and satellite messages. The ESM sensors on it listen for radar pulses, telling the crew if an aircraft or ship is searching nearby. ESM works passively and usually detects a radar long before that radar can see the mast.
keyNumbers: Mast roughly 5 m long
Covers frequencies from HF radio up to many GHz
Raised for minutes rather than hours
details.madeOf: A steel mast with antennas in a glass-fibre radome, which lets radio waves through while keeping the sea out.

parts.name: Radio & ESM mast

parts.description: The nerve centre under the sail, with the steering, diving, sonar and weapons consoles.

details.didYouKnow: Control rooms used red lighting at night so that the officer's eyes stayed adapted to the dark before looking through the periscope.
details.howItWorks: From here the crew steer the boat, hold its depth, manage the ballast and trim, and run the sonar and weapons consoles. One or two operators at the ship-control station handle the rudder and planes, often helped by an autopilot. The commanding officer brings all this together, deciding when to raise masts, when to snort and when to attack.
keyNumbers: About 6 m long
Typically 6 to 10 people on watch
Directly under the sail
details.madeOf: Steel consoles on shock-mounted frames, with flat screens and controls; cabinets are bolted to the deck so they survive the jolt of a nearby explosion.

parts.name: Control room

parts.description: Stacked bunks, a galley and mess where about 35 crew live for weeks at a time.

details.didYouKnow: Submarine food is famously good, partly to keep morale high in a crowded steel tube with no daylight for weeks.
details.howItWorks: This compartment packs sleeping, eating and washing into a space smaller than many flats. Bunks are stacked three high with curtains, and on some patrols junior sailors share a bunk in shifts, known as hot bunking. The galley cooks for the whole crew round the clock, and fresh water is made from seawater with distillers or reverse osmosis.
keyNumbers: About 35 crew
Patrols often several weeks long
Bunks roughly 0.6 m wide
details.madeOf: Light aluminium and plastic fittings with fire-resistant fabrics, all chosen to save weight and space and to give off little toxic smoke in a fire.

parts.name: Crew quarters

parts.description: Hundreds of large lead-acid cells under the deck that power everything when submerged.

details.didYouKnow: If seawater floods a battery compartment it can react with the acid to produce chlorine gas, which is one reason batteries are sealed beneath the deck.
details.howItWorks: Each lead-acid cell gives about 2 volts, so hundreds are wired in series to reach the high voltages that run the propulsion motor. The forward bank sits under the deck below the control room and crew spaces, where its great weight helps keep the boat stable. While charging it gives off hydrogen, so powerful ventilation and catalytic burners keep that gas from building up.
keyNumbers: About 2 V per cell
Each cell roughly half a tonne
Typically a couple of hundred cells in this bank
details.madeOf: Lead plates in dilute sulphuric acid inside tough plastic cases. Lead-acid is heavy but cheap, robust and well understood.

parts.name: Forward battery bank

parts.description: Second battery bank; together they give a few days of slow, silent running.

details.didYouKnow: Batteries make up a large share of a diesel-electric boat's weight, so they double as ballast low in the hull, keeping the boat upright.
details.howItWorks: The aft bank sits just behind the forward one and is wired with it so the boat can draw on both, or isolate one if it is damaged. Together they store enough energy for about a few days at slow speed, but only an hour or so near top speed, because drag rises steeply with speed. The captain always balances the need to move fast against draining the batteries and having to snort.
keyNumbers: About 2 V per cell
Roughly 4 knots for a few days
Up to about 20 knots for an hour or so
details.madeOf: Large lead-acid cells like the forward bank, packed tightly with cable runs and cooling between them.

parts.name: Aft battery bank

parts.description: Diesel engine coupled to a generator that recharges the batteries while snorkelling.

details.didYouKnow: Early submarines used petrol engines, but the fumes caused explosions, so diesels, whose fuel is much less volatile, took over in the early 1900s.
details.howItWorks: The forward diesel generator runs when the boat is surfaced or snorting, turning a generator that recharges the batteries and powers the boat. It sits on a raft of shock mounts that soak up vibration so the hull does not ring. The two generators can run together for a fast charge, or one alone if the other is down for maintenance.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1 MW of output
Typically about 1,000 to 1,500 rpm
Weighs several tonnes
details.madeOf: A cast-iron or alloy engine block with steel crankshaft and pistons, coupled to a generator of copper windings in a steel frame.

parts.name: Diesel generator 1

parts.description: Diesel engine coupled to a generator that recharges the batteries while snorkelling.

details.didYouKnow: The fraction of time a submarine must spend snorting to keep its batteries charged is called the indiscretion rate, and lowering it is a key goal of modern designs.
details.howItWorks: The aft diesel generator is the twin of the first and sits a few metres behind it, closer to the propulsion motor. Running both at once roughly halves the time spent snorting, which is when the boat is most likely to be detected. Its exhaust and air pipes run up through the hull to the snorkel mast.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1 MW of output
Typically about 1,000 to 1,500 rpm
About 3 m long
details.madeOf: Like its twin, a cast block with forged steel moving parts, plus a generator, mounted on resilient isolators.

parts.name: Diesel generator 2

parts.description: Large, slow-turning electric motor that drives the propeller shaft directly, with no gearbox to make noise.

details.didYouKnow: Electric motors are so quiet that at slow speeds a diesel-electric submarine on batteries can be quieter than many nuclear submarines, which have to keep their reactor pumps running.
details.howItWorks: This large electric motor turns the propeller shaft directly at the same slow speed as the propeller, so there is no gearbox. Avoiding gears removes a big source of whine that sonar could hear. It takes power from the batteries, or from the diesels while snorting, and its speed is controlled electronically.
keyNumbers: Typically a few MW
Top speed roughly 200 rpm
Weighs tens of tonnes
details.madeOf: Copper windings and steel laminations, often with permanent magnets in the rotor for high efficiency. The frame is built to be very stiff and is shock-mounted.

parts.name: Propulsion motor

parts.description: Steel shaft from the motor out through a sealed gland in the hull to the propeller.

details.didYouKnow: Shafts are balanced and aligned very precisely, because even a slight wobble makes a regular thump that sonar operators can recognise.
details.howItWorks: The shaft carries the motor's twisting force aft and the propeller's push forward. A thrust bearing inside the hull passes that push into the hull structure, which is what actually drives the boat. Where it leaves the pressure hull, it passes through a stern gland and is supported further aft by water-lubricated bearings, so it never needs oil out in the sea.
keyNumbers: Roughly 0.3 m thick
Up to about 200 rpm
Several metres long
details.madeOf: Forged high-strength steel, often sleeved with corrosion-resistant metal where it runs in seawater.

parts.name: Propeller shaft

parts.description: Bronze boss the blades are fixed to.

details.didYouKnow: When submarines are in dry dock, their propellers are often covered in tarpaulins, because the exact blade shape is a closely guarded secret.
details.howItWorks: The hub is the solid centre of the propeller that fits on a tapered end of the shaft and is held on by a large nut. The blades are cast as one piece with it or bolted on, and the hub must carry their full thrust and twisting load into the shaft. A smooth, rounded cap covers the nut so water flows cleanly off the back of the propeller instead of swirling into a noisy vortex.
keyNumbers: About 1 m across
Carries 7 blades
Weighs several tonnes with blades
details.madeOf: Nickel-aluminium bronze, which resists seawater corrosion and is tough and easy to cast in large pieces.

parts.name: Propeller hub

parts.description: One of seven curved, skewed blades shaped to turn slowly without making bubbles that sonar could hear.

details.didYouKnow: Deeper water presses harder on the blades and stops bubbles forming, so a submarine can usually go faster quietly when it is deeper.
details.howItWorks: Each blade is curved back like a scimitar, so different parts of it meet uneven water from the hull at slightly different times, smoothing out pulses of noise. The large size lets the propeller turn slowly while still pushing plenty of water. Turning slowly keeps the pressure on the blades from dropping so low that the water boils into bubbles, called cavitation.
keyNumbers: 7 blades
Propeller roughly 4 m across
Turns at up to about 200 rpm
details.madeOf: Nickel-aluminium bronze, cast and then carefully ground and polished to an exact shape.

parts.name: Propeller blade

summary: A 65 m patrol submarine with a crew of about 35: diesel generators charge large batteries that drive a single electric motor and propeller, so it can run almost silently underwater for days.

name: Crewed Spacecraft
overview:
A crewed spacecraft is a small, self-contained world that keeps people alive in space and brings them home. It's launched on top of a rocket, then flies itself: it has its own engines to change orbit, solar panels for power, and supplies of oxygen, water and propellant for missions lasting days to weeks.

It comes in two parts. The crew capsule is the cone where the astronauts sit, a sealed pressure vessel with seats, controls, windows and a docking port on top for joining a space station. Below it, the service module carries what the capsule can't: the main engine, propellant tanks, steering thrusters, solar wings and radiators that dump waste heat into space.

Coming home is the dangerous part. Just before re-entry the service module is cast off to burn up, and the capsule hits the atmosphere blunt end first. Its heat shield slowly chars and flakes away, carrying off heat as air in front of it glows at around 2,700 °C. Lower down, small drogue parachutes steady it, the big main parachutes slow it to about 30 km/h, and it splashes down in the sea.

parts.description: Ring-shaped docking system on the nose that latches onto a space station and forms an airtight tunnel.

details.didYouKnow: Apollo used a probe that poked into a cone on the lunar module; today's androgynous docking rings are identical on both sides, so any two spacecraft with the standard ring can join up.
details.howItWorks: As the spacecraft creeps towards a station, a soft-capture ring on springy, motor-driven struts reaches out, absorbs the bump and hooks onto the matching ring on the other side. The struts then pull the two vehicles together, and a circle of hooks clamps them tight against rubber seals. Once the gap between the two hatches is checked for leaks, the crew can open up and float through.
keyNumbers: Passage about 80 cm across
Closing speed typically a few cm per second
Around a dozen structural hooks
details.madeOf: Machined aluminium and steel rings with steel latches and hooks, chosen to stay strong and precise through big temperature swings. The seals are silicone rubber that stays flexible in the cold of space.

parts.name: Docking port

parts.description: Protective cap over the parachutes, thrown off high in the atmosphere so they can deploy.

details.didYouKnow: On Apollo this part was called the forward heat shield, and it had its own little parachute so it would not drift back down onto the capsule's chutes.
details.howItWorks: During launch and re-entry the cover shields the parachutes and docking hardware from heat and air pressure. Once the capsule has slowed below the speed of sound and dropped to several kilometres up, small thrusters or springs push it off and a little parachute pulls it clear. Only then is there an open path for the drogue and main parachutes to fire out of the nose.
keyNumbers: Jettisoned at roughly 7 to 8 km altitude
About 3 m across
Gone within a second or two of the command
details.madeOf: A lightweight composite or aluminium shell covered in the same kind of heat-resistant tiles or ablative coating as the rest of the capsule. It has to be tough but light, since it is thrown away on every flight.

parts.name: Forward bay cover

parts.description: Tightly packed main parachute; three of them open to about 35 m across and slow the capsule to around 30 km/h.

details.didYouKnow: Apollo 15 lost one of its three main parachutes on the way down and landed safely on the remaining two, exactly as the designers had planned for.
details.howItWorks: Once the drogues have slowed and steadied the capsule, small pilot chutes pull the mains out of their bags. Each canopy first opens only partly, held in by cords that are cut in stages, so the jolt on the capsule is spread over several seconds instead of arriving all at once. The three canopies share the load, but the capsule can still splash down safely on two.
keyNumbers: About 35 m across when open
Typically opened around 2 to 3 km up
Each pack weighs well over 100 kg
Splashdown speed about 30 km/h
details.madeOf: Nylon canopy fabric with strong Kevlar or nylon suspension lines and risers. The whole chute is packed into a bag at very high pressure, almost as dense as wood.

parts.name: Main parachute pack

parts.description: Small, tough parachute fired out first at high speed to steady the capsule before the mains open.

details.didYouKnow: A capsule is designed to be stable when falling base-first, but it could also be stable upside-down; one job of the drogues is to make sure it settles the right way up.
details.howItWorks: The drogues are fired out by mortars while the capsule is still falling fast, at around the speed of a racing car. Their small size keeps the opening shock bearable, and they stop the capsule tumbling or swinging so it hangs nose-up and steady. When the speed has dropped enough they are cut loose, pulling the pilot chutes that bring out the mains.
keyNumbers: Roughly 5 to 7 m across
Fired out at several hundred km/h
Deployed at roughly 7 km altitude
details.madeOf: Heavy nylon and Kevlar fabric with very strong lines, because they open at much higher speeds than the mains. Mortar-firing means they deploy instantly and cleanly into the airflow.

parts.name: Drogue parachute pack

parts.description: Outer skin of the cone, covered in heat-resistant tiles; it sees less heating than the shield because it faces away from the flow.

details.didYouKnow: Apollo capsules were wrapped in shiny metallised tape to keep them cool in space; it burned off during re-entry, which is why returned capsules look scorched and brown.
details.howItWorks: The backshell forms the sloping sides of the cone and sits in the wake behind the heat shield during re-entry. Because the hot shock wave forms in front of the blunt base, the sides see far gentler heating, so thinner protection is enough. The panels also carry mounting points and openings for the windows, hatch and capsule thrusters.
keyNumbers: Peak surface heating up to roughly 1,000 °C
Often hundreds of tiles in total
Covers most of the capsule's outside area
details.madeOf: A metal or composite shell covered in silica-fibre tiles, a cousin of the Space Shuttle's tiles, or thin ablative material. These insulate superbly for their weight, which matters because the cone has a large surface area.

parts.name: Backshell panel

parts.description: Multi-pane window of fused silica and toughened glass, each pane able to hold cabin pressure on its own.

details.didYouKnow: The famous Earthrise photograph was taken by Bill Anders through a small window of the Apollo 8 capsule as it orbited the Moon in 1968.
details.howItWorks: Each window is a stack of panes with gaps between them. The outer pane faces the heat of re-entry, while the inner panes are the ones that hold the cabin air in, and each can do so even if another cracks. The crew use the windows to watch docking approaches, check the capsule's attitude by eye and take photographs.
keyNumbers: Typically 3 panes per window
Outer pane faces gases of over 1,000 °C
Each pane holds about 1 atmosphere on its own
details.madeOf: Fused silica for the outer pane, because it shrugs off sudden heating without cracking, and toughened or chemically strengthened glass for the pressure panes. Coatings cut glare and block ultraviolet light.

parts.name: Window

parts.description: Small rocket that steers the capsule after it separates, keeping the heat shield pointed the right way during re-entry.

details.didYouKnow: On the Apollo-Soyuz mission in 1975, a switch left in the wrong position let thruster propellant fumes into the cabin during descent, and the crew needed treatment after splashdown.
details.howItWorks: The capsule's centre of mass is set slightly off-centre, so it flies through the atmosphere at a slight angle and produces some lift. By firing these thrusters to roll the capsule, the computer points that lift up, down or sideways, steering towards the landing spot and easing the g-forces. They also keep the heat shield facing forwards and damp out any wobble.
keyNumbers: Typically 12 thrusters in total
Each a few hundred newtons of thrust
Pulses as short as a few hundredths of a second
details.madeOf: Small steel and niobium-alloy rocket thrusters fed by their own propellant tanks inside the capsule. They have to survive being buried in a hot, ablating skin and still fire reliably.

parts.name: Capsule thruster

parts.description: Main door the crew climb through on the launch pad and after splashdown.

details.didYouKnow: After the Apollo 1 fire in 1967, NASA replaced the slow inward-opening two-part hatch with a single outward-opening one that the crew could open in seconds.
details.howItWorks: The hatch is a thick plug door with an outer heat-protected panel and an inner pressure door, held shut by a ring of latches worked from a single handle. Seals around the edge stop the cabin air escaping. It opens outwards, so in an emergency on the pad or after splashdown it can be flung open quickly without fighting the air pressure inside.
keyNumbers: About 1 m across
Designed to open in well under a minute
Apollo's redesigned hatch opened in under 10 seconds
details.madeOf: Aluminium or titanium structure with an ablative or tiled outer face matching the backshell around it. Every hinge and latch is designed to keep working after the jolts of launch and splashdown.

parts.name: Side hatch

parts.description: Welded aluminium-lithium shell that holds breathable air at sea-level pressure; everything inside it is the crew's living space.

details.didYouKnow: In space, Apollo cabins held pure oxygen at about a third of sea-level pressure; modern capsules use ordinary air at full sea-level pressure, which is safer from fire.
details.howItWorks: This sealed inner shell is the real boundary between the crew and the vacuum of space. It carries the push of the cabin air outwards, plus the loads of launch, re-entry and splashdown, while the heat shield and backshell bolt onto its outside. Every pipe and cable that passes through it has to go through a sealed fitting.
keyNumbers: Holds about 1 atmosphere (101 kPa)
Roughly 10 m³ of living space for four people
Leak rate typically a tiny fraction of the air per day
details.madeOf: Aluminium-lithium alloy, machined into large panels and welded together. Adding lithium makes aluminium both lighter and stiffer, saving weight on a part that has to be very strong.

parts.name: Pressure vessel

parts.description: Contoured couch the astronaut lies back in for launch and landing, cushioning the forces through the whole body.

details.didYouKnow: Being nearest the hatch, the outer-seat crew member is often the first one out after splashdown, helped by recovery teams opening the door from outside.
details.howItWorks: Seat 1 is an outer seat, usually for a mission specialist, next to the side hatch. Lying on their back, the astronaut feels launch and re-entry forces pushing them into the seat chest-to-back, which the body tolerates far better than forces along the spine. Shock-absorbing struts under the seat soften the jolt of splashdown.
keyNumbers: Launch loads around 3 to 4 g
Lunar return re-entry typically 4 to 7 g
Five-point harness
details.madeOf: A carbon-fibre or aluminium frame with a foam liner moulded to the individual astronaut's body, covered in fire-resistant fabric. A custom fit spreads the load evenly across the whole body.

parts.name: Crew seat 1

parts.description: Contoured couch the astronaut lies back in for launch and landing, cushioning the forces through the whole body.

details.didYouKnow: On Apollo, the commander sat in the left seat and the command module pilot in the middle; on four-seat capsules the commander and pilot moved to the middle pair, closest to the screens.
details.howItWorks: Seat 2 is one of the two middle seats, typically the commander's, placed right in front of the main displays and hand controllers. From here the commander can take over steering by hand during docking or if the automatic systems fail. Like all the seats, it holds the body flat so g-forces press chest-to-back rather than draining blood from the head.
keyNumbers: Within arm's reach of the main controls
Re-entry loads typically 4 to 7 g
Seat strokes several centimetres on impact
details.madeOf: A stiff composite or aluminium frame with a body-moulded foam liner and fire-resistant fabric cover. The frame is mounted on energy-absorbing struts that stroke on a hard landing.

parts.name: Crew seat 2

parts.description: Contoured couch the astronaut lies back in for launch and landing, cushioning the forces through the whole body.

details.didYouKnow: Each astronaut's seat liner is shaped to their own body, sometimes from a full-body mould, because a perfect fit lets the body survive higher g-forces without injury.
details.howItWorks: Seat 3 is the other middle seat, usually the pilot's, who shares the controls with the commander and handles many systems tasks. Both middle seats face the same bank of displays so either can fly the spacecraft. The seat carries the astronaut's body through the same g-forces as the rest of the crew, spreading them across the back, legs and head.
keyNumbers: Facing displays about 1 m away
Launch loads around 3 to 4 g
Five-point harness
details.madeOf: Composite or aluminium frame with a custom foam liner and flame-resistant fabric. Lightweight materials matter because every kilogram in the capsule has to be carried to the Moon and back.

parts.name: Crew seat 3

parts.description: Contoured couch the astronaut lies back in for launch and landing, cushioning the forces through the whole body.

details.didYouKnow: Astronauts grow up to a few centimetres taller in weightlessness as their spine stretches, so seats and suits are fitted with that extra height in mind for the trip home.
details.howItWorks: Seat 4 is the far outer seat, typically for a mission specialist who monitors systems and runs experiments. It is the same kind of reclined couch as the others, held on struts that soak up the shock of splashdown. Once in space, seats can often be folded or stowed to make more room for living and working.
keyNumbers: Launch loads around 3 to 4 g
Re-entry loads typically 4 to 7 g
Splashdown at about 30 km/h
details.madeOf: Composite or aluminium frame, body-moulded foam and fire-resistant fabric, the same build as the other seats. Its custom liner is changed for each new crew member.

parts.name: Crew seat 4

parts.description: Glass screens and switches that let the crew monitor every system and fly the spacecraft by hand.

details.didYouKnow: The Apollo guidance computer had about 4 KB of working memory, and its programs were stored in rope memory woven by hand through tiny magnetic rings.
details.howItWorks: A few large screens show the state of every system, from propellant and power to cabin air, and can switch between pages of information. Physical switches and hand controllers sit alongside them for critical actions and manual flying, because they work even if the screens fail. Behind the panel, flight computers talk to the thrusters, engines and sensors throughout the spacecraft.
keyNumbers: Typically 3 main displays
Hundreds of switches and buttons in older capsules
Backup computers running in parallel
details.madeOf: Ruggedised flat-panel displays and switches in a moulded plastic or composite housing, built to survive vibration, radiation and big temperature changes. Everything is tested so nothing breaks loose and floats around.

parts.name: Display & control panel

parts.description: Scrubs carbon dioxide, adds oxygen and controls humidity and temperature in the cabin.

details.didYouKnow: On Apollo 13, the crew had to make square carbon dioxide filters from the command module fit round sockets in the lunar module, using card, plastic bags and tape.
details.howItWorks: Cabin air is constantly drawn through the unit by fans. A chemical bed soaks up the carbon dioxide the crew breathe out, fresh oxygen is fed in from tanks, and a cold heat exchanger condenses excess moisture out of the air. Warm coolant is piped away to the service module radiators, keeping the cabin comfortable.
keyNumbers: Each person breathes out about 1 kg of CO2 a day
Each person uses roughly 0.8 kg of oxygen a day
Cabin kept at about 20 to 25 °C
details.madeOf: Plastic and metal housings containing fans, valves, sensors and absorbent beds. Older capsules used throwaway lithium hydroxide canisters; newer ones use a regenerable bed that dumps carbon dioxide to space and is reused.

parts.name: Life support unit

parts.description: Blunt dish on the base that faces the fire of re-entry; its surface chars and erodes away, carrying heat with it.

details.didYouKnow: After the uncrewed Artemis I flight in 2022, engineers were surprised to find chunks of charred material had broken away from Orion's heat shield, prompting a long investigation.
details.howItWorks: The blunt shape pushes a thick shock wave out in front of the capsule, and most of the heat stays in that glowing layer of gas rather than reaching the surface. What does reach the shield makes its resin char, boil off gases and slowly wear away, carrying the heat with it. Underneath, the structure and the crew stay at a comfortable temperature.
keyNumbers: About 5 m across
Surface reaches roughly 2,800 °C
A few centimetres thick
Hit at about 40,000 km/h
details.madeOf: An ablative material such as Avcoat, a resin filled with silica fibres, or PICA, a carbon-fibre material soaked in resin, laid over a strong carrier structure. Ablators are used because they protect by being sacrificed, which suits a one-time lunar return.

parts.name: Heat shield

parts.description: Ring joining the capsule to the service module, carrying power, data and coolant lines across until separation.

details.didYouKnow: When the Apollo 13 crew jettisoned their crippled service module, they saw for the first time that an entire side panel had been blown off by the oxygen tank explosion.
details.howItWorks: The adapter holds the capsule firmly on top of the service module through launch and the whole journey. Electrical cables, data lines and coolant pipes run through it so the service module can power and cool the capsule. Shortly before re-entry, the lines are disconnected and separation bolts fire, letting the service module drift away to burn up.
keyNumbers: About 5 m across at the capsule end
Separation roughly 20 minutes before re-entry
Carries power and coolant for weeks of flight
details.madeOf: Machined aluminium alloy, chosen because it is light, stiff and easy to work into precise rings and brackets. Separation hardware uses pyrotechnic bolts or nuts that release on command.

parts.name: Crew module adapter

parts.description: Curved outer panel that doubles as a radiator, shedding the spacecraft's waste heat into space.

details.didYouKnow: In space, the side facing the Sun can be over 100 °C while the shaded side drops far below freezing, so spacecraft often roll slowly to even out the temperature.
details.howItWorks: Coolant from the capsule and electronics flows through channels bonded to the inside of these panels. The heat spreads across the outer surface and radiates away as infrared light, the only way to get rid of heat in a vacuum. Valves can bypass the radiators when the spacecraft is cold, so it does not freeze in shadow.
keyNumbers: Service module about 4 m across
Rejects several kW of heat
Coolant loop typically a water-glycol or similar fluid
details.madeOf: Aluminium skin with embedded or bonded tubes, painted with a special white coating. That coating reflects most sunlight while still radiating heat well.

parts.name: Service module skin panel

parts.description: Fold-out wing covered in solar cells; four of them give about 11 kW in sunlight and can turn to track the Sun.

details.didYouKnow: Apollo had no solar panels at all; it made electricity in fuel cells that combined hydrogen and oxygen, and the water they produced was used for drinking.
details.howItWorks: Each wing is a long panel of solar cells that turn sunlight directly into electricity. Power flows back through the hinge and into the service module, where it charges batteries and is passed up through the adapter to the capsule. Because the cells only work in sunlight, batteries carry the spacecraft through any time spent in shadow.
keyNumbers: About 11 kW from all four wings
Each wing roughly 7 m long
Cells about 30 percent efficient
Thousands of cells in total
details.madeOf: Triple-junction gallium arsenide solar cells on lightweight composite panels that fold up for launch. These cells convert a much larger share of sunlight into power than household silicon panels.

parts.name: Solar array wing

parts.description: Motorised hinge that unfolds the wing after launch and swivels it towards the Sun.

details.didYouKnow: Before big engine burns, the wings can be swung back to reduce the strain on them, then returned to face the Sun once the burn is over.
details.howItWorks: For launch the wings are folded flat against the service module and held by restraints. In orbit the restraints release and the hinge swings each wing out and locks it. A motor in the drive then turns the wing to face the Sun as the spacecraft moves, passing power across the rotating joint.
keyNumbers: Wings unfold within about an hour of launch
Can typically turn on two axes
Moves very slowly, a fraction of a degree per second
details.madeOf: Steel and titanium gears, bearings and shafts, with dry lubricants that will not evaporate or freeze in vacuum. Slip rings or flexible cables carry power across the moving joint.

parts.name: Solar wing hinge & drive

parts.description: Tank of storable propellant; one pair holds fuel and the other oxidiser, which ignite on contact.

details.didYouKnow: Apollo's service module carried around 18 tonnes of propellant, more than half the whole spacecraft's weight, to get into and out of lunar orbit.
details.howItWorks: Two tanks hold fuel and two hold oxidiser, and helium pressure pushes the liquids out towards the engines. Inside, metal vanes use surface tension to keep liquid at the outlet even in weightlessness, so no gas bubbles reach the engines. The two propellants burst into flame the instant they meet, so no spark is needed.
keyNumbers: About 2,000 litres each
Total propellant typically around 8 to 9 tonnes
Propellant can be stored for months or years
details.madeOf: Titanium or aluminium alloy, formed and welded into strong, light tanks. The metal is chosen to resist the very corrosive oxidiser for months on end.

parts.name: Propellant tank

parts.description: Carbon-wrapped sphere of high-pressure helium that pushes propellant from the tanks into the engines.

details.didYouKnow: Helium is used because it is light, never reacts with the propellants and stays a gas even at extremely low temperatures, so it will not freeze in space.
details.howItWorks: The helium is stored at very high pressure and released through regulators that drop it to a steady, lower pressure. That gas fills the space above the propellant in the tanks and pushes the liquids into the engine feed lines, doing the job a pump would do. Check valves stop propellant vapour flowing back into the helium system.
keyNumbers: Pressure up to roughly 300 bar
Several times stronger than its working pressure
About 1 m across
details.madeOf: A thin titanium or aluminium liner wrapped in carbon fibre and resin, called a composite overwrapped pressure vessel. The carbon wrap carries most of the pressure at a fraction of the weight of solid metal.

parts.name: Helium pressurant tank

parts.description: One of eight backup engines around the base that trim the trajectory and can take over if the main engine fails.

details.didYouKnow: The design these engines are based on, the R-4D, first flew as a steering thruster on Apollo's service module and lunar module in the 1960s.
details.howItWorks: These engines share the same propellant tanks as the main engine. They fire for small course corrections and to settle propellant at the bottom of the tanks before the main engine lights. If the main engine fails, they can fire together to perform the critical burns and bring the crew home, more slowly.
keyNumbers: About 500 N of thrust each
8 engines, about 4 kN together
Fire for seconds to minutes at a time
details.madeOf: Steel and niobium or platinum-alloy combustion chambers and nozzles that tolerate heat and repeated firing. They are a long-proven design used on many spacecraft.

parts.name: Auxiliary engine

parts.description: Cluster of small thrusters that turn and nudge the spacecraft for docking and pointing.

details.didYouKnow: Apollo's service module had four boxes of four thrusters, called quads, and the same arrangement shows up on many spacecraft today.
details.howItWorks: Each pod holds several small thrusters pointing in different directions. Fired in pairs on opposite pods, they rotate the spacecraft about any axis; fired the same way, they push it gently sideways, forwards or back. This fine control is what lets the crew line up the docking port with a station to within a few centimetres.
keyNumbers: About 220 N per thruster
Typically 4 to 6 thrusters per pod
Pulse lengths down to a few hundredths of a second
details.madeOf: Metal thrusters on an aluminium mounting frame inside a heat-protective cover. Short, quick pulses mean the valves have to open and close millions of times reliably.

parts.name: Thruster pod

parts.description: Gimballed rocket engine for the big manoeuvres: entering and leaving lunar orbit and heading home.

details.didYouKnow: The main engine on the first uncrewed Orion lunar mission was a refurbished Space Shuttle manoeuvring engine that had already flown on Shuttle missions.
details.howItWorks: Fuel and oxidiser are fed into the combustion chamber, where they ignite on contact and blast out of the bell-shaped nozzle. The engine sits on a gimbal, so actuators tilt it a few degrees to keep the thrust pointed through the spacecraft's centre of mass as propellant is used up. It needs no pumps or igniter, which makes it simple and dependable.
keyNumbers: About 27 kN of thrust
Gimbals a few degrees each way
Burns can last up to several minutes
details.madeOf: A combustion chamber of high-temperature alloy, often niobium or nickel based, with a nozzle extension of niobium alloy. These metals stay strong while glowing red hot.

parts.name: Main engine

parts.description: Structural deck that the engines, tanks and wiring are mounted to.

details.didYouKnow: On Orion, the service module is built in Europe by the European Space Agency, the first time Europe supplied a critical system for a NASA crew vehicle.
details.howItWorks: This deck is the backbone of the service module. It carries the engines, tanks, pipework and wiring, and passes the weight of the whole spacecraft down to the rocket during launch. During engine burns, it takes the push from the main engine and spreads it into the rest of the structure.
keyNumbers: About 4 m across
Carries several g during launch
Supports tonnes of propellant and hardware
details.madeOf: Machined or cast aluminium alloy, often with ribbed or honeycomb sections, giving high stiffness for little weight. Its precise mounting points keep engines and tanks aligned.

parts.name: Service module floor

summary: A four-seat spacecraft for trips to the Moon and back: a cone-shaped crew capsule that survives re-entry at 40,000 km/h, riding on a service module that supplies power, air and propulsion and is discarded before landing.

name: Sailing Yacht
overview:
A sailing yacht is a boat that uses the wind to move, including into the wind at an angle, which surprises most people. Its sails aren't just bags that catch the breeze: they're curved wings. Air flowing around their curve creates lift, the same force that holds up an aircraft, and that lift pulls the boat forwards and sideways.

Below the water, the keel stops the sideways part. It's a deep fin that resists sliding through the water, so the boat goes forward instead of drifting downwind, and its heavy lead bulb at the bottom keeps the boat upright against the push of the wind on the sails. Together, sails and keel let a yacht sail about 45 degrees off the wind; to go straight upwind it zigzags, which sailors call tacking.

This one is a sloop: one mast carrying a mainsail behind it, on a boom, and a jib in front. Wire stays and shrouds hold the mast up, ropes called sheets trim the sails through winches, and the helmsman steers with a wheel connected to the rudder. Inside the hull are berths, a galley, fresh water and fuel tanks, and a small diesel engine for getting in and out of harbour.

parts.description: Glass-fibre shell shaped to slip through the water; its curved sides give stability as it heels.

details.didYouKnow: A displacement hull has a natural speed limit set by its waterline length: in knots it is about 1.34 times the square root of the waterline length in feet, roughly 7 knots for a boat this size.
details.howItWorks: The hull is a stiff, watertight shell that floats the whole boat by pushing aside its own weight of water. When the wind heels the yacht, the wide, rounded sides dip in on one side and lift on the other, shifting the centre of buoyancy outwards so the boat resists tipping further. Inside, a moulded grid of floors and frames spreads the big point loads from the keel, mast and rigging into the shell.
keyNumbers: About 10 m long overall
Roughly 3.3 to 3.5 m beam at its widest
Hull shell typically 8 to 15 mm thick below the waterline
Displacement about 5 to 6 tonnes
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre reinforced plastic: layers of glass cloth soaked in polyester or vinyl ester resin and laid into a polished female mould. It is strong, does not rot or rust, and one mould can make hundreds of identical hulls.

parts.name: Hull

parts.description: Painted underwater band that stops weed and barnacles growing on the hull.

details.didYouKnow: Wooden warships of the 1700s were sheathed in copper to stop shipworm and weed, which is said to be the origin of the phrase 'copper-bottomed' for something completely reliable.
details.howItWorks: Antifouling paint slowly releases biocides, usually copper compounds, into a thin layer of water right against the hull, so weed spores and barnacle larvae cannot settle. Many modern paints are self-polishing: the surface wears away gradually as the boat moves, always exposing fresh biocide. A clean bottom matters because even a light coat of slime or weed can make the hull noticeably slower and the engine burn more fuel.
keyNumbers: Typically 2 to 3 coats each season
Roughly 2.5 to 4 litres per coat on a 10 m yacht
Usually a few centimetres above the waterline
details.madeOf: A resin binder loaded with cuprous oxide and booster biocides, applied over an epoxy barrier coat that keeps water out of the glass-fibre. It is usually redone every year or two.

parts.name: Antifouling band

parts.description: Flat stern panel, often with a swim ladder; the boat's name is painted here.

details.didYouKnow: Painting the name and home port on the transom is a long seafaring tradition, and in many countries a registered yacht is required to show them there.
details.howItWorks: The transom closes off the back of the hull and ties the two sides and the deck together at the stern, stiffening the whole aft end. On this yacht it also anchors the backstay chainplate, so it carries part of the load that holds the mast up. Many cruising boats have a stepped or drop-down transom that makes a bathing platform and makes boarding from a dinghy easier.
keyNumbers: About 2.5 m wide at deck level
Swim ladder typically 3 to 4 steps
Backstay load up to several hundred kg
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre laminate, usually cored with foam or balsa and reinforced where fittings like the backstay plate and ladder are bolted through. The core adds stiffness without much weight.

parts.name: Transom

parts.description: Deep fin under the hull that resists sideways drift so the boat sails forward, not downwind.

details.didYouKnow: A keel only produces sideways lift when the boat makes leeway, so every sailing yacht slides a few degrees sideways as it goes, typically about 3 to 5 degrees upwind.
details.howItWorks: As the boat moves slightly sideways through the water, the keel meets the flow at a small angle and acts like an underwater wing, producing lift that pushes back against the sideways force from the sails. A deep, narrow fin does this efficiently with little drag, which lets the yacht point closer to the wind. It also holds the ballast bulb low down, turning the bulb's weight into a righting lever.
keyNumbers: Draft about 2 m from waterline to keel tip
Fin roughly 1.2 to 1.5 m deep below the hull
Typically 10 to 15 cm thick
details.madeOf: Usually cast iron or lead, sometimes a fabricated steel fin, faired with filler and painted. Iron is cheaper and stiff; lead is denser and gentler if the keel hits the ground.

parts.name: Fin keel

parts.description: Torpedo of lead at the bottom of the keel; its weight, low down, keeps the yacht upright.

details.didYouKnow: A well-ballasted keelboat like this is self-righting: knocked flat, the lead pulls the mast back up, and most yachts can recover even from about 110 to 130 degrees of heel.
details.howItWorks: When the sails push the boat over, the heavy bulb swings up to windward and its weight pulls back down, creating a righting moment that grows as the boat heels further. Putting the weight in a bulb at the very bottom of the fin gives the longest lever arm, so the same mass does more work. The streamlined torpedo shape keeps drag low and adds a little extra lift at the keel tip.
keyNumbers: Ballast roughly 1.5 to 2 tonnes
About 30 to 35 percent of the boat's weight
Lead density about 11.3 tonnes per cubic metre
details.madeOf: Cast lead, often hardened with a little antimony. Lead is very dense, so a lot of weight fits in a small, low shape, and it is soft enough to dent rather than crack on a rock.

parts.name: Lead ballast bulb

parts.description: Row of stainless studs that clamp the keel to a stiffened section of the hull floor.

details.didYouKnow: Hard groundings are the main enemy of keel bolts, which is why surveyors check for rust weeping and cracks at the keel joint, often called a 'keel smile'.
details.howItWorks: Threaded studs are cast or screwed into the top of the keel, pass up through the hull bottom and are tightened with large nuts and backing plates inside the bilge. They clamp the keel's flat top hard against a stub on the hull, so the joint carries the huge sideways bending load when the boat heels. A grid of glassed-in floors spreads that load across the hull bottom.
keyNumbers: Typically 6 to 10 bolts
Roughly 20 to 30 mm diameter each
Tightened to several hundred newton-metres
details.madeOf: Stainless steel or sometimes galvanised mild steel, with stainless washers and backing plates. Stainless resists rust in a wet bilge but must be inspected because it can corrode where starved of oxygen.

parts.name: Keel bolts

parts.description: Balanced blade behind the keel that steers the boat; part of it sits ahead of its pivot so the helm feels light.

details.didYouKnow: A rudder only works while water flows over it, so a yacht with no speed through the water cannot steer at all, a common surprise when manoeuvring slowly in a marina.
details.howItWorks: The rudder is a symmetrical foil on a vertical stock that runs up through the hull to the steering quadrant. Turning it puts the blade at an angle to the water flow, creating lift that pushes the stern sideways and swings the bow round. Because a spade rudder hangs free with no skeg, a slice of blade ahead of the stock balances the water pressure, making the wheel light to turn.
keyNumbers: Blade about 1.2 m deep
Roughly 15 to 20 percent of the area ahead of the stock
Turns about 35 degrees each way
details.madeOf: Two glass-fibre half-shells filled with foam around a stainless or aluminium stock and internal web. The stock carries all the bending load into bearings in the hull.

parts.name: Spade rudder

parts.description: Two-blade propeller whose blades fold flat when sailing to cut drag.

details.didYouKnow: Propellers turning in one direction push the stern sideways in reverse, an effect called prop walk, which sailors learn to use to tuck the boat neatly into a berth.
details.howItWorks: Under engine the spinning hub flings the hinged blades open by centrifugal force, and the thrust of the water keeps them out. When the engine stops, the flow of water past the boat folds the blades back together into a slim, streamlined shape. A fixed propeller left in the water can add noticeable drag, so folding versions are popular on cruisers that sail a lot.
keyNumbers: Diameter about 35 to 40 cm
2 blades
Can cut sailing drag by up to about 1 knot compared with a fixed prop
details.madeOf: Cast bronze, nickel-aluminium bronze or a similar marine copper alloy. These resist corrosion in seawater and are protected further by a zinc anode on the shaft.

parts.name: Folding propeller

parts.description: Moulded sandwich deck bonded to the hull along the gunwale; its non-slip surface keeps crew footing.

details.didYouKnow: Leaky deck fittings are the classic problem on older yachts: water gets into a balsa core and rots it, which is why builders now pot fittings in solid epoxy.
details.howItWorks: The deck closes the hull into a stiff box, much like a lid makes a shoebox far harder to twist. It is bonded and bolted to the hull at the hull-to-deck joint, and it carries the loads from winches, cleats, chainplates and the mast. The moulded non-slip pattern gives grip even when wet and heeled.
keyNumbers: Typically 20 to 25 mm thick
Roughly 25 square metres of area
Hull-to-deck joint about 30 m round
details.madeOf: A sandwich of two thin glass-fibre skins either side of a balsa or foam core. The core spaces the skins apart, which makes the deck very stiff for little weight.

parts.name: Deck

parts.description: Raised cabin top that gives standing headroom below, with windows letting light into the saloon.

details.didYouKnow: Many cruising yachts step the mast on deck like this rather than down to the keel, which keeps the cabin dry and makes it simpler to lower the mast.
details.howItWorks: The coachroof lifts part of the deck up so people can stand inside without making the whole hull taller. Its flat top carries the mast step on this yacht, with a compression post below transferring the huge downward load from the rig to the keel area. Ropes from the mast are often led aft along it to clutches near the cockpit.
keyNumbers: Gives about 1.8 to 1.9 m headroom below
Raised roughly 40 to 50 cm above the deck
Mast compression load up to several tonnes
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre sandwich moulded as part of the deck. Extra laminate is added under the mast step to stop it crushing.

parts.name: Coachroof

parts.description: Long acrylic window in the coachroof side.

details.didYouKnow: The word port for the left side comes from boats tying up with that side to the harbour wall, so the steering oar on the other side stayed clear.
details.howItWorks: This window lights the left-hand side of the saloon and, on this layout, the galley area below it. It is bonded and screwed into a cut-out in the coachroof side, with sealant keeping water out. On starboard tack the port side is the low, leeward side, so this window often has the sea rushing past just below it.
keyNumbers: About 1.5 m long
Typically 8 to 10 mm thick
Sealant usually needs renewing every 10 to 15 years
details.madeOf: Tinted cast acrylic, bonded with flexible marine sealant. Acrylic is lighter and much tougher than glass, and the tint keeps the saloon cool.

parts.name: Saloon window (port)

parts.description: Geared drum that multiplies the crew's pull so they can trim a jib sheet loaded with hundreds of kilos.

details.didYouKnow: Racing yachts once used open-handled coffee grinder winches worked by two crew at once; the same idea drives the sails of today's America's Cup boats.
details.howItWorks: The jib sheet is wrapped clockwise around the drum, and a crew member turns a removable handle on top. Inside, gears give two speeds: fast for pulling in slack and slow for powerful final trimming. A ratchet stops the drum running backwards, and a self-tailing jaw on top grips the rope. This port winch does the work when the jib sits on the port side, which happens on starboard tack.
keyNumbers: Power ratio roughly 30 to 40 to 1 in low gear
Handle about 25 cm long
Jib sheet load typically up to 300 to 500 kg
details.madeOf: A chromed bronze or anodised aluminium drum over stainless steel and bronze gears. The metals resist seawater and the drum surface is textured to grip the rope.

parts.name: Sheet winch (port)

parts.description: Wire safety rail on posts around the deck edge to stop crew going overboard.

details.didYouKnow: Guardrails stop people tripping over the edge, but they are not designed to be clipped to; offshore crews attach their harness to separate jackstays running along the deck.
details.howItWorks: Vertical stainless posts, called stanchions, are bolted through the deck along the port side and carry two wires at about knee and thigh height. The wires run from the bow pulpit to the stern rail, forming a fence. On starboard tack this is the low, leeward side, where a crew member is most likely to slip towards the water.
keyNumbers: Typically about 60 cm high
Posts roughly every 2 m
Wire usually 4 to 5 mm thick
details.madeOf: Stainless steel tube posts in sockets with stainless wire, often coated in plastic for comfort. Stainless is strong and corrosion resistant without paint.

parts.name: Guardrail (port)

parts.description: Long acrylic window in the coachroof side.

details.didYouKnow: Starboard comes from the Old English 'steorbord', the side where the steering oar hung, because most people were right-handed.
details.howItWorks: This window lights the right-hand side of the saloon, above the settee on that side. Like its partner it is sealed into the coachroof side so it can survive green water washing over the deck. On port tack the starboard side is the low, leeward side and this window often looks out at the waves.
keyNumbers: About 1.5 m long
Typically 8 to 10 mm thick
Light transmission roughly 20 to 50 percent depending on tint
details.madeOf: Tinted cast acrylic set in flexible marine sealant. Cast acrylic is preferred to extruded sheet because it scratches and crazes less in strong sunlight.

parts.name: Saloon window (starboard)

parts.description: Geared drum that multiplies the crew's pull so they can trim a jib sheet loaded with hundreds of kilos.

details.didYouKnow: The small spring-loaded pawls are what make a winch click; dropping one overboard while servicing is a rite of passage for many sailors.
details.howItWorks: This winch works the jib sheet when the jib is on the starboard side, which happens on port tack. After every tack the crew let the sheet off one winch and haul in on the other, so the two take turns doing the heavy work. Its two-speed gearing and self-tailing jaw are the same as on the port side.
keyNumbers: Typically 2 speeds
Drum about 10 cm across
Holds loads of up to roughly half a tonne
details.madeOf: Chromed bronze or anodised aluminium drum on a stainless base, with grease-lubricated gears and pawls. Regular servicing keeps salt from seizing the pawls.

parts.name: Sheet winch (starboard)

parts.description: Wire safety rail on posts around the deck edge to stop crew going overboard.

details.didYouKnow: Offshore racing rules set minimum heights and spacings for guardrails, and many cruising designs follow the same standards.
details.howItWorks: The starboard guardrail mirrors the port one, with stanchions bolted through the deck carrying the upper and lower wires. On port tack this becomes the leeward side, and crew going forward to the mast or bow hold it as they move. Gates in the rail near the cockpit let people step aboard from a pontoon.
keyNumbers: Typically about 60 cm high
Two wires, roughly 25 and 60 cm above deck
Posts usually 2 m or less apart
details.madeOf: Stainless steel posts with backing plates under the deck and plastic-coated stainless wire. The backing plates spread the load so the posts do not tear out.

parts.name: Guardrail (starboard)

parts.description: Sheltered seating well at the back where the crew steer, trim the sails and spend most of the voyage.

details.didYouKnow: Cockpits on offshore yachts are kept fairly small on purpose, because a big cockpit filled by a breaking wave holds tonnes of water.
details.howItWorks: The cockpit is a sunken well with seats either side and raised coamings that act as backrests and keep spray out. It holds the wheel, winches and rope clutches so the boat can be sailed from one place. It is self-draining: any water that comes in runs out through drains to the sea above the waterline.
keyNumbers: About 2 m long
Seats typically 40 to 45 cm high
Drains usually at least 2 of about 40 mm each
details.madeOf: Glass-fibre sandwich moulded as part of the deck, often with teak or synthetic teak on the seats. The non-slip finish helps on a wet, heeling boat.

parts.name: Cockpit

parts.description: Wheel linked by cables to the rudder stock; turning it swings the rudder blade.

details.didYouKnow: Smaller yachts often use a tiller instead, a simple stick on the rudder head; ships switched widely from tillers to wheels in the early 1700s.
details.howItWorks: Turning the wheel winds a chain over a sprocket in the steering pedestal, and cables from the chain run over pulleys to a quadrant clamped on top of the rudder stock. The quadrant acts as a lever, swinging the rudder. A large wheel gives the helmsman leverage and lets them sit out to one side to see the sails and the waves.
keyNumbers: About 80 cm diameter
Roughly 1.5 to 2 turns from lock to lock
Rudder swing about 35 degrees each way
details.madeOf: Stainless steel tube rim and spokes, often wrapped in leather or plastic for grip. The cables are stainless wire rope.

parts.name: Steering wheel

parts.description: Stainless frame around the bow that gives crew something to hold when handling the jib or anchor.

details.didYouKnow: The red and green sidelights mean that at night you can tell which way another boat is heading just by which colour you can see.
details.howItWorks: The pulpit is a welded tubular frame bolted through the foredeck that wraps around the bow. It anchors the front ends of the guardrail wires and gives crew a firm handhold when they are changing sails, untangling the jib or handling the anchor. Navigation lights are often mounted on it: red to port and green to starboard.
keyNumbers: Typically about 60 to 70 cm high
Tube roughly 25 mm diameter
Navigation lights visible for about 1 to 2 nautical miles
details.madeOf: Welded stainless steel tube on bolted feet with backing plates. Stainless is strong, needs no paint and looks smart polished.

parts.name: Bow pulpit

parts.description: Plough-shaped anchor stowed on the bow roller, ready to drop.

details.didYouKnow: The plough or CQR anchor shape was patented in the 1930s by the physicist Geoffrey Ingram Taylor, and its name CQR is a pun on the word secure.
details.howItWorks: Dropped on the seabed, the anchor is dragged a little until its pointed blade digs in and buries itself, so pulling harder only drives it deeper. It holds best when the pull is nearly horizontal, which is why plenty of chain is let out so the weight lies along the bottom. To lift it, the boat motors over it so the pull becomes vertical and the anchor breaks free.
keyNumbers: Typically 12 to 16 kg
Chain usually 8 mm, often 30 to 50 m long
Let out at least 4 to 5 times the water depth
details.madeOf: Galvanised forged or fabricated steel, sometimes stainless. Galvanising protects it from rust when dragged through mud and sand.

parts.name: Anchor

parts.description: Aluminium spar about 14 m tall standing on the coachroof; it carries the sails and their loads.

details.didYouKnow: This is a Bermuda rig, named after the triangular sails used on fast boats in Bermuda in the 1600s; it largely replaced gaff rigs on yachts in the 20th century.
details.howItWorks: The mast is a tall column held in place by tension wires, rather than a stiff pole standing on its own. Stays and shrouds pull on it from every direction, putting it in heavy compression that the step and compression post carry down to the hull. Sails attach in a groove up its back, and halyards run inside it to lift them.
keyNumbers: About 14 m tall
Section roughly 20 by 13 cm
Weighs around 60 to 90 kg
Compression load up to several tonnes
details.madeOf: Extruded aluminium alloy tube, anodised or painted. Aluminium is light, strong and cheap to extrude in a long, aerodynamic section; carbon fibre is lighter still but much more expensive.

parts.name: Mast

parts.description: Horizontal spar holding the foot of the mainsail; the mainsheet pulls it in or lets it out.

details.didYouKnow: An uncontrolled gybe can swing the boom across the cockpit hard enough to injure people, which is why the cry 'boom' or 'gybe-oh' warns everyone to duck.
details.howItWorks: The boom is fixed to the mast at a hinge called the gooseneck and holds the bottom edge of the mainsail out. The mainsheet, a rope through a set of pulleys to the cockpit, pulls it in towards the centreline or lets it swing out. A kicker or vang below it stops the boom rising and keeps the sail's shape in control.
keyNumbers: About 4 m long
Mainsheet tackle typically 4 to 6 to 1
Sits roughly 1.7 m above the deck
details.madeOf: Extruded aluminium tube like the mast. The mainsail's foot attaches to a slot or the corners only, and lines for reefing run inside.

parts.name: Boom

parts.description: Strut that holds the shroud out from the mast, giving it a better angle to brace the mast sideways.

details.didYouKnow: Many spreaders have tips wrapped in tape or rubber boots so the jib does not tear when it rubs against them during tacks.
details.howItWorks: The port spreader is a short strut jutting out from the mast that pushes the port shroud outwards, widening its angle to the mast. A wider angle means the shroud can hold the mast upright with less tension. When the wind comes from the port side, this is the windward spreader and it is squeezed in compression by the loaded shroud.
keyNumbers: About 75 cm long
Swept back typically 15 to 25 degrees
Mounted roughly halfway up the mast
details.madeOf: Aluminium aerofoil-section extrusion or casting, bolted into a bracket on the mast. The tip is clamped to the shroud and padded to protect the sails.

parts.name: Spreader (port)

parts.description: Steel wire from the masthead over the spreader down to a chainplate at the deck edge, holding the mast up sideways.

details.didYouKnow: Stainless rigging often fails without warning at the end fittings, so many insurers ask for standing rigging to be replaced by age even if it looks fine.
details.howItWorks: The port shroud runs from the masthead, over the port spreader tip, down to a chainplate on the port side deck. When wind blows from the port side and the boat heels to starboard, this wire takes the load and stops the mast bending away. A rigging screw at its base adjusts the tension.
keyNumbers: Wire typically 7 to 8 mm diameter
Breaking load roughly 4 to 5 tonnes
Usually replaced every 10 to 15 years
details.madeOf: 1 by 19 stainless steel wire with swaged or mechanical end fittings. This construction stretches very little and resists corrosion.

parts.name: Shroud (port)

parts.description: Strut that holds the shroud out from the mast, giving it a better angle to brace the mast sideways.

details.didYouKnow: If a spreader is not angled to split the shroud angle evenly, the wire can push it down and fold it, which can bring the mast down.
details.howItWorks: The starboard spreader does the same job on the right side, holding the starboard shroud out from the mast. When the wind is from the starboard side, it becomes the windward spreader and carries a strong compressive load. It is angled slightly upwards so it bisects the angle the shroud makes over its tip.
keyNumbers: About 75 cm long
Roughly 7 m above the deck
Compression load up to about 1 tonne
details.madeOf: Aluminium aerofoil section, bolted to the mast. The aerofoil shape reduces wind drag and turbulence above the mainsail.

parts.name: Spreader (starboard)

parts.description: Steel wire from the masthead over the spreader down to a chainplate at the deck edge, holding the mast up sideways.

details.didYouKnow: A yacht on starboard tack, with wind over the starboard side, generally has right of way over one on port tack under the international collision rules.
details.howItWorks: The starboard shroud mirrors the port one, running from masthead to a chainplate on the starboard deck edge. It takes the load when wind comes from the starboard side, which sailors call starboard tack. The two shrouds are tuned to equal tension so the mast stands straight.
keyNumbers: Wire typically 7 to 8 mm diameter
Tensioned to about 15 to 20 percent of breaking load
Roughly 14 m long
details.madeOf: Stainless steel wire terminated in swaged fittings, with a bronze or stainless rigging screw at the deck. Chainplates carry the load into bulkheads or the hull.

parts.name: Shroud (starboard)

parts.description: Wire from the masthead to the bow that holds the mast forward; the jib is attached along it.

details.didYouKnow: Roller furling headsails became common on cruising yachts from the 1970s and 80s, making it possible to reduce sail without going onto the foredeck.
details.howItWorks: The forestay runs from the masthead to the stemhead fitting at the bow and stops the mast falling backwards. On this yacht the jib is fitted to a furling foil around it, so the sail can be rolled away like a blind by pulling a line from the cockpit. A tight forestay keeps the jib's leading edge straight, which helps upwind.
keyNumbers: About 14 m long
Wire typically 8 mm diameter
Breaking load roughly 5 tonnes
details.madeOf: Stainless steel wire, usually slightly thicker than the shrouds, with an aluminium furling extrusion over it. Stainless keeps stretch low under heavy load.

parts.name: Forestay

parts.description: Wire from the masthead to the stern; tightening it bends the mast to flatten the mainsail in strong wind.

details.didYouKnow: Before satellite phones, offshore yachts commonly used an insulated backstay as the aerial for their single sideband radios.
details.howItWorks: The backstay runs from the masthead to the stern and balances the pull of the forestay. Many yachts have an adjuster, so tightening the backstay bends the top of the mast aft, which flattens the mainsail and tightens the forestay for better upwind performance in a breeze. Easing it in light wind gives fuller, more powerful sails.
keyNumbers: About 15 m long
Wire typically 6 to 7 mm diameter
Adjuster tension up to roughly 1 tonne
details.madeOf: Stainless steel wire, sometimes with insulators so it can serve as a long-range radio aerial. An adjuster may be a tackle, wheel screw or hydraulic ram.

parts.name: Backstay

parts.description: Big triangular sail behind the mast; it works like a vertical wing, generating lift from the wind flowing round it.

details.didYouKnow: Sails pull hardest with the wind at an angle, not from behind; a yacht reaching across the wind is usually faster than one running straight downwind.
details.howItWorks: The mainsail is cut with a built-in curve so air flowing over the back speeds up and lowers pressure, creating lift that pulls the boat forward and sideways. The keel resists the sideways part, leaving forward drive. Reefing lines let the crew lower part of the sail and tie it to the boom in strong wind, shrinking it so the boat does not heel too much.
keyNumbers: About 25 to 30 square metres
Typically 2 or 3 reef points
Cloth roughly 250 to 350 g per square metre
details.madeOf: Woven polyester sailcloth, usually Dacron, with stitched reinforcing patches at the corners. Polyester resists stretch, sunlight and abrasion well for the price.

parts.name: Mainsail

parts.description: Front sail set on the forestay; it speeds up the air flowing past the mainsail, making both work better.

details.didYouKnow: Sailors long believed the jib forced air through the slot onto the mainsail, but the modern explanation is that each sail improves the airflow around the other.
details.howItWorks: The jib is attached along the forestay and its sheets lead back to the cockpit winches. It bends the airflow so that air leaving it streams smoothly past the back of the mainsail, delaying stall and helping both sails make more lift together. It rolls up on its furler, so it can be shortened in seconds.
keyNumbers: About 20 to 30 square metres
Overlaps the mast by roughly 0 to 30 percent
Sheet loads up to about 500 kg
details.madeOf: Polyester sailcloth with UV-resistant strips along the edges that face outwards when furled. The strips protect the rolled-up sail from sunlight damage.

parts.name: Jib

parts.description: Small three-cylinder marine diesel of around 20 kW under the cockpit, for harbours and calm days.

details.didYouKnow: Diesel replaced petrol for yacht engines largely for safety: diesel fumes do not explode easily in a closed bilge, unlike petrol vapour.
details.howItWorks: The diesel compresses air in each cylinder until it is hot enough to ignite injected fuel, with no spark plugs needed. Seawater pumped through a heat exchanger cools a sealed freshwater circuit, and then leaves with the exhaust. A gearbox on the back gives forward, neutral and reverse, and an alternator charges the batteries while it runs.
keyNumbers: About 20 kW (roughly 27 hp)
3 cylinders
Uses roughly 2 to 3 litres of fuel per hour cruising
Pushes the boat at about 6 knots
details.madeOf: Cast iron block and head, often based on an industrial or tractor engine. Cast iron is durable and damps vibration, and marinised parts resist salt.

parts.name: Auxiliary diesel

parts.description: Stainless shaft from the gearbox out through a watertight seal to the propeller.

details.didYouKnow: An old-style stern gland is supposed to drip slightly while the shaft turns, roughly a drop every few seconds, because the water lubricates and cools the packing.
details.howItWorks: The shaft carries the engine's twisting force from the gearbox coupling, through a seal in the hull, to the propeller. The seal lets the shaft spin while keeping the sea out, either with greased packing rings or a modern dripless face seal. A flexible coupling at the engine end absorbs small misalignments and vibration.
keyNumbers: Typically 25 mm diameter
Roughly 1 m long
Typically turns at roughly half engine speed after the gearbox
details.madeOf: Stainless steel or high-strength marine alloy bar. Stainless resists corrosion and is protected further by a sacrificial zinc anode clamped to the shaft.

parts.name: Propeller shaft

parts.description: Aluminium tank of about 100 litres of diesel under the cockpit seats.

details.didYouKnow: Bacteria can grow at the boundary between diesel and condensed water in a tank, forming a slimy sludge nicknamed diesel bug that can clog filters.
details.howItWorks: The tank stores the diesel low and near the middle of the boat so its weight does not upset trim. A pick-up pipe draws fuel from just above the bottom, through a water-separating filter, to the engine. A vent line lets air in as fuel is used and lets fumes out when filling from a deck fitting.
keyNumbers: About 100 litres
Range roughly 200 to 250 nautical miles under engine
Weighs about 85 kg full
details.madeOf: Welded aluminium or sometimes rotomoulded plastic. Aluminium is light and strong, but it must sit dry and well supported to avoid corrosion.

parts.name: Fuel tank

parts.description: Flexible or plastic tank under a berth holding drinking and washing water.

details.didYouKnow: Long-distance cruisers often fit a watermaker, a reverse-osmosis filter that turns seawater into drinking water by forcing it through a membrane at high pressure.
details.howItWorks: Fresh water is stored below a berth, low in the hull to help stability. An electric pump pressurises the system, so taps in the galley and heads work like at home, with a hand or foot pump as backup. Some yachts also heat water with the engine's cooling circuit through a calorifier.
keyNumbers: Typically 150 to 250 litres
About 1 kg per litre when full
Roughly 5 to 10 litres per person per day when careful
details.madeOf: Food-grade polyethylene or a flexible rubber bladder. Plastic is light, does not corrode and is easy to keep clean.

parts.name: Freshwater tank

parts.description: Bank of 12-volt batteries powering lights, instruments, fridge and autopilot, charged by the engine and solar.

details.didYouKnow: A fridge is often the biggest energy user on a small cruising yacht, using a large share of the daily battery budget in warm weather.
details.howItWorks: The house bank stores energy so lights, instruments, the fridge and the autopilot can run while the engine is off. It is kept separate from the engine starting battery, so draining it at anchor never leaves you unable to start the engine. Solar panels, the engine alternator or shore power top it up.
keyNumbers: 12 volts
Typically 200 to 400 amp-hours
Lead-acid weighs roughly 25 to 30 kg per 100 Ah
details.madeOf: Lead-acid batteries (flooded, gel or AGM) or, increasingly, lithium iron phosphate. Lithium is lighter and can be drained deeper but costs more.

parts.name: House batteries

parts.description: Long settee cushions either side of the cabin that double as sea berths.

details.didYouKnow: Sailors call bunks used underway sea berths; the forward cabin is often too bumpy to sleep in when sailing hard upwind.
details.howItWorks: By day the saloon berths are sofas around the table; at sea they become the best beds on the boat, because the middle of the hull moves least. Canvas lee cloths can be clipped up along the edge to stop a sleeper rolling out when the boat heels. Lockers under the cushions hold stores and often the water tank.
keyNumbers: About 1.9 to 2 m long
Cushions typically 10 to 12 cm thick
Sleep 2 people
details.madeOf: Foam cushions in hard-wearing upholstery fabric on plywood or glass-fibre bases. The fabric is chosen to resist damp and mildew.

parts.name: Saloon berths

parts.description: Folding table built around the mast support post.

details.didYouKnow: Teak has been prized in boatbuilding for centuries because its natural oils and silica help it shrug off water, rot and wear.
details.howItWorks: The table is mounted around the compression post that carries the mast's downward load to the hull, so it is very firmly fixed. Hinged leaves fold down to make room to move around, and a raised edge, called a fiddle, stops plates sliding off when the boat heels. On some yachts it drops down to make an extra double berth.
keyNumbers: About 1 m long
Seats roughly 4 to 6
Fiddles typically 1 to 3 cm high
details.madeOf: Teak or teak-veneered marine plywood, varnished. Teak is naturally oily, which helps it resist water and rot.

parts.name: Saloon table

parts.description: Triangular double bed in the bow cabin.

details.didYouKnow: In rough weather the bow can drop several metres into each trough, which is why sailors joke that the forward cabin is for use in harbour only.
details.howItWorks: The V-berth fills the narrow bow cabin with a triangular double bed that follows the shape of the hull. It is often the private owner's cabin in harbour, with a hatch overhead for light and air. At sea it is the bumpiest place on board, because the bow rises and falls the most over waves.
keyNumbers: About 2 m long
Roughly 1.8 m wide at the head end
Narrows to about 0.5 m at the foot
details.madeOf: Foam mattress pieces on plywood boards, with lockers or the anchor chain locker beneath. Ventilation under the foam helps stop condensation.

parts.name: Forward V-berth

parts.description: Compact kitchen with a gimballed stove that swings to stay level as the boat heels.

details.didYouKnow: Bottled gas is heavier than air and can pool in a boat's bilge, so galley gas systems are fitted with sniffers and the bottle lives in a locker that drains overboard.
details.howItWorks: The stove is hung on pivots so it stays level as the boat heels, keeping pans on the burners, with clamps or rails called fiddles to hold them in place. Gas is supplied from a bottle in a sealed, drained locker, with a shut-off valve near the cooker. A small sink, a top-loading fridge and deep lockers complete the kitchen.
keyNumbers: Typically 2 burners and an oven
Gimbals typically allow 30 degrees or more of swing
Gas bottle usually about 3 to 6 kg
details.madeOf: Stainless steel stove and sink set into a laminate or solid-surface worktop. These materials are easy to clean and resist heat and salt.

parts.name: Galley

summary: A 10 m cruising yacht for four to six people: a sloop rig with mainsail and jib on a 14 m mast, a deep fin keel with a lead bulb, and a cabin with berths, galley and a small diesel engine for calm days and harbours.

name: Farm Tractor
overview:
A tractor is a machine for pulling and powering other machines. On its own it doesn't plough, mow or bale; it supplies the pulling force and the power for implements that do.
