That's why it's built for grip and torque rather than speed: a big, slow-revving diesel engine, a gearbox with many low ratios, and enormous rear tyres with deep lugs that bite into soft soil.

Power leaves a tractor three ways. The drawbar and three-point hitch at the back pull and carry implements, and the hitch can lift them clear of the ground. The power take-off, a splined shaft spinning at a fixed speed, drives the moving parts of things like mowers and balers through a shaft. And a hydraulic pump sends pressurised oil out through couplings to work cylinders and motors on the implement.

The engine, gearbox and rear axle are bolted end to end into one rigid casting that is the tractor's backbone, so there's no separate frame. The front axle pivots in the middle so all four wheels stay on uneven ground. Heavy weights hang on the front to balance the pull at the back, and the cab gives the driver a sealed, quiet seat for long days in the field.

parts.description: Huge low-pressure radial tyre, about 1.7 m tall; running soft spreads the weight so it doesn't pack down the soil.

details.didYouKnow: For decades farmers added weight by part-filling rear tyres with water, often with calcium chloride mixed in so it wouldn't freeze in winter.
details.howItWorks: The left rear tyre carries a large share of the tractor's weight and turns the engine's torque into pulling force at the ground. Its flexible sidewalls let it bulge into a long, wide footprint, so the load is spread over a big area and the lugs have more soil to push against. The left and right rear tyres are linked through the differential, which lets them turn at different speeds on corners unless the driver engages the diff lock.
keyNumbers: About 1.7 m tall
Roughly 0.5 m wide
Typically 0.8 to 1.6 bar of pressure
Fits a 38-inch rim on many tractors this size
details.madeOf: Layers of rubber-coated textile cords laid radially across the tyre, under steel or textile belts and a thick rubber tread. Radial construction keeps the sidewall supple and the tread flat on the ground.

parts.name: Rear tyre (left)

parts.description: Chevron-shaped rubber bars that dig into soft ground like paddles to give grip.

details.didYouKnow: Before rubber tyres caught on in the 1930s, tractors ran on steel wheels with bolted-on spade lugs, which had to be removed or covered before driving on a public road.
details.howItWorks: These bars form the inner half of the left rear tyre's chevron, the half nearest the tractor's body. As the wheel turns, each bar sinks into the soil and shoves backwards against it, much like a paddle in water. The bars are angled so that soil trapped between them is squeezed out sideways as the tyre rolls, letting the tread clean itself rather than clogging into a slick.
keyNumbers: About 20 bars on this half
Typically 40 to 60 mm tall when new
Set at roughly 45 degrees to the tyre's centreline
details.madeOf: A tough, cut-resistant rubber compound moulded as one piece with the tyre. It needs to grip in mud yet survive stones, stubble and road miles.

parts.name: Rear tread lugs (left, inner half)

parts.description: Chevron-shaped rubber bars that dig into soft ground like paddles to give grip.

details.didYouKnow: Fit a tractor tyre the wrong way round and the chevrons pack with soil instead of clearing it, which is why the tyre sidewall carries an arrow showing the direction of rotation.
details.howItWorks: The outer half of the left tyre's chevron mirrors the inner half and is staggered from it, so a bar is always starting to bite somewhere across the width. Because the outer edge sweeps the widest path, these bars do a lot of the work of resisting sideways slip on slopes and when pulling round headland turns. Together the two halves form a V that is meant to point forward at the top of the tyre.
keyNumbers: About 20 bars on this half
Typically 40 to 60 mm tall when new
Tread often regarded as worn out below roughly a third of its height
details.madeOf: The same moulded rubber as the rest of the tread, vulcanised onto the tyre carcass. Heat and pressure in the mould bond the bars permanently to the body.

parts.name: Rear tread lugs (left, outer half)

parts.description: Steel rim bolted to the axle hub; its centre can be reset to change the track width between crop rows.

details.didYouKnow: Heavy cast-iron wheel weights are often bolted to the rear rim centres; they add grip without the drawbacks of filling the tyres with water.
details.howItWorks: The rim holds the tyre's beads and is bolted to the wheel centre, which in turn bolts to the hub at the end of the left axle housing. Many rims can be unbolted and refitted in different positions on their centres, or the dished centre flipped over, to slide the wheel in or out. That lets a farmer set the wheels to run between crop rows or spread them wider for stability on hills.
keyNumbers: About 38 inches (965 mm) bead diameter
Rear track typically adjustable from about 1.5 to 2 m
Wheel and tyre together weigh roughly 200 to 300 kg
details.madeOf: Rolled and welded steel plate, painted against rust. Steel is cheap, strong and tough enough to take knocks without cracking.

parts.name: Rear wheel rim (left)

parts.description: Smaller steering tyre; on four-wheel-drive tractors it's driven too.

details.didYouKnow: On four-wheel-drive tractors the front wheels are geared to run around 1 to 5 per cent faster than the rears, so the front axle slightly pulls the tractor along rather than being dragged.
details.howItWorks: The left front tyre steers the tractor, swivelling on a kingpin at the end of the front axle. On a four-wheel-drive tractor it is also driven, through a shaft from the gearbox and a small reduction gear in the hub. Its tread is the same chevron style as the rears, so it pulls the tractor along as well as pointing it.
keyNumbers: About 1.1 to 1.3 m tall
Typically 1 to 1.6 bar of pressure
Fits a 24- or 28-inch rim on tractors this size
details.madeOf: A radial rubber tyre built like the rear one but smaller and lighter, with textile and steel reinforcement under the tread.

parts.name: Front tyre (left)

parts.description: Steel rim of the front wheel.

details.didYouKnow: Early tractors often had their two front wheels tucked close together in a tricycle layout so they could run between rows of crops like maize.
details.howItWorks: The left front rim mounts the tyre on the hub of the steering knuckle, so it turns with every movement of the steering wheel. Because the left wheel sits on the inside of a left turn, it swings through a tighter angle than the right one. The rim's dished shape leaves room for the hub and steering parts inside it.
keyNumbers: About 24 to 28 inches bead diameter
Front wheels steer up to about 50 to 55 degrees
Wheel and tyre roughly 100 kg
details.madeOf: Pressed and welded steel, painted. A steel rim shrugs off stones and impacts that would dent a lighter wheel.

parts.name: Front wheel rim (left)

parts.description: Curved guard over the rear tyre that stops mud and stones flying onto the cab.

details.didYouKnow: Those outside hitch buttons save lots of climbing in and out: the driver can creep the lower links up to the implement's pins while standing right beside them.
details.howItWorks: The left mudguard arches over the rear tyre and catches mud, water and stones thrown up and forwards by the turning lugs. It also forms a safety barrier between the cab steps and the moving wheel. On many tractors it carries the rear indicator and work lights, and buttons on it let someone standing at the back raise or lower the hitch while lining up an implement.
keyNumbers: Spans roughly 1.6 to 1.8 m of arc
Clearance of typically 10 cm or more above the tyre
Often carries 1 or 2 work lights
details.madeOf: Pressed steel or tough moulded plastic. Steel can carry lights and handles securely; plastic shrugs off dents and doesn't rust.

parts.name: Rear mudguard (left)

parts.description: Huge low-pressure radial tyre, about 1.7 m tall; running soft spreads the weight so it doesn't pack down the soil.

details.didYouKnow: A little wheel slip is actually good: tyres pull best when they are slipping slightly, but much above about 15 per cent they mostly waste fuel and smear the soil.
details.howItWorks: The right rear tyre shares the pull with the left. When ploughing, it is often the one running in the furrow bottom, so the tractor leans slightly to the right and this tyre carries a bit more load. If it starts to spin on wet ground, the driver can engage the diff lock to force both rear wheels to turn together.
keyNumbers: About 1.7 m tall
Carries roughly 1.5 tonnes or more
Typically 10 to 15 per cent wheel slip is ideal when ploughing
details.madeOf: A radial casing of rubberised textile cords under stabilising belts and a deep rubber tread, chosen for supple sidewalls and a long, flat footprint.

parts.name: Rear tyre (right)

parts.description: Chevron-shaped rubber bars that dig into soft ground like paddles to give grip.

details.didYouKnow: Wide gaps between the bars matter as much as the bars themselves; they give the soil somewhere to go so the tread can clean itself every revolution.
details.howItWorks: These bars make up the inner half of the right rear tyre's chevron, nearest the transmission. They bite into the soil and push back against it, while their slant sweeps loose soil outward between them. They mirror the left tyre's lugs, so the two rear wheels pull evenly and the tractor tracks straight.
keyNumbers: About 20 bars on this half
Typically 40 to 60 mm tall when new
Gap between bars roughly 15 to 25 cm at the shoulder
details.madeOf: Hard-wearing tread rubber with carbon black for strength, moulded with the tyre. The compound balances grip, cut resistance and road wear.

parts.name: Rear tread lugs (right, inner half)

parts.description: Chevron-shaped rubber bars that dig into soft ground like paddles to give grip.

details.didYouKnow: Lots of road work at high speed wears tractor lugs far faster than field work, because the bars squirm and scrub on tarmac.
details.howItWorks: The outer half of the right tyre's chevron overlaps the inner half at the centre, so there is always some rubber in contact on a hard road. In the field these outer bars, at the tyre's shoulder, also help it climb out of ruts and resist sliding sideways on a hillside. Lugs on road-heavy tractors wear fastest on their leading edges.
keyNumbers: About 20 bars on this half
Typically 40 to 60 mm tall when new
Worn lugs can cut drawbar pull noticeably on wet ground
details.madeOf: Moulded rubber tread compound, bonded to the tyre carcass during vulcanisation.

parts.name: Rear tread lugs (right, outer half)

parts.description: Steel rim bolted to the axle hub; its centre can be reset to change the track width between crop rows.

details.didYouKnow: Wheel nuts on tractor rear wheels are tightened to several hundred newton metres and are checked again after the first few hours of work, as the joint settles.
details.howItWorks: Like the left rim, the right rim bolts to an adjustable wheel centre on the hub of the right axle housing. Setting both sides to the same track matters, since an uneven track makes the tractor crab sideways and implements run off line. A valve stem through the rim lets the tyre pressure be checked and changed.
keyNumbers: About 38 inches (965 mm) bead diameter
Rim width roughly 16 to 18 inches
Usually held by 8 to 10 wheel studs
details.madeOf: Welded steel plate rolled into a hoop and painted, with a pressed steel or cast centre. Steel tolerates the huge twisting load of the axle.

parts.name: Rear wheel rim (right)

parts.description: Smaller steering tyre; on four-wheel-drive tractors it's driven too.

details.didYouKnow: Some modern tractors can change their tyre pressures on the move, letting them down for soft fields and pumping them up for the road.
details.howItWorks: The right front tyre is linked to the left by a track rod, so both steer together. When the front axle pivots over a bump, this wheel can rise while the left one drops, keeping both in contact with the ground. Its pressure is usually set a little differently from the rears to suit the load the front weights put on it.
keyNumbers: About 1.1 to 1.3 m tall
Roughly 0.4 m wide
Carries typically 1 tonne or more with front weights fitted
details.madeOf: A smaller radial rubber tyre with textile cords and a moulded chevron tread.

parts.name: Front tyre (right)

parts.description: Steel rim of the front wheel.

details.didYouKnow: The geometry that steers the inner and outer wheels through different angles is called Ackermann steering, patented in the early 1800s for horse-drawn carriages.
details.howItWorks: The right front rim bolts to its hub and turns on the right steering knuckle. On a left turn this is the outer wheel, so it steers through a slightly smaller angle than the left one, which keeps both wheels rolling around the same centre point instead of scrubbing.
keyNumbers: About 24 to 28 inches bead diameter
Usually held by 6 to 8 studs
Front track typically about 1.5 to 1.9 m
details.madeOf: Pressed steel, welded and painted, sized to clear the hub reduction gears and brake parts inside it.

parts.name: Front wheel rim (right)

parts.description: Curved guard over the rear tyre that stops mud and stones flying onto the cab.

details.didYouKnow: Rear mudguards on older open tractors had to double as a footrest and handhold, and sometimes a perch for a second person, which was never a safe place to ride.
details.howItWorks: The right mudguard shields the cab and the right door from spray off the rear tyre. It often carries a socket panel, lights and an indicator, and its shape follows the tyre so it still clears when the wheels are set out wide. Like the left guard, it is bolted to the cab structure or axle housing.
keyNumbers: Spans roughly 1.6 to 1.8 m of arc
Typically 10 cm or more above the tyre
Lights on it often LED, about 20 to 40 W each
details.madeOf: Pressed steel or moulded plastic composite, with steel brackets. Plastic versions bend and spring back after a knock from a gatepost.

parts.name: Rear mudguard (right)

parts.description: Hinged sheet-steel hood over the engine, cooling pack and air filter.

details.didYouKnow: Many tractor makers became known by their paint colour alone; a field of tractors can often be identified from a long way off just by the shade of the bonnets.
details.howItWorks: The bonnet covers the engine, cooling pack and air filter and tilts up on hinges, usually helped by gas struts, for servicing. Its sides slope inwards and its nose drops away so the driver can see the ground just ahead of the front wheels. Vents along its sides let hot air from the engine bay escape.
keyNumbers: About 2 m long
Opens to roughly 60 to 80 degrees
Weighs roughly 30 to 50 kg
details.madeOf: Pressed sheet steel or moulded plastic composite, painted in the maker's colours. Composite is lighter and doesn't rust; steel is cheaper and easy to repair.

parts.name: Bonnet

parts.description: Mesh panel letting cooling air into the radiator while keeping out chaff and crop debris.

details.didYouKnow: In dusty, chaff-filled work some tractors run their cooling fan briefly in reverse to blow the debris back off the grille and coolers.
details.howItWorks: The grille is the first thing the cooling air passes through on its way to the radiator stack. Its fine mesh stops straw, chaff and seeds from matting onto the cooler fins, where they would block airflow and let the engine overheat. It usually hinges or slides out so it can be brushed or blown clean.
keyNumbers: Mesh openings typically a few millimetres across
Passes several cubic metres of air a second
Often cleaned daily at harvest
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic with a fine metal or plastic mesh. Plastic is light, can be shaped to the bonnet nose, and won't rust.

parts.name: Front grille

parts.description: Road light set into the front of the bonnet.

details.didYouKnow: A front loader or front-mounted mower can hide the bonnet lights completely, which is why road rules often require extra lights mounted high when a front implement is fitted.
details.howItWorks: The left headlight lights the road ahead and, with its partner, shows other drivers the tractor's width. Its lens and reflector shape a dipped beam that throws light down and to the near side so oncoming drivers aren't dazzled. Because front implements can block bonnet lights, many tractors carry a second set of road lights higher up on the cab.
keyNumbers: Halogen bulb typically 55 to 60 W
LED units roughly 20 to 40 W
Runs on 12 volts
details.madeOf: A glass or polycarbonate lens over a mirrored reflector, with a halogen bulb or LEDs. Polycarbonate resists stones better than glass.

parts.name: Headlight (left)

parts.description: Road light set into the front of the bonnet.

details.didYouKnow: Electric headlights only became common on farm tractors from around the 1930s and 40s; before that much night work was done by paraffin lamp or not at all.
details.howItWorks: The right headlight works with the left as a matched pair, wired through the same light switch, dip control and fuse box. On full beam both reach far down the road; on dip each is aimed slightly down so the light pattern stays below oncoming drivers' eyes. Its aim is set by small adjusting screws behind the housing.
keyNumbers: Typically 55 to 60 W halogen or about 20 to 40 W LED
Main beam reaches roughly 100 m
Sealed to resist hosing down
details.madeOf: A clear lens of glass or polycarbonate over a reflector of metallised plastic, sealed against water and dust.

parts.name: Headlight (right)

parts.description: Four-cylinder turbo-diesel of about 4.5 litres, tuned for strong pulling power at low revs.

details.didYouKnow: Building a tractor with no separate frame, with the engine and gearbox bolted together as the backbone, became standard from around 1917 and is still how most tractors are made.
details.howItWorks: Each of the four cylinders squeezes air so hard it gets hot enough to ignite diesel sprayed in at very high pressure, with no spark needed. The engine is tuned so its torque rises as the revs drop under load, so it digs in rather than stalling when the plough hits heavy soil. Its block bolts directly to the front axle support and the transmission, making it a load-bearing part of the tractor's backbone.
keyNumbers: About 4.5 litres from 4 cylinders
Roughly 100 hp (75 kW) at about 2,200 rpm
Peak torque around 400 to 450 Nm
Compression ratio about 17:1
details.madeOf: A cast-iron block and cylinder head, with a forged steel crankshaft and connecting rods. Cast iron is strong and stiff enough to carry chassis loads and damps vibration well.

parts.name: Diesel engine

parts.description: Exhaust-driven fan that packs extra air into the cylinders for more power.

details.didYouKnow: Drivers are taught to let a hard-worked tractor idle for a minute before switching off, so the turbo's bearings aren't left glowing hot with no oil flowing through them.
details.howItWorks: Hot exhaust gas spins a small turbine wheel, which drives a compressor wheel on the same shaft on the intake side. The compressor pushes extra air into the cylinders, so more fuel can be burned cleanly and the engine makes more power from the same size. The compressed air is cooled in the intercooler at the front of the tractor before it enters the engine.
keyNumbers: Spins at up to roughly 100,000 rpm or more
Exhaust gas up to about 600 to 700 degrees C
Boost typically 1 to 2 bar above outside air
details.madeOf: A cast-iron or steel turbine housing with a nickel-alloy turbine wheel that survives red-hot exhaust, and an aluminium compressor wheel. The shaft runs in oil-fed bearings.

parts.name: Turbocharger

parts.description: Stack of radiator, intercooler and oil cooler at the front, cooled by a large engine-driven fan.

details.didYouKnow: Some early tractors were cooled by evaporating water: the driver simply topped up a hopper as it boiled away during the day's work.
details.howItWorks: Several coolers sit stacked at the nose of the tractor: the radiator for engine coolant, an intercooler for the compressed intake air, and coolers for gearbox and hydraulic oil, and often the air-conditioning. A large fan driven from the engine pulls air through all of them in turn. Because a tractor often works flat out at walking pace, there is little natural airflow, so the fan does nearly all the work.
keyNumbers: Engine holds roughly 15 to 20 litres of coolant
Fan about 50 to 60 cm across
Intercooler can cool intake air by about 100 degrees C
details.madeOf: Aluminium tubes and thin aluminium fins brazed together, with plastic or aluminium tanks. Aluminium conducts heat very well and is light.

parts.name: Radiator & cooling pack

parts.description: Large dry filter that cleans the very dusty air of a working field before the engine breathes it.

details.didYouKnow: Older tractors used oil-bath air cleaners, in which incoming air was forced through a pool of oil that caught the dust; the sludge in the bottom showed how dirty the day had been.
details.howItWorks: Field air is full of dust, which would grind the inside of the engine like sandpaper. Air first passes a pre-cleaner that spins out heavy dirt, then a pleated main element that traps fine dust, with a smaller safety element behind it in case the main one fails. A sensor warns the driver when the filter is clogged and needs cleaning or changing.
keyNumbers: Engine draws roughly 8 to 10 cubic metres of air a minute at full power
Typically traps over 99.9 per cent of dust
Main element often changed every few hundred to 1,000 hours
details.madeOf: A plastic housing with pleated filter paper elements bonded into rubber or polyurethane seals. Paper pleats pack a large filtering area into a small space.

parts.name: Air filter

parts.description: Upright pipe that releases exhaust above the cab, with a flap that closes when the engine stops.

details.didYouKnow: The flap is just a loose hinged lid with no spring or motor: the first puff of exhaust on starting flips it open, often with a little clatter.
details.howItWorks: The exhaust runs from the turbo, through the silencer and any after-treatment unit, and up the stack beside the windscreen pillar so the fumes clear the cab. The hinged flap on top is pushed open by the exhaust flow and drops shut when the engine stops, keeping rain out of the turbo. Modern tractors clean the exhaust with a catalyst, a particulate filter and a urea injection system before it leaves the stack.
keyNumbers: Exhaust gas typically 300 to 600 degrees C
Top of stack roughly 2.8 to 3 m above ground
Pipe about 10 to 13 cm across
details.madeOf: Stainless or aluminised steel tube, which resists heat and corrosion, often with a perforated guard to stop the driver touching the hot pipe.

parts.name: Exhaust stack

parts.description: Stack of cast-iron weights hung on the nose to balance a heavy implement on the back and keep the front wheels down.

details.didYouKnow: Too much ballast is as bad as too little: extra weight compacts the soil and burns fuel, so farmers try to add only enough to keep wheel slip in the efficient range.
details.howItWorks: A heavy implement hanging on the rear hitch acts like a lever, lifting weight off the front wheels and making the steering light and dangerous. The front weights push the nose back down so the front tyres keep grip for steering and, on four-wheel drive, for pulling. Individual slabs hang on a carrier at the nose, so the driver can add or remove them to suit each job.
keyNumbers: Each slab typically about 40 to 50 kg
A full stack roughly 400 to 900 kg
Aim is often about 40 per cent of the weight on the front axle
details.madeOf: Cast iron, which is dense, cheap and can be cast into interlocking slabs with handholds. Some tractors use a single large weight block hung on a front hitch instead.

parts.name: Front ballast weights

parts.description: Cast housing holding the gearbox and rear differential; with the engine it forms the tractor's backbone.

details.didYouKnow: Tractors often have a shuttle lever beside the steering wheel that flips between forward and reverse without using the clutch, making loader work far quicker.
details.howItWorks: Behind the clutch, the gearbox splits the engine's narrow speed range into many ratios, from creeping speeds for planting to about 40 km/h for the road. A powershift gearbox changes between some ratios using hydraulic clutch packs, so the driver can shift under load without stopping. At the back of the housing, a crown wheel and pinion turn the drive sideways into the rear axle, and the same oil usually feeds the hydraulic system.
keyNumbers: Typically 16 to 32 forward speeds
Top road speed usually about 40 km/h
Holds roughly 50 to 70 litres of oil
Creep speeds can be well under 1 km/h
details.madeOf: A large iron casting, machined to hold shafts, bearings and gears precisely. Its walls must be thick and stiff because it carries the weight of the tractor between the engine and rear axle.

parts.name: Transmission housing

parts.description: Long trumpets carrying the half-shafts and final-drive gears out to the rear wheels.

details.didYouKnow: Tractor brakes usually work on each rear wheel separately, so the driver can brake just the inside wheel to turn very tightly on a headland.
details.howItWorks: From the differential, half-shafts run out through these trumpet housings to the rear wheels. Near each hub a planetary gearset gives a final big speed reduction, multiplying torque just before it reaches the wheel so the shafts and gears inboard can be smaller. The housings also carry the rear brakes, the lift linkage brackets and the cab mounts.
keyNumbers: Final drive reduction often around 4:1 to 6:1
Wheel torque can reach tens of thousands of Nm
Carries roughly 60 per cent of the tractor's weight unballasted
details.madeOf: Cast iron or cast steel housings with forged and hardened steel shafts and gears. Hardened gear teeth survive huge, repeated loads.

parts.name: Rear axle housings

parts.description: Beam that pivots on a central pin so the front wheels can follow bumps while the rear stays level.

details.didYouKnow: Some tractors add suspension to the front axle, which lets them travel faster on the road and keeps the front tyres pressed to bumpy ground for better grip.
details.howItWorks: The axle beam hangs from a single pivot pin at its centre, so it rocks like a see-saw as the front wheels ride over ridges and furrows. This keeps all four tyres on the ground without twisting the tractor's body. On four-wheel drive it contains a differential, half-shafts and hub reduction gears, and a hydraulic cylinder on it steers the wheels.
keyNumbers: Pivots roughly 10 to 12 degrees each way
Turning circle roughly 9 to 11 m
Front axle often carries roughly 1.5 to 2.5 tonnes with weights fitted
details.madeOf: A cast-iron or cast-steel beam with forged steel steering knuckles and hardened gears inside. The beam must take hard knocks from rough ground and the weight of the front ballast.

parts.name: Front axle

parts.description: Tank of about 200 litres of diesel beside the cab steps, enough for a long working day.

details.didYouKnow: In the UK, farm tractors can run on red diesel, ordinary fuel dyed red and taxed at a lower rate; the dye lets officials check that it isn't being used in road cars.
details.howItWorks: The tank stores diesel beside the cab steps, low down to keep the centre of gravity low. A lift pump draws fuel through filters and a water separator before the high-pressure pump forces it to the injectors; spare fuel used to cool the injectors returns to the tank. Modern tractors also have a smaller blue-capped tank for the urea solution the exhaust system needs.
keyNumbers: About 200 litres of diesel
Full fuel weighs roughly 170 kg
Typically burns 10 to 20 litres an hour in heavy work
details.madeOf: Rotationally moulded polyethylene plastic. It can't rust, can be shaped to fill odd spaces around the steps and axle, and flexes rather than splits if knocked.

parts.name: Fuel tank

parts.description: Heavy-duty 12-volt battery for starting the cold diesel.

details.didYouKnow: Many old tractors started on petrol and switched to cheaper paraffin once the engine was warm, because they had no battery strong enough to crank a cold diesel.
details.howItWorks: The battery supplies the big current the starter motor needs to turn the stiff, high-compression diesel over until it fires. In cold weather, heater plugs or an intake grid warm the air first, drawing more current. Once the engine runs, the alternator recharges the battery and powers the lights, cab and electronics.
keyNumbers: 12 volts
Typically 100 to 180 amp-hours
Cold cranking current roughly 800 to 1,000 A
Weighs about 25 to 45 kg
details.madeOf: Lead plates in sulphuric acid inside a tough polypropylene case. Lead-acid batteries are cheap, robust and deliver very high starting currents.

parts.name: Battery

parts.description: One of the two lower arms of the three-point hitch; their ends hook onto the implement's pins.

details.didYouKnow: The modern hook-ended lower links let a driver collect an implement without leaving the seat: back up, lift, and the hooks catch the balls and latch automatically.
details.howItWorks: The left lower link pivots at the rear axle and hooks onto the left pin of an implement. A lift rod from the left lift arm hangs from its middle, so raising the arms raises the link. A stabiliser or check chain on its outside stops the implement swinging into the tyre, and on many tractors a load sensor in its mounting measures the pull for automatic draft control.
keyNumbers: Category 2 ball takes a 28 mm pin
Lower link ends spaced about 825 mm apart
Link roughly 0.8 to 1 m long
details.madeOf: Forged steel bar, sometimes with a hook end and a separate ball, chosen for strength in both pulling and bending.

parts.name: Lower link arm (left)

parts.description: Arm swung by the hydraulic lift that raises and lowers the lower links and whatever hangs on them.

details.didYouKnow: Harry Ferguson's hydraulic lift, introduced in the 1930s, let the driver lift a plough out of the ground with a lever, ending the hard work of hauling ploughs around by hand.
details.howItWorks: The left lift arm is fixed to a cross-shaft (the rockshaft) on top of the transmission, which is turned by hydraulic cylinders. As the shaft rotates, both lift arms swing up together, pulling the lift rods and lower links with them. The left lift rod is usually a fixed length, while the right one can be adjusted to tilt the implement level.
keyNumbers: Hitch lifts roughly 3.5 to 4.5 tonnes at the link ends
Swings through about 60 to 70 degrees
Hydraulic system pressure around 180 to 200 bar
details.madeOf: Forged steel, shaped to carry a heavy bending load at the end of a short lever.

parts.name: Lift arm (left)

parts.description: One of the two lower arms of the three-point hitch; their ends hook onto the implement's pins.

details.didYouKnow: Before the three-point hitch, implements were simply towed on a chain or bar, and a plough that snagged a root could flip a tractor over backwards.
details.howItWorks: The right lower link matches the left one and hooks onto the implement's right pin. Its lift rod usually includes a screw or hydraulic adjuster, so the driver can raise this side slightly to keep a plough level when the right wheel runs in the furrow. A stabiliser on its outer side controls side-to-side sway.
keyNumbers: Category 2 ball takes a 28 mm pin
Levelling adjustment typically several centimetres
Rated for several tonnes of pull and lift
details.madeOf: Forged steel, heat-treated for toughness, with a hardened steel ball or hook at its end.

parts.name: Lower link arm (right)

parts.description: Arm swung by the hydraulic lift that raises and lowers the lower links and whatever hangs on them.

details.didYouKnow: Draft control transfers some of the implement's weight onto the tractor's rear wheels as it pulls, giving extra grip without carrying extra ballast.
details.howItWorks: The right lift arm turns with the left on the same rockshaft, sharing the lifting load. On many tractors the right lift rod has a crank or hydraulic cylinder so its length can be changed for levelling. The hitch can work in position mode, holding a set height, or draft mode, raising and lowering automatically to keep the pull steady as soil changes.
keyNumbers: Hitch lifts roughly 3.5 to 4.5 tonnes at the link ends
Lift from fully down to fully up in a couple of seconds
Typically worked by 1 or 2 hydraulic cylinders
details.madeOf: Forged steel, splined or keyed onto the rockshaft so it can't slip under load.

parts.name: Lift arm (right)

parts.description: Adjustable strut forming the third point of the hitch; its length sets the implement's angle.

details.didYouKnow: Harry Ferguson patented the core ideas of his three-point linkage in the 1920s, and today almost every tractor in the world uses a hitch descended from it.
details.howItWorks: The top link joins a bracket at the back of the tractor to the top point of the implement's mast, completing a triangle with the two lower links. Turning its central barrel, which has opposite threads at each end, lengthens or shortens it and tips the implement forwards or back. In Ferguson's original design, the push and pull on this link signalled the hydraulics to adjust the plough's depth.
keyNumbers: Category 2 top pin about 25 mm
Length typically adjustable over about 15 to 20 cm
Roughly 0.5 to 0.8 m long
details.madeOf: Steel tube with threaded steel rods at each end and forged ball or hook ends. Some top links are hydraulic cylinders that can be adjusted from the seat.

parts.name: Top link

parts.description: Splined stub spinning at 540 or 1,000 rpm that drives mowers, balers and pumps through a shaft.

details.didYouKnow: An unguarded spinning PTO shaft can catch clothing in an instant, which is why every shaft must have a plastic guard and the tractor has a metal shield over the stub.
details.howItWorks: The power take-off is driven straight from the engine through its own clutch and gears, so its speed depends on engine revs, not on the tractor's travel speed. A telescopic drive shaft with universal joints at each end connects it to the implement, so mowers, balers and pumps can be powered while the tractor stands still or moves. The driver selects 540 or 1,000 rpm, and often an economy setting that reaches the same speed at lower engine revs.
keyNumbers: 540 rpm stub has 6 splines
1,000 rpm stub has 21 splines
Stub about 35 mm (1 3/8 inch) across
Can deliver most of the engine's roughly 75 kW
details.madeOf: Hardened alloy steel stub with machined splines. It must survive sudden shock loads when a baler or mower jams.

parts.name: Power take-off shaft

parts.description: Heavy steel bar with a pin for towing trailers and pulled implements.

details.didYouKnow: Since 1920, tractors sold in the US state of Nebraska have had to pass an official test, including measuring their maximum drawbar pull, making it one of the oldest tractor test programmes in the world.
details.howItWorks: The drawbar sits low under the rear axle and carries trailers and trailed implements on a vertical pin. Many swing from side to side and can be pinned in different positions, so a trailed implement can be offset or centred. Hitching low and close to the axle lets the tractor pull hard without the pull trying to tip its nose up.
keyNumbers: Hitch pin typically 30 to 40 mm thick
Allowed vertical load often 1 to 2 tonnes
Can pull tonnes of force in low gears
details.madeOf: Forged or thick plate steel with a hardened steel hitch pin, built to take shock loads when a heavy trailer starts or stops.

parts.name: Drawbar

parts.description: Quick-release couplings that feed pressurised oil to rams and motors on an implement.

details.didYouKnow: A pinhole leak at this pressure can inject oil through the skin, so you should never feel along a hydraulic hose for leaks with bare hands.
details.howItWorks: Each coupler is a self-sealing socket fed by a valve the driver controls from the cab. Pushing in an implement's hose opens matching valves in both halves, so oil can flow without leaking; pulling it out seals both ends. They usually come in pairs, one pressure and one return, to work double-acting cylinders, such as folding a cultivator or tilting a trailer.
keyNumbers: Typically 2 to 4 double-acting pairs
System pressure around 180 to 200 bar
Pump flow roughly 60 to 110 litres a minute
Standard 1/2-inch coupler size
details.madeOf: Plated steel bodies with internal poppet valves and rubber seals, with colour-coded plastic dust caps to show which lever controls which pair.

parts.name: Hydraulic couplers

parts.description: Moulded roof with the air-conditioning unit, radio and a ring of work lights for night working.

details.didYouKnow: Old open tractors could expose drivers to over 90 dB(A) all day; a modern cab is quieter than many family cars were a few decades ago.
details.howItWorks: The roof ties the tops of the four pillars together into a rigid safety cage. Inside it sits the heating and air-conditioning unit, which draws fresh air through filters and blows it into the cab under slight pressure. A ring of work lights around its edges lights the ground all round the tractor for night work, and an opening hatch lets in fresh air on cool days.
keyNumbers: Top of cab roughly 2.7 to 3 m above ground
Often 8 to 12 work lights
Cab noise typically around 70 to 75 dB(A)
details.madeOf: A moulded plastic or glass-fibre shell over a steel frame. Plastic keeps weight down high on the tractor and is easy to mould around ducts and lights.

parts.name: Cab roof

parts.description: Steel pillar of the rollover protective structure that keeps the driver safe if the tractor tips over.

details.didYouKnow: Overturns have long been the leading cause of tractor deaths, and studies show a protective cab or frame plus a fastened seat belt prevents nearly all of them.
details.howItWorks: The front left pillar is one corner of the rollover protective structure. If the tractor rolls, it and the other pillars must hold up the roof and keep a survival space around the seat. It also frames the windscreen and the front edge of the left door, and on many tractors carries a mirror arm.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1.5 to 1.7 m tall
The whole cab frame must absorb several tonnes of crush load
Cab weighs roughly 500 to 800 kg
details.madeOf: Pressed and welded steel tube, kept slim to block as little of the view as possible while still being strong enough to pass rollover tests.

parts.name: Cab pillar (front left)

parts.description: Steel pillar of the rollover protective structure that keeps the driver safe if the tractor tips over.

details.didYouKnow: Sweden was among the first countries to require rollover protection on new tractors, in the late 1950s, and tractor deaths there fell sharply afterwards.
details.howItWorks: The front right pillar mirrors the left, framing the windscreen and the right door. Pillars are designed together with the roof so that in a roll the energy goes into bending the structure in a controlled way rather than collapsing onto the driver. Wiring for lights and indicators often runs up inside it to the roof.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1.5 to 1.7 m tall
Tested to standard OECD codes
Typically just a few centimetres wide
details.madeOf: High-strength welded steel tube, painted. Steel can bend and absorb energy without snapping, which is exactly what is needed in a crash.

parts.name: Cab pillar (front right)

parts.description: Steel pillar of the rollover protective structure that keeps the driver safe if the tractor tips over.

details.didYouKnow: In the UK, new tractors have had to be fitted with safety cabs or frames since 1970, after rules introduced in the late 1960s.
details.howItWorks: The rear left pillar carries the back corner of the cab and is usually where the left door hinges. It bolts down through rubber mounts towards the rear axle housing, and it takes much of the load when the cab is tested from behind and from the side. The rear window latches or hinges onto the rear pillars too.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1.6 to 1.8 m tall
Door hinges usually carry a 25 to 40 kg door
Mounted on rubber blocks to cut vibration
details.madeOf: Welded steel section, often a little heavier than the front pillars, since it sits nearer the main load path to the rear axle.

parts.name: Cab pillar (rear left)

parts.description: Steel pillar of the rollover protective structure that keeps the driver safe if the tractor tips over.

details.didYouKnow: A four-post cab with no central pillars gives almost unbroken all-round glass, which drivers value when checking implements on both sides.
details.howItWorks: The rear right pillar completes the four-post cage and hangs the right door. Close by on many tractors are the electrical sockets and cable entries that let implement control boxes and monitors be plugged in from outside. It shares the rollover load with the other three pillars through the roof and floor frames.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1.6 to 1.8 m tall
One of 4 posts in the safety cage
Cabs are tested by crushing and side-loading to set forces
details.madeOf: Welded steel tube, painted, with threaded inserts for mirrors, sockets and handholds.

parts.name: Cab pillar (rear right)

parts.description: Tall front glass giving a clear view down to the front wheels and the work ahead.

details.didYouKnow: Some tractors have a tall one-piece windscreen curving into the roof, purely so drivers can watch a loader bucket overhead without craning their necks.
details.howItWorks: The windscreen gives the driver a view forward over the sloping bonnet and down to the front wheels. It is usually curved and reaches up into the roof line so the driver can also see a front loader at full height. A large wiper and a heated screen or fan blower keep it clear in rain and frost.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1.2 to 1.5 m tall
Glass typically 5 to 8 mm thick
Wiper often sweeps over 1 m of screen
details.madeOf: Safety glass, usually toughened so it breaks into small blunt pieces, and sometimes laminated. Glass stays clear and scratch-free better than plastic.

parts.name: Windscreen

parts.description: Glass door hung on the cab pillars; the cab is sealed and pressurised to keep dust out.

details.didYouKnow: Cabs approved for spraying pesticides use carbon filters as well as dust filters, and keeping the doors shut is what lets them protect the driver.
details.howItWorks: The left door is the main way in on most tractors, reached by the steps beside the fuel tank. It swings on hinges at the rear pillar and latches at the front, held open by a gas strut. Rubber seals all round it, plus filtered fan air keeping the cab slightly above outside pressure, stop dust and spray from getting in.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1.6 to 1.8 m tall
Glass about 6 to 8 mm thick
Cab overpressure typically a fraction of a millibar to a few millibars

parts.name: Cab door (left)

parts.description: Glass door hung on the cab pillars; the cab is sealed and pressurised to keep dust out.

details.didYouKnow: Rules require a tractor cab to have an emergency exit on a different side from the main door, which a second door or an opening window provides.
details.howItWorks: The right door gives a second exit, useful in an emergency or when working alongside a hedge or trailer. Many drivers leave it partly open on hot days, though that breaks the seal that keeps dust out. Like the left door it hangs on the rear pillar and latches to the front one, with a handle inside and out.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1.6 to 1.8 m tall
Opens to about 90 degrees or more
Weighs about 25 to 40 kg

parts.name: Cab door (right)

parts.description: Opening rear glass so the driver can watch the hitch and the implement.

details.didYouKnow: Tractor drivers spend so much time looking backwards that many seats swivel, and some tractors even have a reversible driving position for working backwards.
details.howItWorks: The rear window lets the driver keep an eye on the hitch, PTO shaft and implement, which on a tractor matters almost as much as looking ahead. It hinges at the top and props open, so cables and hoses for implement controls can be passed in and fresh air let through. A rear wiper keeps it clear when spray and dust are kicked up behind.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1 to 1.2 m tall
Opens roughly 30 to 45 degrees
Glass typically 5 to 6 mm thick

parts.name: Rear window

parts.description: Air-suspended seat that soaks up jolts from rough fields over a long working day.

details.didYouKnow: Early tractor seats were pressed-steel pans on a springy steel bar, and today those old seats are popular collectors' items.
details.howItWorks: The seat sits on a scissor linkage with an air spring and a shock absorber, fed by a small compressor. It adjusts automatically or at the touch of a lever to suit the driver's weight, then floats so jolts from the field are absorbed instead of passing into the spine. A switch under the cushion tells the tractor whether anyone is sitting there, so things like the PTO can stop if the driver leaves.
keyNumbers: Suspension travel about 80 to 100 mm
Adjusts for drivers of roughly 50 to 130 kg
Swivels about 15 to 20 degrees
details.madeOf: A steel frame and suspension with foam padding and hard-wearing fabric cover. Fabric breathes better than vinyl on hot days.

parts.name: Driver's seat

parts.description: Turns the front wheels through hydraulic power steering.

details.didYouKnow: Because hydrostatic steering has no mechanical link, a steering wheel's spokes slowly drift out of line as you drive, which is normal on a tractor.
details.howItWorks: The wheel drives a hydraulic steering valve rather than a mechanical box. As it turns, the valve meters oil to a cylinder on the front axle in proportion to how far the wheel moves, so there is no solid link between the wheel and the front wheels. The column usually tilts and telescopes to suit the driver, and a horn button sits in the centre.
keyNumbers: About 4 to 5 turns lock to lock
Wheel roughly 40 cm across
Steering oil typically at up to around 150 to 200 bar
details.madeOf: A steel core rim covered in moulded plastic or polyurethane foam for grip. The steel core keeps it from breaking if leant on hard.

parts.name: Steering wheel

parts.description: Instrument panel and armrest console with the gear, PTO and hitch controls.

details.didYouKnow: Many tractors share a standard data plug, called ISOBUS, so one cab screen can run a sprayer, seed drill or baler from any maker.
details.howItWorks: The dashboard shows engine revs, forward speed, PTO speed, fuel, coolant temperature and warning lights. Beside the seat an armrest console carries the gear and shuttle controls, the hitch height and draft dials, the PTO switches and levers for each pair of hydraulic couplers. Electronics link these controls to valves and clutches all over the tractor, and a screen can show settings and implement data.
keyNumbers: Engine rev counter usually reads to about 3,000 rpm
PTO speed marked at 540 and 1,000 rpm
Often 2 to 4 hydraulic levers
details.madeOf: Injection-moulded plastic panels around electronic displays, switches and wiring. Plastic can be moulded into ergonomic shapes and doesn't conduct electricity.

parts.name: Dashboard & controls

parts.description: Platform the cab sits on, isolated from the chassis on rubber mounts, with steps up to the door.

details.didYouKnow: Mounting the whole cab on rubber blocks was one of the biggest steps in cutting the noise and vibration reaching tractor drivers.
details.howItWorks: The cab floor is the base of the cab structure, carrying the seat, pedals and controls. It sits on rubber isolation mounts on the transmission and rear axle, so engine and gearbox vibration is filtered out before it reaches the driver. The steps up to the door are fixed to it and usually lit so the driver can climb in safely in the dark.
keyNumbers: Floor roughly 1 to 1.2 m above ground
Usually 3 or 4 steps
Typically 4 rubber cab mounts
details.madeOf: Welded steel plate and sections, covered inside with a rubber mat for grip and sound damping. The steps are open steel grating that lets mud fall through.

parts.name: Cab floor & steps

summary: A 100-horsepower farm tractor: a turbo-diesel engine and a many-speed gearbox drive huge rear tyres for grip in soft fields, while the hitch, power take-off and hydraulics drive and lift the implements it pulls.

name: Shinkansen Bullet Train
overview:
The Shinkansen is Japan's high-speed railway, opened in 1964 between Tokyo and Osaka as the world's first dedicated bullet-train line. Its trains run on their own fenced, level-crossing-free tracks at up to 300 km/h or more, and on the busiest line a train leaves every few minutes, with average delays measured in seconds.

Each train is an electric multiple unit: instead of one locomotive pulling coaches, most of the cars have their own motors in their bogies, so power and grip are spread along the whole train. A pantograph on the roof picks up 25,000-volt alternating current from the overhead wire; transformers and converters under the floor turn it into three-phase power for the traction motors, and those same motors act as generators when braking, feeding energy back into the line.

The long, flattened nose is shaped mainly for tunnels. A blunt train entering a tunnel at speed shoves a pressure wave ahead of it that can bang out of the far end like a sonic boom; stretching and shaping the nose eases the air in gradually and also cuts drag and noise. Underneath, air springs and active dampers keep the ride smooth, and each car tilts slightly on curves so passengers barely feel the turn.

parts.description: Ten-metre-long sculpted nose that eases the train into tunnels and through the air.

details.didYouKnow: Engineer Eiji Nakatsu, a keen birdwatcher, modelled the 500 Series nose on the beak of a kingfisher, which dives into water with barely a splash. The result was quieter at tunnel exits and used less energy.
details.howItWorks: When a train rushes into a tunnel it pushes a wall of air ahead of it, and a blunt front squeezes that air suddenly. The long, gradually widening nose lets the cross-section grow slowly, so the pressure rises gently instead of in one sharp jump. The flattened, winged shape also steers air smoothly over the windscreen and around the sides, cutting drag and wind noise, and it houses the headlights and the hidden emergency coupler.
keyNumbers: About 10 m long
Roughly a third of the car's 27 m length
Shaped for speeds up to about 300 km/h
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy panels shaped over a frame, often hand-finished by skilled panel beaters because the complex curves are hard to press in one go. Aluminium keeps the overhanging nose light.

parts.name: Aerodynamic nose

parts.description: Hinged tip of the nose that opens to reveal an emergency coupler for towing a failed train.

details.didYouKnow: Because a Shinkansen lead car almost never couples at the front, this cover can spend years without being opened except during maintenance checks.
details.howItWorks: The very tip of the nose is a separate cover that stays shut and flush in normal running, keeping the airflow smooth. If a train breaks down, crews open it to swing out the coupler inside so a rescue train can push or pull it clear. Latches hold it tight against the buffeting air at full speed.
keyNumbers: Opened only a handful of times in a typical train's life
Has to stay sealed at up to about 300 km/h
Sits roughly at buffer height, about 1 m above the rail
details.madeOf: Painted aluminium or fibre-reinforced plastic, matched exactly to the surrounding nose so there is no step for the air to catch on.

parts.name: Coupler cover

parts.description: Folding coupler kept inside the nose; normally the lead car never couples at this end.

details.didYouKnow: Shinkansen trains run as fixed sets and are almost never split in service on the Tokaido line, so the front coupler exists mainly as insurance.
details.howItWorks: The coupler folds away inside the nose and is swung out and locked in position only when a failed train needs rescuing. It mates with the coupler of the rescue train so the two can be moved together at low speed. Between cars inside the train, separate permanent couplers do the everyday work.
keyNumbers: A 16-car set weighs roughly 700 tonnes
Rescue moves are made at walking to modest speeds
Coupler parts weigh up to a few hundred kilograms
details.madeOf: Forged and cast high-strength steel, because it must carry the full pulling and pushing load of a heavy train without cracking.

parts.name: Emergency coupler

parts.description: Curved, heated laminated windscreen tough enough to stop a bird strike at 300 km/h.

details.didYouKnow: Railway windscreens are certified by firing objects, such as a weighted projectile, at them at high speed to prove they will stop a bird or debris strike.
details.howItWorks: The windscreen gives the driver a wide view of the line ahead while forming part of the pressure-tight cab. Thin heating elements in the layers keep it clear of mist and ice. Its curve follows the nose so air flows smoothly over it, and the layers are bonded so that if the outer pane cracks, the inner ones still hold.
keyNumbers: Several centimetres thick in total
Tested against impacts at up to about 300 km/h
Heated to stay clear in sub-zero weather
details.madeOf: Several layers of glass bonded with tough plastic interlayers, sometimes with polycarbonate, so it resists impacts without shattering into the cab.

parts.name: Driver's windscreen

parts.description: LED headlight and red tail light in one unit, faired smoothly into the nose.

details.didYouKnow: Because the end cars swap roles every trip, each Shinkansen spends about half its life with these lamps glowing red as tail lights.
details.howItWorks: The left lamp unit shines white when this car leads and switches to red when it is the rear of the train, so the same car works in either direction. It sits low on the nose to light the track and make the train visible from far away. Together with the right lamp it gives a recognisable pair of lights to track workers and stations.
keyNumbers: LEDs typically last tens of thousands of hours
Visible from well over a kilometre away
One of two lamps on the nose
details.madeOf: LED modules behind a clear polycarbonate cover shaped to match the nose. LEDs last far longer than old filament bulbs and use less power.

parts.name: Headlight (left)

parts.description: LED headlight and red tail light in one unit, faired smoothly into the nose.

details.didYouKnow: The lamp lenses are shaped into the nose rather than sticking out, because even a small bump at 300 km/h would add drag and noise.
details.howItWorks: The right lamp mirrors the left, and the pair are switched together from the driver's desk. Having two lamps set wide apart helps people judge the train's distance and speed as it approaches. When the train runs the other way, the cab at the far end takes over and this lamp shows red.
keyNumbers: Power draw of tens of watts rather than hundreds
Sealed against pressure swings in tunnels
Faired flush into the nose curve
details.madeOf: LEDs and reflectors in a sealed housing with a polycarbonate lens, sealed against rain and the pressure changes of tunnels.

parts.name: Headlight (right)

parts.description: Controls and screens: a single power/brake handle, speed readouts and the in-cab signalling display.

details.didYouKnow: There are no traffic-light signals beside Shinkansen tracks; at these speeds a driver could not read them in time, so the signal is shown on the desk instead.
details.howItWorks: The desk brings together power and brake controls, screens showing speed and the permitted speed from the in-cab signalling, and the train's monitoring system. The automatic train control system tells the driver the safe speed and will apply the brakes itself if the train goes too fast. Screens also show the status of doors, motors and brakes along the whole train.
keyNumbers: Controls a train of 16 cars
Signalling updates continuously as speed limits change
Automatic braking steps in above the permitted speed
details.madeOf: Moulded plastic and composite panels over a metal frame, with industrial-grade displays and switches built to last decades of daily use.

parts.name: Driver's desk

parts.description: Seat for the single driver, who watches a cab display rather than lineside signals.

details.didYouKnow: Japanese train drivers are famous for pointing and calling: they point at gauges and signals and say the reading aloud, a habit shown to cut mistakes.
details.howItWorks: The seat holds one driver in a comfortable, adjustable position for long stints at the controls, which on the busiest line can mean running from Tokyo to Osaka in about two and a half hours. It is set so the driver can see the track ahead over the long nose and reach every control. A conductor elsewhere on the train handles the doors and passengers.
keyNumbers: One driver per train
Tokyo to Shin-Osaka is about 515 km
Fastest services take roughly 2 hours 20 minutes
details.madeOf: A steel frame with foam padding and hard-wearing fabric, designed to support good posture and absorb vibration.

parts.name: Driver's seat

parts.description: Long aluminium double-skinned tube forming the passenger saloon; light, stiff and airtight.

details.didYouKnow: The first 0 Series trains in 1964 had steel bodies; moving to aluminium helped later trains become far lighter while carrying the same number of people.
details.howItWorks: The body is built from long hollow aluminium extrusions, each with two skins joined by internal ribs, welded side by side to form the floor, sides and roof. This double skin makes a light but very stiff tube that carries the loads without a heavy separate frame. It is sealed airtight so that tunnel pressure changes do not hurt passengers' ears.
keyNumbers: About 27 m long
About 3.4 m wide
Roughly 3.6 m tall
Weighs a few tonnes as a bare shell
details.madeOf: Aluminium alloy extrusions, often joined by friction stir welding, which fuses the metal without melting it and gives smoother, stronger seams. Aluminium cuts weight compared with steel, saving energy and track wear.

parts.name: Car body shell

parts.description: The classic blue band along the side, with a thinner pinstripe; painted, not structural.

details.didYouKnow: The blue-on-white colour scheme goes back to the original 0 Series of 1964, and the Tokaido line has kept a version of it ever since.
details.howItWorks: The left stripe is just paint or film, but it makes the train instantly recognisable as a Tokaido Shinkansen. A broad blue band runs beneath the windows with a thin pinstripe below it, and it sweeps up into the nose. It has no structural job at all.
keyNumbers: Runs the full 27 m length
Usually repainted every several years
Paint adds only a few tens of kilograms per car
details.madeOf: Durable polyurethane paint or adhesive vinyl over primer on the aluminium, chosen to keep its colour through sun, rain and frequent washing.

parts.name: Blue stripe (left)

parts.description: Row of small, double-glazed windows, kept small to keep the pressure-tight body strong.

details.didYouKnow: None of the passenger windows open; the whole car is sealed and air conditioned, which is what lets it pass through tunnels at speed without ear-popping.
details.howItWorks: Each window is a sealed double-glazed unit set into the body, with an air gap that keeps heat and noise out. Keeping the openings small leaves more aluminium between them, so the pressure-tight tube stays strong. The left windows face north on the run from Tokyo to Osaka.
keyNumbers: Roughly 1 m wide each
Two panes with an insulating gap
Must survive repeated tunnel pressure swings
details.madeOf: Two panes of toughened or laminated glass sealed into a frame, chosen for strength, insulation and resistance to pressure changes.

parts.name: Passenger windows (left)

parts.description: Door that swings out and slides along, then pulls in to seal flush and airtight against the body.

details.didYouKnow: On the Tokaido line platform screen doors and gates line up with the train doors, so trains have to stop within tens of centimetres of their mark.
details.howItWorks: When opening, the door first pushes out from the body, then slides along the outside. When closing, it slides back and pulls inward to seal flush, with seals pressed tight around the edges. This keeps the side smooth for the airflow and the car pressure-tight in tunnels.
keyNumbers: About 1 m wide opening
Opens and closes in a few seconds
Station stops are often only about 1 minute
details.madeOf: An aluminium skin over a light frame with rubber seals, moved by electric or pneumatic actuators.

parts.name: Plug door (left)

parts.description: Smooth panel hiding the equipment under the floor to cut drag and noise.

details.didYouKnow: In winter, snow around Sekigahara can pack into the underfloor area, so tracks there have sprinklers to keep the snow wet and stop it building up on trains.
details.howItWorks: The left skirt covers the boxes, cables and pipes under the floor so the air sees a smooth surface instead of rough equipment. That cuts drag and the roaring noise that rough shapes make at speed. Panels lift or unclip so maintenance staff can reach the equipment behind.
keyNumbers: Panels each a metre or two long
Run most of the 27 m car length
Hang a few tens of centimetres above the rail
details.madeOf: Aluminium or fibre-reinforced plastic panels, light and easy to shape to the body's curve.

parts.name: Side skirt (left)

parts.description: The classic blue band along the side, with a thinner pinstripe; painted, not structural.

details.didYouKnow: Different Shinkansen lines use their own colours, such as green or red, so the blue stripe quietly signals that this is a Tokaido-style train.
details.howItWorks: The right stripe matches the left exactly so the train looks the same from either platform. Along with the white body it helps staff and passengers tell which line or operator a train belongs to at a glance. Like its twin, it is decoration rather than structure.
keyNumbers: About 27 m long on this car
Repeated on all 16 cars of the train
A train is roughly 400 m long, stripe and all
details.madeOf: Weather-resistant paint or vinyl film, kept thin and smooth so it does not add drag.

parts.name: Blue stripe (right)

parts.description: Row of small, double-glazed windows, kept small to keep the pressure-tight body strong.

details.didYouKnow: Mount Fuji appears on the right-hand side heading west from Tokyo, so seat E, the window seat on the three-seat side, is a favourite.
details.howItWorks: The right-hand windows match those on the left and are sealed into the same airtight body. On a journey from Tokyo towards Osaka, seats on this side are the ones passengers book for a view of Mount Fuji. Small windows also keep the cabin cooler in sunshine.
keyNumbers: Each roughly 1 m wide
Glazing several millimetres thick per pane
details.madeOf: Double-glazed safety glass with a tinted or coated outer pane to cut glare and solar heat.

parts.name: Passenger windows (right)

parts.description: Door that swings out and slides along, then pulls in to seal flush and airtight against the body.

details.didYouKnow: At Tokyo station, cleaning crews have only about seven minutes between arrival and departure to tidy a whole train, a routine nicknamed the 'seven-minute miracle'.
details.howItWorks: The right door works the same way as the left, and the conductor opens only the side facing the platform. Interlocks stop the train from taking power until every door on the train is shut and locked. Inflatable or compressed seals around the frame keep tunnel pressure out.
keyNumbers: Typically one or two doors per side on a car
Tens of thousands of cycles per year
Seals hold against pressure swings in tunnels
details.madeOf: Aluminium panels, rubber seals and a steel mechanism, built to open and close many thousands of times a year.

parts.name: Plug door (right)

parts.description: Smooth panel hiding the equipment under the floor to cut drag and noise.

details.didYouKnow: Shinkansen operators measure noise beside the line carefully, and smoothing the underside is one way trains have become quieter even as they got faster.
details.howItWorks: The right skirt mirrors the left, enclosing the underfloor space so the side of the train is smooth all the way down. Openings and louvres let cooling air reach the transformer and converter while keeping the outline sleek. Partial covers around the bogies also help reduce noise near the wheels.
keyNumbers: Cuts drag on a train that runs at up to about 300 km/h
Covers equipment weighing several tonnes
Removable in sections for servicing
details.madeOf: Light aluminium or composite panels, fixed with quick-release fasteners for inspection access.

parts.name: Side skirt (right)

parts.description: Folding arm that presses a carbon strip up against the overhead wire to collect power (on real trains it rides on a middle car; it's shown here to complete the picture).

details.didYouKnow: Nakatsu also borrowed from owls: the 500 Series pantograph had serrated, feather-like edges that broke up the airflow and made it much quieter.
details.howItWorks: A spring or air-driven arm pushes a carbon contact strip up against the overhead wire with a steady light force, collecting current as the strip slides along. Current flows down to the main transformer. On real trains only a couple of pantographs are raised on middle cars of the 16-car set, not on the lead car; one is shown here so you can see the whole power path.
keyNumbers: Collects 25,000 volts AC at 60 Hz
Wire about 5 m above the rails
Typically two raised per 16-car train
details.madeOf: A steel or aluminium arm with a carbon strip on the head, because carbon conducts well, lubricates itself and wears gently on the copper wire.

parts.name: Pantograph

parts.description: Flexible, sealed connection leading passengers through to the next car.

details.didYouKnow: Smooth covers over the gaps between cars cut drag and noise, because every gap along a 400 m train adds turbulence.
details.howItWorks: The bellows link the end of this car to the next, giving passengers and crew a covered walkway through the train. It flexes as the cars move relative to each other on curves and over bumps. It is sealed so the whole train stays pressure-tight in tunnels, and outer covers smooth over the gap for the airflow.
keyNumbers: Gap between cars under about 1 m
One at the rear of the lead car
About 15 between the 16 cars of a train
details.madeOf: Rubber-coated fabric bellows on metal frames, flexible but airtight and fire-resistant.

parts.name: Gangway bellows

parts.description: Floating floor isolated from the body to keep the cabin quiet at speed.

details.didYouKnow: Tests of noise inside the car help decide the thickness and mounts of the floor, because much of the sound at speed comes up from the wheels and rails.
details.howItWorks: The floor sits on rubber mounts above the body's structural floor, so vibration from the bogies and noise from below are not passed straight to passengers' feet. Seats bolt into rails in the floor, and cables and ducts can run in the gap underneath. It is part of what makes a 300 km/h ride feel calm enough to rest a drink on the table.
keyNumbers: Floor roughly 1.3 m above the rail
Panels a few centimetres thick
Covers about 25 m of saloon length
details.madeOf: Honeycomb or composite panels with an aluminium or plywood core, topped with a hard-wearing, fire-resistant covering.

parts.name: Passenger floor

parts.description: Rows of three seats on one side of the aisle; whole rows rotate to face the direction of travel at the terminus.

details.didYouKnow: During the turnaround at Tokyo, the cleaning crew swivels every seat row as part of the seven-minute clean, often with a single push of a pedal.
details.howItWorks: Each three-seat row sits on a pivoting base, and at the terminus the rows are turned around so everyone faces forward for the return trip. Backrests recline and there is a fold-down table on the seat in front. Three-plus-two seating across the wide 3.4 m body is what lets a train carry so many people.
keyNumbers: Seat pitch about 1 m
Around 1,300 seats per 16-car train
Rows turn 180 degrees at the terminus

parts.name: Seat rows (three-seat side)

parts.description: Rows of two seats on the other side of the aisle.

details.didYouKnow: The middle seat on the three-seat side is a little wider on some trains, a small touch to make the least-loved seat more comfortable.
details.howItWorks: The two-seat rows sit on the other side of the aisle and turn around at the end of the line just like the three-seat ones. The narrower block leaves room for an aisle down the car. Many passengers travelling in pairs choose this side.
keyNumbers: 2 seats per row
Recline of a few tens of degrees
Five seats across with the three-seat side

parts.name: Seat rows (two-seat side)

parts.description: Overhead shelves running the length of the saloon.

details.didYouKnow: Since 2020 the Tokaido line has asked passengers with very large suitcases to reserve a seat with oversized-luggage space, because racks fill up fast.
details.howItWorks: The racks run along both sides above the windows, keeping bags off the floor and out of the aisle. They are fixed to the body's side and roof structure and designed to hold their load through acceleration, braking and gentle tilting on curves. Lips at the edge stop items sliding off.
keyNumbers: Run nearly the full saloon length
Sit roughly 1.8 m above the floor
Each section carries tens of kilograms

parts.name: Luggage racks

parts.description: Welded steel frame carrying two wheelsets, their motors and brakes, with springs between it and the body.

details.didYouKnow: Some newer Shinkansen bogies carry sensors that watch temperatures and vibrations in service, warning of trouble long before a fault could develop.
details.howItWorks: The front bogie sits under the cab end, so it carries the weight of the nose and is the first to meet every curve and bump in the track. It holds two wheelsets in axle boxes with springs, and the body rests on it through the air springs. Dampers between bogie and body stop the side-to-side wobble called hunting that can build up at high speed.
keyNumbers: Wheelbase about 2.5 m
Weighs several tonnes
Bogie centres roughly 17.5 m apart
details.madeOf: Welded steel plates formed into box-section beams, chosen for strength, stiffness and resistance to fatigue over millions of kilometres.

parts.name: Bogie frame (front bogie)

parts.description: Two steel wheels pressed onto a solid axle; their tapered treads steer the train along the rails without flanges touching.

details.didYouKnow: Lead wheelsets are re-profiled on a lathe more often than those further back, because they meet every rail joint and curve first.
details.howItWorks: This is the very first axle of the whole train, so it guides the car into curves and takes the most wear. Its coned treads mean the outer wheel rolls on a larger diameter in a curve, steering the axle around without the flanges scraping. Brake discs are mounted on the wheels.
keyNumbers: About 860 mm wheel diameter when new
Spaced for 1,435 mm standard gauge
Turns over 1,800 times a minute at 300 km/h
details.madeOf: Forged or rolled steel wheels pressed onto a solid steel axle, hardened at the tread to resist wear.

parts.name: Wheelset (front bogie, axle 1)

parts.description: Two steel wheels pressed onto a solid axle; their tapered treads steer the train along the rails without flanges touching.

details.didYouKnow: Shinkansen tracks are laid on fenced, dedicated routes with no level crossings, which removes a whole class of accidents that ordinary railways face.
details.howItWorks: The second axle shares the front bogie with the first, following it through every curve. Because the first axle has already guided the bogie, it usually sees a little less flange contact and wear. It carries its own brake discs and is driven by its own motor through a gearbox.
keyNumbers: Wheels replaced after wearing down by several centimetres
Axle load roughly 11 to 14 tonnes
Gauge 1,435 mm

parts.name: Wheelset (front bogie, axle 2)

parts.description: Pair of three-phase motors, one per axle, that drive the wheels through gears and act as generators when braking.

details.didYouKnow: On many recent 16-car sets the end cars are actually unpowered and 14 cars carry motors; the model shows them here so you can see how the drive works.
details.howItWorks: Each motor hangs from the front bogie and turns its axle through a gearbox and flexible coupling. The converter feeds it three-phase current, and changing the frequency changes the speed. When the driver brakes, the motors become generators, slowing the train while sending electricity back up to the wire.

Two per bogie, one per axle
Spin several thousand rpm at top speed

parts.name: Traction motors (front bogie)

parts.description: Rubber bellows of compressed air between the bogie and the body; it can lift one side slightly to tilt the car into curves.

details.didYouKnow: Tilting by just a degree on curves lets recent trains keep up 270 km/h on the twisty Tokaido line where older ones had to slow.
details.howItWorks: This bellows sits on the left side of the front bogie, under the cab end. It holds the body at a constant height whatever the passenger load by adding or releasing air. On curves bending right, it can be inflated a little more than its partner to lean the car into the bend.
keyNumbers: Body tilt of up to about 1 degree
Air pressure typically a few bar
Supports several tonnes of car

parts.name: Air spring (front bogie, left)

parts.description: Rubber bellows of compressed air between the bogie and the body; it can lift one side slightly to tilt the car into curves.

details.didYouKnow: The tilt is triggered from a stored map of the line, so the train starts leaning as it enters a curve rather than waiting to feel it.
details.howItWorks: The right-hand front air spring partners the left one under the cab end. On curves bending left it is pumped up a little to tilt the car into the turn, so passengers feel less sideways push. Valves level it automatically as passengers board and leave.

Works with an air supply of about 8 to 9 bar
One of four on this car

parts.description: Welded steel frame carrying two wheelsets, their motors and brakes, with springs between it and the body.

details.didYouKnow: A yellow inspection train nicknamed Doctor Yellow has run along the line for decades measuring track and wire, so problems are found before the bogies meet them.
details.howItWorks: The rear bogie sits about 17.5 m behind the front one, near the gangway end of the car. It carries less of the nose's overhang but more of the passenger saloon. It follows in the track already taken by the front bogie, and it holds its own wheelsets, motors, brakes and dampers.

Overhauled roughly every few years

parts.description: Two steel wheels pressed onto a solid axle; their tapered treads steer the train along the rails without flanges touching.

details.didYouKnow: Each wheel rests on the rail on a patch of steel only about the size of a small coin, carrying several tonnes.
details.howItWorks: This is the last axle of the lead car, and when the train runs the other way it is no longer at the front at all. It shares the rear bogie with axle 3 and carries brake discs on its wheels. Like every axle, its coned treads self-centre it on straight track.

Load per axle roughly 11 to 14 tonnes
Wheels replaced once worn by several centimetres

parts.name: Wheelset (rear bogie, axle 2)

parts.description: Pair of three-phase motors, one per axle, that drive the wheels through gears and act as generators when braking.

details.didYouKnow: The first 0 Series trains of 1964 ran at 210 km/h; today's trains are much faster yet use far less energy per seat, thanks largely to lighter bodies and regenerative braking.
details.howItWorks: The rear motors drive the third and fourth axles, sharing the job of pushing and braking the train with motors in other cars. Spreading drive across most axles of a 16-car train gives strong grip and acceleration without heavy locomotives. In braking, they return energy to the wire for other trains to use.

A whole train totals around 17,000 kW

parts.name: Traction motors (rear bogie)

parts.description: Rubber bellows of compressed air between the bogie and the body; it can lift one side slightly to tilt the car into curves.

details.didYouKnow: Before tilting, curves on the old Tokaido line forced trains down to around 250 km/h, because the route was laid out in the early 1960s.
details.howItWorks: The rear left air spring works as a team with the front left one, so the whole left side of the car lifts evenly when tilting. It cushions small bumps that the bogie springs pass up and keeps the floor level as the load changes. Dampers alongside it stop the body bouncing.

Supports several tonnes

parts.name: Air spring (rear bogie, left)

parts.description: Rubber bellows of compressed air between the bogie and the body; it can lift one side slightly to tilt the car into curves.

details.didYouKnow: Shinkansen trains also carry earthquake protection: early-warning seismometers can cut power and trigger the brakes within seconds of detecting a quake.
details.howItWorks: The fourth air spring, rear right, completes the set that carries the car body. With its three partners it lets the body float on air while the bogies take the shocks from the rails. In a curve to the left it rises with the front right spring to bank the car.
keyNumbers: One of four on the car
Tilt up to about 1 degree
Height held to within a few millimetres
