parts.name: Air spring (rear bogie, right)

parts.description: Steps the 25,000-volt supply from the overhead wire down to a level the converters can use.

details.didYouKnow: Japan's grid runs at 50 Hz in the east and 60 Hz in the west, yet the Tokaido Shinkansen uses 60 Hz all the way, with converter stations feeding the eastern part.
details.howItWorks: The transformer takes 25,000-volt alternating current from the pantograph and steps it down through coils wound on an iron core. Its output feeds the converters that drive the motors, and other windings supply lighting and air conditioning. It is cooled by oil pumped through a radiator.
keyNumbers: Input 25,000 V at 60 Hz
Weighs a few tonnes
Several transformers spread along a 16-car train
details.madeOf: Copper or aluminium windings on a laminated steel core, sealed in a steel or aluminium tank filled with insulating oil.

parts.name: Main transformer

parts.description: Power electronics that turn the transformer's output into variable-frequency three-phase power for the motors.

details.didYouKnow: Shinkansen trains are remarkably punctual: on the Tokaido line the average delay per train is typically well under a minute, including weather and other disruption.
details.howItWorks: The converter first turns the transformer's AC into DC, then uses fast-switching transistors to build three-phase AC at whatever frequency and voltage the motors need. Raising the frequency speeds the motors up. In braking it runs in reverse, sending power from the motors back towards the wire.
keyNumbers: Switches thousands of times a second
Feeds motors totalling over 1,000 kW per car
Weighs up to about a tonne
details.madeOf: Silicon or silicon-carbide power transistors on cooled heat sinks, inside a sealed metal box. Newer silicon-carbide chips waste less heat, so the boxes can be smaller and lighter.

parts.name: Traction converter

parts.description: Supplies compressed air for the air springs, doors and backup brakes.

details.didYouKnow: Because the motors do most of the braking, the air brakes on a Shinkansen mostly work at low speed and in emergencies, so the brake pads last a long time.
details.howItWorks: A motor-driven compressor fills reservoirs with dry compressed air for the air springs, the door mechanisms, horns and the backup air brakes. A dryer removes moisture so valves do not corrode or freeze. A pressure switch starts and stops it as air is used.
keyNumbers: Typically about 8 to 9 bar
Several per 16-car train
Delivers hundreds of litres of air a minute
details.madeOf: Cast aluminium or iron housings with steel internals, often a screw or scroll design for quiet, smooth running.

parts.name: Air compressor

summary: The lead car of a Japanese Shinkansen: 27 m long with a 10 m aerodynamic nose, part of a 16-car electric train that carries about 1,300 passengers at up to 300 km/h.

name: Eiffel Tower
overview:
The Eiffel Tower was built in just over two years for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, the World's Fair marking a century since the French Revolution. Designed by the engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier and the architect Stephen Sauvestre at Gustave Eiffel's company, it was the tallest structure in the world for 41 years. It was meant to stand for only 20; it survived because its height made it useful for radio.

It's a wind-shaped lattice. Four huge legs, each a curved box of iron girders, rise from masonry foundations and lean in to meet in a single tapering tower. Their curve follows the forces that wind puts on the tower, so the open lattice lets air through and the whole thing weighs surprisingly little for its size: about 7,300 tonnes of iron, less than the air in a box the same size. The decorative arches between the legs carry almost no load.

Visitors climb or ride up to three levels: the first floor at 57 m, the second at 116 m and the top at 276 m, where Eiffel kept a small apartment. Lifts run up the curving legs on inclined tracks, and today antennas on the very top broadcast radio and television across Paris. The tower is repainted by hand about every seven years to stop it rusting.

parts.description: Block of limestone and concrete under each leg corner, spreading the leg's weight into the ground.

details.didYouKnow: The two legs nearest the Seine sit on wetter ground, so their foundations were dug inside sealed iron boxes pumped full of compressed air to keep river water out while men worked below.
details.howItWorks: Each leg ends in iron shoes that sit on solid masonry blocks, so the curved corner girders press straight down into stone rather than onto soil. The blocks spread the load over a wide area, keeping the pressure on the ground surprisingly gentle. During building, hydraulic jacks set into the shoes let engineers raise or lower each leg slightly so all four met the first floor girders perfectly level.
keyNumbers: About 125 m between the outer corners of the base
Construction began on the foundations in about January 1887
Pressure on the soil roughly like a person sitting on a chair
details.madeOf: Cut limestone blocks laid on beds of concrete. Stone and concrete are excellent in compression and do not rust, which suits a part that only ever gets pushed down on and sits close to damp ground.

parts.name: Masonry foundation pier

parts.description: Outer corner girder of a leg, the curved edge you see in every photograph; it follows the line of wind forces down to the ground.

details.didYouKnow: While the legs were being built they leaned out unsupported, so wooden scaffolding towers and sand boxes propped them up until they could be joined at the first floor.
details.howItWorks: This is one of the two girders on the outside face of a leg, and its sweeping curve is the tower's signature line. Eiffel's engineers shaped the curve so that the forces from wind pushing on the tower run down through the legs and into the foundations without bending them. It joins the other corner girders through lattice bracing and, higher up, the horizontal belt of girders under the first floor.
keyNumbers: About 57 m of climb to the first floor
Rises roughly 116 m before the legs merge into one shaft
One of 16 corner girders across the four legs
details.madeOf: Puddled iron, a very pure wrought iron worked by hand in the furnace. It is tough and forgiving rather than brittle, and the real girder is a riveted box built up from plates and angle sections, simplified here into a single bar.

parts.name: Leg corner girder (outer)

parts.description: The other outer corner girder of the leg.

details.didYouKnow: Every hole for every rivet was drilled in Eiffel's workshop at Levallois-Perret before delivery, so pieces arrived ready to bolt and rivet with almost no fitting on site.
details.howItWorks: The second outer corner girder forms the other edge of the leg's outward-facing side, so together the pair frames the face you see from the street. Because the two outer girders splay apart at the base and close in as they rise, each leg is widest at the ground where loads are greatest. Lattice bars between them stop either one from buckling sideways.
keyNumbers: Each leg roughly 25 m across at its foot
Rests on its own masonry block
Part of about 7,300 tonnes of ironwork
details.madeOf: Puddled iron plates and angles joined by hot-driven rivets. In reality it is a hollow box girder, which gives a lot of stiffness for little weight.

parts.name: Leg corner girder (outer (second))

parts.description: Inner corner girder of a leg, facing the middle of the tower.

details.didYouKnow: Hydraulic jacks under the legs could nudge them by millimetres, letting the builders bring all four legs to the first floor girders with very little error.
details.howItWorks: The inner corner girders face the middle of the tower and are the ones that meet the great horizontal girders carrying the first floor. They curve more gently than you might expect, leaning in to meet their partners from the other legs. Getting the four inner sets to line up at about 57 m up was the trickiest moment of construction.
keyNumbers: About 57 m up to where it meets the first floor girders
Legs joined at the first floor by about early 1888
Some 2.5 million rivets in the whole tower
details.madeOf: Puddled iron box girder, riveted from flat plates and angle sections. Wrought iron was chosen over cast iron because it copes well with the pulling forces that wind creates on the inward side.

parts.name: Leg corner girder (inner)

parts.description: The other inner corner girder of the leg.

details.didYouKnow: Rivets were heated red hot and hammered in by teams of about four men; as each rivet cooled it shrank and pulled the plates tightly together.
details.howItWorks: This second inner girder completes the box-shaped leg, so each leg is really a tall, tapering four-sided column. With its partner it frames the inside face, which looks across the open space under the tower. When wind blows, the leeward inner girders are squeezed while those on the windward side are pulled, and the lattice shares the load between them.
keyNumbers: About 18,000 individual iron parts in the tower
Most pieces light enough for a small crane
Top of the tower sways only a few cm in wind
details.madeOf: Riveted puddled iron. Its plates were made in many small pieces light enough to lift with simple cranes, then joined in place.

parts.name: Leg corner girder (inner (second))

parts.description: Criss-cross of small iron bars bracing the leg's girders; it's what makes the tower look like lace.

details.didYouKnow: If all the tower's iron were melted down and spread over the square of its base, it would make a layer only about 6 cm thick.
details.howItWorks: On the lower outer face, these crossing bars tie the two outer corner girders together so neither can bow outward under load. The open criss-cross lets wind pass straight through instead of pushing on a solid wall, which is why such a tall tower needs so little metal. Near the base the bracing is at its largest, matching the wide spread of the leg.
keyNumbers: Spans legs up to roughly 25 m wide
Bracing below about 57 m
Repainted about every 7 years
details.madeOf: Puddled iron flats and angles riveted at every crossing. Many small, thin members are lighter than a few big ones yet still very stiff when triangulated.

parts.name: Leg lattice (lower, outer face)

parts.description: Criss-cross of small iron bars bracing the leg's girders; it's what makes the tower look like lace.

details.didYouKnow: The tower is painted in graded shades, darkest at the bottom and lightest at the top, so that it looks one even colour against the sky.
details.howItWorks: This lattice braces the inner face of a leg below the first floor, the side that looks into the great open space under the tower. It keeps the inner girders working as a team and stops the leg from twisting. It also forms part of the screen through which the leg lifts and stairs can be glimpsed as they climb.

parts.name: Leg lattice (lower, inner face)

parts.description: Criss-cross of small iron bars bracing the leg's girders; it's what makes the tower look like lace.

details.didYouKnow: Because the open lattice catches so little air, the tower's top moves only a few centimetres even in strong winds.
details.howItWorks: Between the first and second floors, the outer faces of the legs narrow and lean inward more steeply, and this lattice keeps them rigid. The bars are smaller here because the legs carry less weight than they do lower down. They also help pass the push of wind from the upper tower down into the leg girders.
keyNumbers: Spans roughly 57 m to 116 m up
Legs merge into one shaft at about 116 m

details.didYouKnow: On a sunny day the side facing the sun expands more than the shaded side, so the whole top of the tower leans gently away from the sun.
details.howItWorks: This bracing stiffens the inner face of each leg between the first and second floors, where the four legs bend towards each other. It works with the second floor girders to lock the legs together as they converge. Visitors riding the leg lifts pass close beside it on the way up.

In Eiffel's design the real work of tying the legs together is done by the straight girders above, so the arches carry little load. details.didYouKnow: The modern pavilions were designed to use energy efficiently, with features such as solar panels and rainwater collection added during the renovation.

details.didYouKnow: Eiffel used the second floor for experiments on air resistance, dropping objects on a cable to measure how air pushed on them.

details.howItWorks: The top floor has an enclosed, glazed level with a panoramic view and a smaller open-air level above it behind safety mesh. It sits where the four upper girders meet, so it is supported from all corners. Visitors also find a champagne bar and Eiffel's restored apartment here.

keyNumbers: About 276 m above Paris
