name: Acoustic Guitar
overview:
An acoustic guitar makes sound with nothing but wood, strings and air. Plucking a string sets it vibrating, but a string on its own is almost silent: it's too thin to push much air. The trick is the bridge, which passes the string's vibration into the soundboard, the guitar's thin wooden top. The big top flexes in and out like a loudspeaker cone and moves enough air to be heard.

The body is a resonating box. Air inside it vibrates too, breathing in and out of the soundhole, which strengthens the low notes. The top has to be thin enough to move freely yet strong enough to resist the strings, which pull with a combined force of about 70 kg, so it's stiffened from underneath with a pattern of thin wooden braces. The X-shaped bracing pattern used here was popularised in the 19th century and shapes much of the guitar's tone.

You change the note by pressing a string against a fret, a metal bar across the fretboard, which shortens the part of the string that vibrates. Frets are spaced so that each one raises the pitch by a semitone, and twelve frets up, halfway along the string, the note is exactly an octave higher. A steel truss rod inside the neck counters the strings' pull so the neck stays straight.

parts.description: String 1, tuned to low E; its length between saddle and nut sets the pitch of the open string.

details.didYouKnow: The guitar body radiates the 82 Hz fundamental only weakly, so much of what you hear as low E is its overtones, with your brain filling in the missing low pitch.
details.howItWorks: The thickest string vibrates slowest, giving the lowest note on the guitar. Its pitch depends on three things: the vibrating length between nut and saddle, the tension set by the tuner, and the string's mass per length. The heavy bronze wrap adds mass so it can sound low while still being tight enough to play cleanly.
keyNumbers: Open note E2, about 82 Hz
Typically about 0.053 in (1.35 mm) thick
Roughly 11 kg of tension
Vibrating length about 645 mm
details.madeOf: A hexagonal high-carbon steel core wrapped in bronze wire. The wrap adds weight without making the string much stiffer, so it still bends easily and stays in tune along its length.

parts.name: Low E string

parts.description: String 2, tuned to A; its length between saddle and nut sets the pitch of the open string.

details.didYouKnow: Open A on a guitar is exactly two octaves below the 440 Hz A that orchestras tune to, so 110 Hz is a quarter of that frequency.
details.howItWorks: The A string sits a perfect fourth above the low E, so pressing the low E at the 5th fret gives the same note, which players use to tune one string from the next. Like the low E it is wound, and its vibration passes through the saddle into the top. Its open note is the root of many common chords, from A major to A minor.
keyNumbers: Open note A2, 110 Hz
Typically about 0.042 in (1.07 mm) thick
Roughly 13 to 14 kg of tension
details.madeOf: A steel core wrapped in bronze wire, slightly thinner than the low E. The wrap keeps the string flexible while giving it enough mass for a low pitch.

parts.name: A string

parts.description: String 3, tuned to D; its length between saddle and nut sets the pitch of the open string.

details.didYouKnow: So-called 80/20 bronze strings are really brass, an alloy of about 80 per cent copper and 20 per cent zinc, while phosphor bronze is copper with tin and a trace of phosphorus.
details.howItWorks: The D string is the thinnest of the heavily wound bass strings and bridges the low and middle range. It vibrates nearly twice as fast as the low E, and because each string is pulled to a similar tension, its thinner gauge is what lets it reach the higher note at the same length. Its ball end hooks under the bridge plate, held in place by a bridge pin.
keyNumbers: Open note D3, about 147 Hz
Typically about 0.032 in (0.81 mm) thick
Roughly 14 kg of tension
details.madeOf: A steel core wrapped in bronze wire, usually phosphor bronze or 80/20 bronze. Bronze gives a bright, ringing tone and resists corrosion better than plain steel.

parts.name: D string

parts.description: String 4, tuned to G; its length between saddle and nut sets the pitch of the open string.

details.didYouKnow: Electric guitar sets usually have a plain G string, which is easier to bend, but acoustic sets wind it because a plain G that thick would sound dull and play out of tune.
details.howItWorks: The G string is the last wound string, sitting in the middle of the guitar's range. Being wound makes it thicker and more flexible than a plain string of the same mass would be, which keeps it from sounding stiff and out of tune when fretted. It sits right at the changeover between the bronze-wound bass strings and the plain treble strings.
keyNumbers: Open note G3, about 196 Hz
Typically about 0.024 to 0.025 in (0.6 mm) thick
Roughly 14 kg of tension
details.madeOf: A thin steel core with a fine bronze wrap. On light-gauge acoustic sets the G is almost always wound, giving a warmer sound that blends with the bass strings.

parts.name: G string

parts.description: String 5, tuned to B; its length between saddle and nut sets the pitch of the open string.

details.didYouKnow: Because of the odd major third between G and B, a chord shape moved across from the lower strings to the B string has to shift up by one fret to give the same notes.
details.howItWorks: The B string is the first plain, unwound string and carries much of the melody in chords. Most neighbouring strings are tuned a perfect fourth apart, but the B sits only a major third above the G. That small step is what makes common chord shapes fit comfortably under the fingers.
keyNumbers: Open note B3, about 247 Hz
Typically about 0.016 in (0.41 mm) thick
Roughly 10 to 11 kg of tension
details.madeOf: A single strand of high-carbon steel music wire, often tin-plated to slow rusting. Plain steel is strong enough to hold its tension at a small diameter.

parts.name: B string

parts.description: String 6, tuned to high E; its length between saddle and nut sets the pitch of the open string.

details.didYouKnow: The high E is exactly two octaves above the low E. Touching it lightly over the 12th fret and plucking gives a chiming harmonic one octave higher still, about 659 Hz.
details.howItWorks: The thinnest and highest string vibrates four times as fast as the low E. Being so light, it starts and stops quickly, giving a bright, clear attack that cuts through. It bears on the saddle and nut in very narrow slots, and its tension pulls on the top just like the bass strings.
keyNumbers: Open note E4, about 330 Hz
Typically about 0.012 in (0.3 mm) thick
Roughly 10 to 11 kg of tension
details.madeOf: Plain high-carbon steel wire, drawn very fine for a high tensile strength. A small brass ball end is wound onto one end to anchor it at the bridge.

parts.name: High E string

parts.description: Three geared tuners: turning a button winds its string round a post through a worm gear that won't slip back.

details.didYouKnow: Geared machine heads were already in use by the early 1800s; before that, guitars were tuned with plain wooden friction pegs, like a violin.
details.howItWorks: These three tuners hold the low E, A and D strings. Each button turns a small worm screw that drives a gear on the string post, so many turns of the button make a small, precise change in tension. Because the worm's thread is shallow, friction stops the string's pull from turning it backwards, so the guitar stays in tune without a lock.
keyNumbers: 3 tuners on this side
Gear ratio typically about 14:1 to 18:1
Each post holds roughly 11 to 14 kg of pull
details.madeOf: Steel or brass gears in a die-cast or stamped metal housing, usually chrome- or nickel-plated. Metal gears last for decades of tuning and resist wear.

parts.name: Tuning machines (bass side)

parts.description: Three geared tuners: turning a button winds its string round a post through a worm gear that won't slip back.

details.didYouKnow: With an 18:1 gear, one full turn of the button rotates the post only about a twentieth of a turn, which is why fine-tuning is so precise.
details.howItWorks: These three tuners hold the G, B and high E strings. Plain treble strings are slippery and thin, so they need more wraps around the post than the wound strings to stop them creeping. The post's angle and the wraps also help set how firmly each string presses down into its nut slot.
keyNumbers: 3 tuners on this side
Gear ratio typically about 14:1 to 18:1
Plain strings typically need about 3 to 5 wraps on the post
details.madeOf: Plated steel or brass gears and posts, often in a sealed housing packed with grease. Sealed tuners need little maintenance and turn smoothly for years.

parts.name: Tuning machines (treble side)

parts.description: Slotted strip of bone at the top of the fretboard that spaces the strings and ends their vibrating length.

details.didYouKnow: A pinging or clicking sound while tuning is usually a string catching in its nut slot, often fixed with a little pencil graphite as a dry lubricant.
details.howItWorks: The nut is one end of every string's vibrating length; the saddle is the other. Each string sits in its own slot, cut just deep enough that the string clears the first fret without buzzing but is not so high that it is hard to press down. If a slot is too tight, the string sticks and jumps in pitch as you tune.
keyNumbers: Typically about 43 to 44 mm wide
String clearance at the 1st fret about 0.5 mm
6 slots, each sized to its string
details.madeOf: Usually bone, which is hard, dense and slightly slippery, so it transmits vibration well and lets strings slide. Cheaper guitars use plastic or synthetic substitutes.

parts.name: Nut

parts.description: Angled-back head that holds the tuners and presses the strings down onto the nut.

details.didYouKnow: The angled join between neck and headstock is the most common place for a guitar to break when it falls, because the wood grain runs short across the angle there.
details.howItWorks: The headstock is tilted back from the neck so that the strings bend down over the nut on their way to the tuners. That bend gives each string enough downward pressure to sit firmly in its slot and stop it buzzing or ringing beyond the nut. It also has to resist the whole string pull concentrated at the tuner posts.
keyNumbers: Back angle typically about 14 to 17 degrees
About 14 to 15 mm thick
Holds 6 tuners, 3 per side
details.madeOf: Usually carved from the same mahogany as the neck, often faced with a thin veneer of rosewood or ebony. Some makers join it on with an angled glue joint, called a scarf joint, for strength.

parts.name: Headstock

parts.description: Mahogany neck carved to a comfortable round back; it has to stay straight under the strings' steady pull.

details.didYouKnow: Big-leaf mahogany has been protected under international trade rules since 2003, so many modern necks use related woods such as sapele or other African mahoganies.
details.howItWorks: The neck is a long lever that must hold the strings at the right height along their whole length. The strings pull it forward with roughly 70 kg of force, so it relies on its own stiffness plus the truss rod to stay nearly straight. Its rounded back shape and thickness decide how comfortable it feels in the hand.
keyNumbers: About 21 to 23 mm deep at the 1st fret
Typically 14 frets clear of the body
Resists roughly 70 kg of string pull
details.madeOf: Mahogany, which is fairly light, stable and resists warping as humidity changes. The grain runs along the neck for stiffness.

parts.name: Neck

parts.description: Adjustable steel rod buried in the neck that pushes back against the strings to keep the neck straight.

details.didYouKnow: Adjustable truss rods were patented in the early 1920s, and C. F. Martin used a fixed, non-adjustable steel bar in its necks until the mid-1980s.
details.howItWorks: The rod runs in a channel under the fretboard and is tightened with a nut at one end. Tightening it bends the neck backwards slightly, against the strings' forward pull, so a player can set just a little forward bow, called relief, for clean playing. Changes in humidity or string gauge are corrected with small turns.
keyNumbers: Typical relief about 0.2 to 0.3 mm
Adjusted in steps of about a quarter turn
Rod typically about 5 mm thick
details.madeOf: Steel rod, sometimes a double-action design with two rods that can push the neck either way. Steel is far stiffer than wood, so a thin rod can control the whole neck.

parts.name: Truss rod

parts.description: Block at the base of the neck that joins it to the body, traditionally with a dovetail or bolts.

details.didYouKnow: Over decades the string pull slowly rolls the neck forward, so old guitars often need a neck reset, where the joint is taken apart and refitted at a steeper angle.
details.howItWorks: The heel is where the neck meets the body, and its joint sets the neck angle. That small tilt decides how high the strings sit above the frets and how tall the bridge and saddle must be. The joint carries the whole twisting load of the strings into the neck block.
keyNumbers: Neck meets body at the 14th fret
Neck angle typically about 1 to 2 degrees
details.madeOf: Mahogany, built up from the neck blank or from glued layers. The traditional joint is a glued dovetail; many modern guitars use a bolted mortise and tenon, which is easier to adjust later.

parts.name: Neck heel & joint

parts.description: Strip of dark hardwood glued to the neck that you press the strings against.

details.didYouKnow: Brazilian rosewood was placed under the strictest international trade protection in 1992, which is why most rosewood fretboards now come from India.
details.howItWorks: The fretboard holds the frets and gives your fingertips a hard surface to press the strings against. Its surface is gently curved across its width, which makes chords more comfortable to hold. It also adds stiffness to the neck and covers the truss rod channel.
keyNumbers: About 6 mm thick
Width about 43 mm at the nut, about 55 mm at the 14th fret
Curve radius typically about 400 mm
details.madeOf: Rosewood, a dense, oily hardwood that wears slowly under fingers and holds fret slots tightly without needing a finish. Ebony is the classic premium alternative.

parts.name: Fretboard

parts.description: Nickel-silver wires set across the fretboard; pressing just behind one shortens the string by a semitone.

details.didYouKnow: Nickel-silver contains no silver at all: it is roughly 60 per cent copper, 18 per cent nickel and the rest zinc, named for its silvery colour.
details.howItWorks: Each fret is a raised metal bar; pressing a string just behind it makes the fret the new end of the vibrating length. Each step shortens the string by about 5.6 per cent, raising the pitch one semitone, so the gaps shrink toward the body and the 12th fret sits exactly halfway. The model draws them evenly spaced as a simplification.
keyNumbers: 20 frets
12th fret about 322 mm from the nut, half the scale
1st fret gap about 36 mm, shrinking to about 12 mm near the 20th
Wire typically about 1 mm tall
details.madeOf: Nickel-silver wire with a T-shaped section whose barbed tang grips a slot in the fretboard. Harder stainless steel frets last longer but are harder to shape.

parts.name: Frets

parts.description: Thin, quarter-sawn spruce top that flexes like a loudspeaker cone; it does most of the guitar's sound-making.

details.didYouKnow: Spruce is roughly ten to twenty times stiffer along its grain than across it, which is why the braces underneath run at an angle to the grain to strengthen the top crosswise.
details.howItWorks: The strings rock the bridge, and the bridge pumps the lower part of the top in and out, pushing on the air around it. Because the top is large and light, it turns tiny string movements into sound you can hear across a room. It has to be thin enough to move freely but, with its bracing, strong enough not to bulge under the strings.
keyNumbers: About 2.5 to 3 mm thick
Lower bout about 40 cm across
Body about 50 cm long
details.madeOf: Solid spruce, split into two book-matched halves and quarter-sawn so the grain runs straight and upright. Spruce has one of the best stiffness-to-weight ratios of any wood.

parts.name: Soundboard

parts.description: Round opening that lets the air inside the body breathe in and out, boosting the bass.

details.didYouKnow: Players amplifying a guitar on stage sometimes plug the soundhole with a rubber cover, which kills that air resonance and helps stop feedback howl.
details.howItWorks: The air inside the body acts like a spring and the plug of air in the soundhole like a mass bouncing on it. This forms a resonance, the same effect as blowing across a bottle, that boosts the guitar's bass. The size of the hole and the volume of the body set its pitch.
keyNumbers: About 10 cm across
Air resonance typically about 100 Hz
Body volume roughly 15 to 20 litres
details.madeOf: An opening cut out of the spruce top; its edge is strengthened by the rosette and the braces around it. A round hole is the most common and least likely to start cracks.

parts.name: Soundhole

parts.description: Decorative inlaid ring round the soundhole that also reinforces its edge against cracking.

details.didYouKnow: The name comes from the lute, whose soundhole was covered by a carved wooden grille shaped like a rose.
details.howItWorks: The rosette is set into a shallow channel cut around the soundhole, crossing the grain of the top. Because spruce splits easily along its grain, the ring of inlay acts as a barrier that helps stop cracks running out from the soundhole edge. Its pattern is mainly a maker's decorative signature.
keyNumbers: Channel typically about 1 mm deep
Usually under 1 cm wide
details.madeOf: Thin rings of wood, plastic purfling or shell such as abalone, glued in and scraped flush. These materials are easy to cut into fine strips and contrast well with spruce.

parts.name: Rosette

parts.description: Thin plastic plate that protects the soft spruce from a pick's scratches.

details.didYouKnow: Old celluloid pickguards can shrink with age and pull on the spruce beneath them, which is a classic cause of cracks on vintage guitars.
details.howItWorks: Strumming with a pick drags its tip across the top just below the soundhole, and over the years that would gouge the soft spruce. The pickguard takes those knocks instead. It is so thin and light that it barely affects how the top vibrates.
keyNumbers: Typically about 0.5 mm thick
Weighs only a few grams
details.madeOf: Thin plastic sheet, often celluloid or acetate in a tortoiseshell pattern, stuck on with adhesive. Plastic is cheap, tough and easy to replace.

parts.name: Pickguard

parts.description: Hardwood block glued to the top that anchors the strings and passes their vibration into the soundboard.

details.didYouKnow: On most steel-string guitars the bridge is held on by glue alone, so a back edge that starts lifting is a common warning sign that needs a repair.
details.howItWorks: The bridge holds the saddle and anchors the string ends, and it is the only path from the strings into the top. The strings pull it forward and twist it, trying to roll its front edge down and lift its back edge up. Its broad glued footprint spreads that load over the top, and its mass shapes the tone.
keyNumbers: About 15 cm long and 3 cm wide
Roughly 9 to 10 mm tall
Resists roughly 70 kg of string pull
details.madeOf: Rosewood or ebony, both dense, hard woods that resist the strings' pull and wear. It is glued directly to bare spruce for the strongest bond.

parts.name: Bridge

parts.description: Thin strip of bone in the bridge that the strings bear down on; it ends their vibrating length at the body end.

details.didYouKnow: When a guitar has a pickup, a thin strip of piezo crystal is often hidden right under the saddle, turning the pressure of the strings into an electrical signal.
details.howItWorks: The saddle is where the strings leave their vibrating length at the body end, pressing down hard enough to pass vibration into the bridge. It is set at a slight slant so the bass strings are a little longer, which corrects for strings going slightly sharp when pressed down. Its height sets how high the strings sit over the frets.
keyNumbers: About 3 mm thick and 75 mm long
String height at the 12th fret typically about 2 to 2.5 mm on the bass side
Bass end set back a few mm
details.madeOf: Usually bone, which is hard and dense and carries vibration efficiently. Plastic saddles are cheaper but absorb more of the vibration.

parts.name: Saddle

parts.description: Six tapered pegs that wedge the ball ends of the strings into holes in the bridge.

details.didYouKnow: The pin does not carry the string tension itself: the ball end hooks against the bridge plate, and the pin mostly just keeps it in place.
details.howItWorks: Each string passes down through a hole in the bridge, and its ball end is pushed in after it by a tapered pin. The pin wedges the ball end against the underside of the bridge plate, where it catches. A groove in each pin lets the string pass alongside.
keyNumbers: 6 pins, one per string
Shaft roughly 5 mm across
Each ball end pulls with roughly 10 to 14 kg
details.madeOf: Plastic on most guitars, with ebony or bone on more expensive ones. They only need to be firm and smooth enough to grip without cracking the bridge.

parts.name: Bridge pins

parts.description: One arm of the X of spruce struts under the top, crossing just below the soundhole; it carries much of the strings' pull.

details.didYouKnow: X-bracing was popularised by C. F. Martin in the mid-1800s, and it later proved strong enough for steel strings when they replaced gut in the early 1900s.
details.howItWorks: This leg runs diagonally from one side of the upper bout across to the opposite side of the lower bout, passing close to the bridge. Together with the second leg it forms a stiff frame that stops the top bulging behind the bridge and sinking in front of it. Where the legs cross, they are notched halfway into each other so they lock together.
keyNumbers: About 7 to 8 mm wide
Typically about 15 to 18 mm tall at its peak
Legs cross at roughly 90 to 100 degrees
details.madeOf: Quarter-sawn spruce, the same light, stiff wood as the top, glued with its grain running along the brace. Tall and narrow sections give a lot of stiffness for very little weight.

parts.name: X-brace (first leg)

parts.description: One arm of the X of spruce struts under the top, crossing just below the soundhole; it carries much of the strings' pull.

details.didYouKnow: Scalloped braces went out of fashion in the mid-1940s as makers worried about tops failing under heavier strings, and they came back into wide use from the 1970s.
details.howItWorks: The second leg mirrors the first, crossing it just below the soundhole. Its ends taper and are thinned between their tallest points, a technique called scalloping, letting the top flex more freely around the bridge for a bigger bass response. Together the two legs carry most of the strings' pull around the soundhole.
keyNumbers: About 7 to 8 mm wide
Typically about 40 cm long
Scalloped down to a few mm at the ends
details.madeOf: Quarter-sawn spruce, shaped with chisels and planes after gluing. Removing wood from the brace ends trades a little strength for a livelier, louder top.

parts.name: X-brace (second leg)

parts.description: Smaller diagonal brace in the lower bout that tunes how the top vibrates.

details.didYouKnow: Many luthiers tap the top while carving the braces and listen to the ringing note, shaving wood until it sounds right, a craft method called tap tuning.
details.howItWorks: This small brace stiffens a patch of the lower bout below the bridge, controlling how that area bends. Its size and angle nudge the top's natural vibration patterns, helping balance bass against treble. Makers shave tone bars carefully to fine-tune a guitar's voice.
keyNumbers: About 13 cm long
Typically about 6 mm wide and 8 to 10 mm tall
details.madeOf: Spruce, much smaller than the X-brace legs. A light brace adds stiffness without adding mass that would deaden the top.

parts.name: Tone bar 1

parts.description: Smaller diagonal brace in the lower bout that tunes how the top vibrates.

details.didYouKnow: In traditional X-bracing both tone bars usually sit on the treble side, making that side stiffer to favour the high strings while the bass side stays freer to boom.
details.howItWorks: The second tone bar works with the first to stiffen the lower bout, the area that moves the most air. Changing the stiffness on one side relative to the other lets bass and treble areas of the top vibrate differently. The model shows the two bars mirrored for simplicity.
keyNumbers: About 13 cm long
Typically about 6 mm wide and 8 to 10 mm tall
details.madeOf: Light spruce with its grain running along the bar. Spruce keeps the added weight tiny for the stiffness gained.

parts.name: Tone bar 2

parts.description: Brace across the top above the soundhole, stiffening it where the neck pulls.

details.didYouKnow: Most of a guitar's sound comes from the lower bout around the bridge; the stiffened area above the soundhole contributes comparatively little.
details.howItWorks: This brace runs across the upper bout between the soundhole and the neck block. The strings pull the neck toward the bridge, squeezing the top in this area, so the brace stops it buckling or sinking. The upper bout moves relatively little anyway, so it can be braced stiffly without costing much sound.
keyNumbers: About 26 cm long
Typically about 12 mm tall
details.madeOf: A tall, straight bar of spruce, often with a thin hardwood or spruce patch beside it. It is usually left unscalloped because its job is mostly structural.

parts.name: Upper transverse brace

parts.description: Hardwood plate glued under the bridge so the ball ends of the strings don't wear through the soft top.

details.didYouKnow: On old, well-played guitars the ball ends can chew the plate around the string holes so badly that strings pull up into the bridge, and repairers fit thin replacement pads.
details.howItWorks: The bridge plate is glued under the top, sandwiching the spruce between it and the bridge. The string ball ends press against it, so it takes the wear and the pull that would otherwise tear through the soft top. It also helps resist the top rolling forward under string tension.
keyNumbers: About 2.5 to 3 mm thick
Roughly 4 cm wide
Holds 6 ball ends
details.madeOf: Usually hard maple, which is tough and wears slowly while staying light. Rosewood is also used; too heavy a plate can dull the sound.

parts.name: Bridge plate

parts.description: Strut across the inside of the back that keeps it gently arched and stiff.

details.didYouKnow: Back braces cross over a thin strip of wood glued along the back's centre seam, notched to let it pass, so the seam is reinforced along its whole length.
details.howItWorks: The brace nearest the neck crosses the narrow upper bout and helps keep the back's slight dome in shape. Like all back braces, it is glued to a back that has been gently arched, so the back resists humidity changes and knocks better than a flat panel would. It sits close to the neck block, adding stiffness to that end of the box.
keyNumbers: Roughly 28 cm long, across the upper bout
Typically about 7 mm wide and 12 to 15 mm tall
details.madeOf: Spruce, the same light, stiff wood as the top bracing. Braces are glued across the grain of the back to stop it splitting along its centre seam.

parts.name: Back brace 1

parts.description: Strut across the inside of the back that keeps it gently arched and stiff.

details.didYouKnow: The back is often arched to a curve with a radius of several metres, so slight that you barely notice it, yet enough to make it much stiffer.
details.howItWorks: This brace crosses the back near the waist, the narrowest part of the body. With the others it divides the back into panels whose vibration helps shape the guitar's tone. Its curved top edge holds the back in its gentle dome.
keyNumbers: Roughly 26 cm long, across the waist
Typically about 7 mm wide and 12 to 15 mm tall
details.madeOf: Spruce, shaped with a curved gluing face to match the arch of the back. Spruce keeps the back light while stiffening it across the grain.

parts.name: Back brace 2

parts.description: Strut across the inside of the back that keeps it gently arched and stiff.

details.didYouKnow: This simple pattern of straight braces across the back is called ladder bracing, and it is used on most steel-string guitars.
details.howItWorks: This brace spans the start of the lower bout, where the body widens. The back here is free to vibrate and reflect sound back toward the top and out of the soundhole. Its spacing from the neighbouring braces sets how big the vibrating panels of the back are.
keyNumbers: Roughly 33 cm long
Typically about 7 mm wide and 12 to 15 mm tall
details.madeOf: Spruce, glued across the mahogany grain. Its ends taper down where they meet the sides so they tuck neatly under the linings.

parts.name: Back brace 3

parts.description: Strut across the inside of the back that keeps it gently arched and stiff.

details.didYouKnow: Pressing your ear to the back of a guitar while someone plays shows how much it vibrates; the back adds its own colour to the sound rather than just reflecting it.
details.howItWorks: The brace nearest the tail crosses the widest part of the lower bout, the largest free panel of the back. Keeping this big area stiff and domed stops it bellying in or out and helps it respond evenly. It is the longest of the four back braces.
keyNumbers: Roughly 38 to 40 cm long, across the lower bout
Typically about 7 mm wide and 12 to 15 mm tall
details.madeOf: Spruce, chosen for its high stiffness for its weight. A longer brace like this needs straight grain along its whole length to stay strong.

parts.name: Back brace 4

parts.description: Two thin strips of mahogany bent with heat into the guitar's curved outline and joined at each end.

details.didYouKnow: The dreadnought shape is named after HMS Dreadnought, a huge British battleship of 1906; big, square-shouldered guitars of this type became popular from the 1930s.
details.howItWorks: The sides set the guitar's outline and depth, holding the top and back apart and enclosing the air that resonates inside. Strips of notched wood called kerfed linings are glued along their inside edges to give a wide gluing surface for the top and back. The sides are stiff and move relatively little, giving the vibrating plates a firm frame.
keyNumbers: About 2 mm thick
About 12 cm deep at the tail, tapering toward the neck
2 pieces joined at the neck and end blocks
details.madeOf: Mahogany planed thin, then heated and bent over a hot iron or in a heated mould until it holds its curves. Mahogany bends well and is stable once set.

parts.name: Sides (rims)

parts.description: Two book-matched mahogany plates joined down the middle; the back reflects sound and adds its own warmth.

details.didYouKnow: Book-matching is not just for looks: using two halves of the same board gives both sides the same stiffness, so the back vibrates evenly.
details.howItWorks: The back closes the box and contains the air inside, reflecting sound energy back toward the top and soundhole. It vibrates too, adding to the guitar's tone, especially in the low and middle range. Its gentle arch and bracing let it stay thin without cracking or sinking.
keyNumbers: About 2.5 mm thick
About 40 cm across the lower bout
4 back braces
details.madeOf: Two book-matched pieces of mahogany, cut from one board and opened like a book so the grain mirrors along the centre seam. Mahogany gives a warm, focused sound with a strong midrange.

parts.name: Back

parts.description: Plastic or wood edging round the top that seals the end grain and protects the edges from knocks.

details.didYouKnow: Wood swells and shrinks with humidity much more across its grain than along it, so guitars are happiest kept at roughly 45 to 55 per cent relative humidity.
details.howItWorks: The binding fits in a small step routed around the edges where the top and back meet the sides. It seals the exposed end grain of the wood there, slowing moisture getting in and out, and covers the joint. It takes the knocks that would otherwise chip the soft spruce edge.
keyNumbers: Typically about 2 mm thick
About 6 mm tall
details.madeOf: Usually plastic such as celluloid or ABS, or a hardwood strip, often with thin decorative lines called purfling alongside. Plastic bends easily round the curves and resists chips.

parts.name: Binding

parts.description: Solid block inside the top of the body where the neck is attached.

details.didYouKnow: Many makers stamp the guitar's serial number on the neck block, where you can read it through the soundhole with a small mirror.
details.howItWorks: The neck block is glued inside the body where the sides meet at the upper end. It anchors the neck joint and spreads the string pull into the sides, top and back. On many guitars the truss rod nut is reached through the soundhole at this end.
keyNumbers: Roughly 7 to 8 cm wide
Nearly the full body depth, about 10 cm at this end
Carries roughly 70 kg of string pull
details.madeOf: Solid mahogany, chosen to match the neck and because it is strong yet easy to cut accurately. The dovetail socket or bolt holes are cut straight into it.

parts.name: Neck block

parts.description: Block at the tail where the two sides meet; it also holds the strap button.

details.didYouKnow: When a pickup is fitted, the strap button is usually replaced by an endpin jack drilled through this block, which doubles as the strap button and the cable socket.
details.howItWorks: The end block joins the two sides at the tail of the guitar and keeps the box square. The strap button screws into it, so it takes the weight of the guitar when played standing. It also stops the joint between the sides pulling apart.
keyNumbers: About 12 cm tall, the full depth at the tail
Holds 1 strap button
details.madeOf: Solid mahogany or another light hardwood, glued between the sides. Its thickness gives a strap screw plenty of wood to bite into.

parts.name: End block

summary: A steel-string dreadnought acoustic guitar: a hollow wooden box whose thin spruce top, braced from inside, turns the vibration of six strings into sound loud enough to fill a room.

name: Grand Piano
overview:
A piano is a percussion instrument with strings: pressing a key flings a small felt-covered hammer up at a string, which rings out at one fixed note. Its full name, pianoforte, means soft-loud, because unlike the harpsichord before it, how hard you press decides how loud it sounds. Bartolomeo Cristofori in Florence built the first around 1700.

Behind the keys are about 230 steel strings, one to three per note, stretched so tight that together they pull with a force of roughly 20 tonnes. A cast-iron plate takes that strain. The strings rest on bridges glued to the soundboard, a large, thin sheet of spruce that vibrates with them and moves enough air to fill a hall. In a grand, the bass strings cross diagonally over the others, which fits longer strings into the case.

Each key works a small mechanism called the action: levers, springs and felts, about 50 parts per note. The hammer strikes the string and immediately falls back so it doesn't mute the sound, and it can repeat a note before the key is fully up. When you let go, a felt damper drops onto the string to silence it. The pedals change all this: the right pedal lifts every damper so notes keep ringing, the left shifts the hammers to strike fewer strings for a softer tone, and the middle one sustains only the notes being held.

parts.description: Big hinged lid that, propped open, reflects sound out towards the audience.

details.didYouKnow: Many pianists rehearse with the lid on the short stick or closed, because full lid can sound overwhelming in a small room even though it is ideal in a hall.
details.howItWorks: The lid is hinged along the straight, bass side of the case and opens towards the curved treble side. Propped up, its underside acts as an angled mirror, catching sound rising off the soundboard and throwing it sideways towards listeners. That is why a concert grand is placed with its curved side facing the audience. Closed, it muffles and evens out the sound, and the front section usually folds back on its own hinges so the music desk can be used with the main lid shut.
keyNumbers: Roughly 2 m long on a piano this size
Typically three brass hinges along the straight side
Heavy enough that lifting it is a two-handed job
details.madeOf: A stable core of solid or laminated wood such as spruce, poplar or birch plywood, veneered and finished, often in black polyester or lacquer. A flat, rigid panel reflects sound cleanly without buzzing.

parts.name: Lid

parts.description: Stick that holds the lid open, usually with a choice of a tall and a short position.

details.didYouKnow: A propped lid falling is one of the more common piano accidents, which is why movers and technicians are taught to always check the prop is seated in its cup before letting go.
details.howItWorks: The prop is a hinged stick that swings up from the case rim, and its tip sits in a small cup screwed to the underside of the lid. The tall position opens the lid wide for maximum projection, while the short one gives a gentler angle for accompanying singers or playing in smaller rooms. Because the whole weight of the lid bears down through it at an angle, the cup is what stops it slipping.
keyNumbers: Usually two lengths, tall and short
Short stick roughly half the height of the tall one
Holds up a lid of roughly 2 m
details.madeOf: A hardwood such as maple or beech, finished to match the case, with a brass or rubber-tipped end. Hardwood is strong enough to take a heavy, slanted load on a slim stick.

parts.name: Lid prop

parts.description: Curved case made of many thin layers of hardwood bent round a form while the glue sets; it gives the piano its shape and stiffness.

details.didYouKnow: Bending a whole rim in one continuous piece was patented in 1878; before that, grand cases were usually built up from separate sections joined together.
details.howItWorks: The rim is the curved wall that defines the grand's wing shape and holds everything together. The soundboard is glued to a ledge, called the liner, around its inside edge, and the iron plate is bolted down onto it. A very stiff, heavy rim stays still while the soundboard moves, so less of the string energy leaks away into the case and more becomes sound, giving longer sustain.
keyNumbers: Typically 15 to 20 layers of veneer
Several centimetres thick
Left to rest for weeks after bending
details.madeOf: Many thin layers of hardwood veneer, very often hard maple, glued together and bent round a giant clamp form in one go. Laminating the wood makes it far stronger and more stable than a single bent plank.

parts.name: Rim

parts.description: Heavy wooden beams under the case that brace the rim and carry the legs.

details.didYouKnow: If a keybed warps even slightly, the keys can start to feel uneven or the soft pedal can stick, so technicians sometimes check it with a long straightedge.
details.howItWorks: Thick beams run across the underside of the case, tying the rim's curved sides together so the string load cannot slowly squeeze it out of shape. They also give solid anchoring for the three legs and the pedal lyre. At the front, the keybed is a heavy flat panel on which the whole keyboard and action rest and slide.
keyNumbers: Carries a piano of roughly 300 to 350 kg
Usually several beams in a fan or grid
Keybed typically 3 to 5 cm thick
details.madeOf: Solid softwood or hardwood beams, often spruce or maple, joined into the rim, with a laminated keybed at the front. The keybed has to stay perfectly flat, so it is built from stable, cross-grained layers.

parts.name: Case bottom & beams

parts.description: Folding stand that holds the sheet music.

details.didYouKnow: Concert pianists playing from memory often have the desk removed entirely, which also lets slightly more sound escape over the strings.
details.howItWorks: The desk sits on rails over the tuning pin area and can usually be slid forwards or back to suit the player's eyesight. A hinged prop on the back sets its angle, and many fold flat or lift off completely for concerts. A narrow ledge at the bottom holds the pages and often a pencil.
keyNumbers: Typically about 70 to 80 cm wide
Usually two or three angle settings
Weighs only a few kilograms
details.madeOf: Wood or wood veneer matching the case, sometimes with a carved or fretwork panel. It needs to be light enough to lift off, yet stiff enough not to wobble when pages are turned.

parts.name: Music desk

parts.description: Key cover that folds down over the keyboard to protect it.

details.didYouKnow: Closing the fallboard on a piano that will sit unused in a bright room helps prevent the key tops yellowing or fading unevenly.
details.howItWorks: The fallboard hinges over the keys and closes onto the key slip, keeping out dust and stopping keys being knocked by accident. When open, it folds back against the front of the case and frames the top of the keyboard. Many modern versions have a slow-close damper inside the hinge so it settles gently instead of slamming on fingers.
keyNumbers: About 1.25 m long, the width of the keyboard
Slow-close types take a few seconds to settle
Often lockable on older pianos
details.madeOf: Solid or veneered wood, finished like the case, usually with the maker's name inlaid or printed on it. Some have a felt strip along the edge to protect the key tops.

parts.name: Fallboard

parts.description: Row of felt pads resting on the strings; lifting a key lifts its damper so the note can ring.

details.didYouKnow: Even with the sustain pedal up, the undamped top notes ring on slightly, which subtly brightens the sound of the whole instrument.
details.howItWorks: Each damper is a small wooden head carrying felt that rests on its strings from above. When you press a key, its back end lifts the damper clear just before the hammer strikes, and when you let go the damper drops back to silence the note. The sustain pedal lifts all of them at once via a tray underneath. The topmost notes have no dampers at all, because their short strings die away quickly anyway.
keyNumbers: Roughly 65 to 70 notes are damped
Top 18 to 20 notes or so have no dampers
Damper lifts a few millimetres off the strings
details.madeOf: Wooden heads and wires with soft wool felt pads. In the bass and tenor the felts are wedge-shaped to fit between the strings of each note, while in the treble they are flat.

parts.name: Dampers

parts.description: Plain steel strings, three per note in the treble, running straight back from the keyboard to the hitch pins.

details.didYouKnow: Because steel strings are slightly stiff, their overtones run a little sharp, so tuners stretch the octaves, tuning the top a touch higher and the bass a touch lower than simple maths predicts.
details.howItWorks: Each plain string runs from its tuning pin, over a hard edge on the plate, across the long bridge and on to a hitch pin at the back. Only the part between the front edge and the bridge, the speaking length, vibrates to make the note. Having two or three strings per note gives more volume and a richer, slowly evolving tone, since the strings never stay exactly in step with each other.
keyNumbers: Roughly 70 to 90 kg of tension per string
About 0.8 to 1.2 mm thick
Top C8 speaking length about 5 cm
Top note about 4,186 Hz
details.madeOf: High-carbon steel music wire, cold-drawn to be extremely strong. It has to survive tension close to its breaking point for years and be hit thousands of times without stretching.

parts.name: Treble and middle strings

parts.description: Copper-wound strings for the low notes, crossing diagonally over the others to fit more length into the case.

details.didYouKnow: The patent for an overstrung grand with a one-piece iron frame, granted in 1859, set the basic layout that almost every grand built since has followed.
details.howItWorks: Low notes need strings that are heavy for their length. Wrapping a steel core in copper adds mass without making the string stiff, so it can vibrate slowly and still sound musical. Crossing these strings over the tenor strings, called overstringing, lets them run diagonally across the case, which fits in extra length and puts their bridge nearer the lively middle of the soundboard.
keyNumbers: One string per note in the lowest octave or so
Lowest string roughly 1.5 to 1.7 m long here
Several millimetres thick at the very bottom
Bottom note A0 at 27.5 Hz
details.madeOf: A plain steel core wire tightly wound with one or two layers of copper wire. Copper is dense and soft, so it adds weight without adding much stiffness.

parts.name: Bass strings (overstrung)

parts.description: Single huge iron casting that takes the strings' combined pull of about 20 tonnes, which a wooden frame couldn't hold.

details.didYouKnow: A full iron frame was first patented for a square piano in 1825; without it, wooden-framed pianos could not take modern string tension and went out of tune constantly.
details.howItWorks: All the strings are anchored at both ends on the plate, so it, not the wooden case, takes their huge combined pull. It is shaped with struts and a curved outline that spread the load evenly, with large holes to save weight. The plate sits just above the soundboard without touching it, and is bolted to the rim and the pinblock so the whole assembly stays rigid and in tune.
keyNumbers: Roughly 150 to 200 kg
Holds about 18 to 20 tonnes of string tension
Usually the single heaviest part of the piano
details.madeOf: Grey cast iron, poured into a sand mould and cooled slowly, then sanded and usually finished in gold or bronze lacquer. Iron is cheap, very stiff in compression and does not creep under a constant load the way wood does.

parts.name: Cast-iron plate

parts.description: About 230 steel pins, one per string, that the tuner turns to tighten or slacken each string.

details.didYouKnow: A full tuning means adjusting every one of the roughly 230 pins, and a skilled tuner usually does it in about one to two hours.
details.howItWorks: Each string is coiled about three times round its pin, and the pin is driven through the plate into a tight hole in the pinblock below. The tuner fits a lever over the square top and turns it by tiny amounts, and friction alone holds it there afterwards. A good tuner also sets the pin so it is not left twisted, otherwise it slowly unwinds and the note drifts flat.
keyNumbers: About 230, one per string
Roughly 7 mm in diameter
Typically 55 to 65 mm long
details.madeOf: Hardened, blued or nickel-plated steel with a finely threaded or ridged shank that bites into the wood. Steel is needed because each pin is under constant twisting and bending from its string.

parts.name: Tuning pins

parts.description: Laminated hardwood block under the plate that grips the tuning pins tightly enough to hold the strings in tune.

details.didYouKnow: Pinblocks are one of the main things replaced when an old piano is rebuilt, since the wood eventually loses its grip after decades of humidity swings and retunings.
details.howItWorks: The pinblock grips every tuning pin like a vice, and that grip, not any locking mechanism, is what keeps the piano in tune. In a grand it sits under the front of the plate, pressed tightly against it so the pins cannot lean forward under string tension. If the wood dries out or the holes wear, pins turn too easily and the piano will not hold a tuning.
keyNumbers: Typically 5 to 40 or more layers
Roughly 35 to 40 mm thick
Holds about 230 pins
details.madeOf: Many layers of hard maple glued with their grains at different angles. Cross-laminating means each pin is gripped by both end grain and side grain, and the block resists splitting.

parts.name: Pinblock

parts.description: Curved hardwood bridge glued to the soundboard that the treble and middle strings press down on.

details.didYouKnow: The bridge is carefully notched at each pin so the string leaves it at a crisp point; a sloppy notch can make a note sound dull or buzzy.
details.howItWorks: The strings pass over the bridge at a slight downward angle, called downbearing, so they press firmly on it. Each string zigzags between two metal pins on the bridge top, which stops it sliding sideways and defines exactly where its speaking length ends. As the strings vibrate, they rock the bridge, and the bridge passes that motion into the soundboard it is glued to.
keyNumbers: About 1 to 2 degrees of downbearing
Two steel bridge pins per string
Strings press down with several hundred kg in total
details.madeOf: Hard maple, often built up from laminations with a solid cap, and topped with graphite so the strings can slide during tuning. Maple is dense and hard enough to hold hundreds of pins without splitting.

parts.name: Long bridge

parts.description: Separate short bridge for the bass strings, set back near the tail.

details.didYouKnow: The jump from the bass bridge to the long bridge is one of the trickiest areas in piano design, because the tone can change audibly between the last bass note and the first tenor note.
details.howItWorks: Because the bass strings cross over the others, they need their own bridge, sitting on a different part of the soundboard. Placing it away from the stiff edge of the case and nearer the middle helps the low notes drive the board well. On many grands it stands on a raised block or a small cantilever so the overstrung bass strings clear the ones below.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 20 to 30 notes
Usually about 30 to 50 cm long
Uses one or two strings per note
details.madeOf: Hard maple like the long bridge, with steel bridge pins and a graphite-coated top. It has to transmit very large, slow movements from heavy strings without flexing.

parts.name: Bass bridge

parts.description: Large spruce panel under the strings that vibrates with them and turns their energy into sound, like a loudspeaker cone.

details.didYouKnow: A soundboard swells and shrinks with humidity; a cracked board is often the result of very dry winters, though a small crack does not always change the sound much.
details.howItWorks: A string on its own barely moves any air, so the soundboard acts as an amplifier: the bridges shake it and its large area pushes air back and forth. It is made with a slight upward arch, the crown, which pushes back against the string downbearing and keeps the board springy. Thinning the board towards its edges lets it move more freely, a bit like the surround of a loudspeaker cone.
keyNumbers: About 8 to 10 mm thick
Roughly 1.5 to 2 square metres in area
Sound travels along the grain at about 5,000 m/s
details.madeOf: Quarter-sawn spruce boards edge-glued into one panel. Spruce is very stiff for its weight, which means it can be thin and light yet still carry sound quickly through the wood.

parts.name: Soundboard

parts.description: Spruce rib glued across the underside of the soundboard, stiffening it and holding its slight upward crown.

details.didYouKnow: In a real grand the ribs run diagonally, at right angles to the soundboard grain; this model draws them straight across the case to keep things simple.
details.howItWorks: This rib sits nearest the keyboard end of the board, under the treble part of the long bridge. The treble needs a stiff, light board area that can respond to short, fast vibrations, so ribs here are short and relatively deep for their length. It also helps the board resist the strong downward push of the treble strings close to the bridge.
keyNumbers: One of the shortest ribs, under the treble
Roughly 20 to 25 mm wide
Grand soundboards typically have 10 to 15 ribs
details.madeOf: Straight-grained spruce, glued across the soundboard's grain. Crossing the grain gives the board stiffness in both directions.

parts.name: Soundboard rib 1

parts.description: Spruce rib glued across the underside of the soundboard, stiffening it and holding its slight upward crown.

details.didYouKnow: Ribs are often glued on while the board is held over a curved form, and drying the wood first means the board swells slightly afterwards, helping to lock in its crown.
details.howItWorks: The second rib sits a little further back, still under the upper treble and tenor area of the long bridge. Like its neighbour, it helps hold the crown and stiffen the board so high notes stay clear and bright rather than thin. Its ends are usually tapered, or scalloped, so the board can flex more freely where it meets the rim.
keyNumbers: Roughly 20 to 25 mm wide
Typically 20 to 30 mm tall at the centre
Tapered towards each end
details.madeOf: Spruce, chosen to match the soundboard's stiffness and weight. The rib's grain runs along its length, crossing the board's own grain.

parts.name: Soundboard rib 2

parts.description: Spruce rib glued across the underside of the soundboard, stiffening it and holding its slight upward crown.

details.didYouKnow: Piano designers sometimes tap a finished soundboard and listen, or measure how it rings, to check the ribs have given it the stiffness they intended.
details.howItWorks: This rib crosses the board under the middle of the long bridge, where the strings for the most-played notes around middle C press down. The board here has to balance stiffness for clarity against flexibility for warmth and volume. Its job is to spread the bridge's movement across a wide area of the board.
keyNumbers: Near the notes around middle C at about 262 Hz
Roughly 20 to 25 mm wide
Among the longer ribs on the board
details.madeOf: Spruce, sometimes sugar pine in older or specialist pianos. Both are light, resonant softwoods with long, straight grain.

parts.name: Soundboard rib 3

parts.description: Spruce rib glued across the underside of the soundboard, stiffening it and holding its slight upward crown.

details.didYouKnow: Go-bar decks, where dozens of bent poles hold parts down while glue sets, are an old trick that piano and harpsichord makers still use.
details.howItWorks: The fourth rib sits around the middle of the board, where the soundboard is broad and free to move. Mid-board ribs tend to be the longest and are a little shallower for their length than treble ribs, keeping this area flexible enough to sound full and warm. It runs under the tenor section of the long bridge and close to where the bass strings cross above.
keyNumbers: One of the longest ribs
Roughly 20 to 25 mm wide
Crown height of only a few millimetres
details.madeOf: Spruce, glued with a strong wood glue and often clamped with go-bars, springy poles wedged against a ceiling to press the rib down evenly.

parts.name: Soundboard rib 4

parts.description: Spruce rib glued across the underside of the soundboard, stiffening it and holding its slight upward crown.

details.didYouKnow: Where a rib crosses the bridge area matters: makers adjust rib spacing and depth to fine-tune how evenly the board responds from note to note.
details.howItWorks: This rib supports the board in the zone between the tenor of the long bridge and the bass bridge. It helps the crown push back evenly against both bridges, so the downbearing stays consistent across the change from plain to wound strings. A smooth stiffness here helps the tone stay even across that awkward transition.
keyNumbers: Roughly 20 to 25 mm wide
Near the break between bass and tenor
Typically tapered over its last 20 to 30 cm
details.madeOf: Spruce, tapered at its ends. The taper lets this part of the board move while still holding its arch.

parts.name: Soundboard rib 5

parts.description: Spruce rib glued across the underside of the soundboard, stiffening it and holding its slight upward crown.

details.didYouKnow: A soundboard cannot efficiently radiate the very lowest fundamental notes, so much of what you hear as deep bass is actually the overtones, and your ear fills in the rest.
details.howItWorks: The sixth rib sits under the bass bridge region, where the heavy wound strings drive the board with slow, large movements. Ribs here can be a little more flexible, because the bass needs the board to move a lot of air at low frequencies. It still has to hold the crown so the bass bridge keeps pressing firmly on the board.
keyNumbers: Under the bass bridge area
Roughly 20 to 25 mm wide
Helps carry bass notes down to 27.5 Hz
details.madeOf: Spruce, glued across the grain. Light weight here matters, because any extra mass makes the board slower to respond to the strings.

parts.name: Soundboard rib 6

parts.description: Spruce rib glued across the underside of the soundboard, stiffening it and holding its slight upward crown.

details.didYouKnow: A rib that comes unglued from the board is a classic cause of a mysterious buzz in a grand piano, and finding it can take a technician quite some detective work.
details.howItWorks: The last rib sits nearest the tail, where the board narrows towards the back of the case. It is shorter because the board is narrower here, and it stiffens the edge area behind the bass bridge. With little string load right at the tail, its main job is keeping the board's outer region from flapping or buzzing.
keyNumbers: Shortest rib in this model
Roughly 20 to 25 mm wide
Nearest the tail of a 2.1 m case
details.madeOf: Spruce like the others, often with heavily tapered ends. Tapering helps the board edge blend smoothly into the rim liner.

parts.name: Soundboard rib 7

parts.description: The 52 natural keys, each a long wooden lever covered with a smooth top; the front end goes down, the back end lifts the action.

details.didYouKnow: One octave of seven white keys measures about 16.5 cm, a size that has hardly changed in well over a century, so pianists can move between instruments easily.
details.howItWorks: Each key is a lever that pivots on a balance pin near its middle. Pressing the front down lifts the back, which pushes up on the action and the damper. Small lead weights set into the key sticks balance them so that every key needs about the same push to go down and comes back up at the same speed.
keyNumbers: 52 white keys
About 23 mm wide at the front
Typically about 10 mm of key dip
Roughly 50 g to press a key down
details.madeOf: Long sticks of spruce or basswood with tops of acrylic or other plastic. Ivory key tops were once standard but were phased out after international bans on the ivory trade.

parts.name: White keys

parts.description: The 36 sharps and flats, raised and set back in groups of two and three.

details.didYouKnow: On many 18th-century keyboards the colours were reversed, with dark naturals and light sharps.
details.howItWorks: The black keys are shorter at the front and sit higher, set back between the white keys, so fingers can reach them without catching the naturals. They are levers just like the white keys and drive their own sets of action parts. Their pattern of twos and threes repeats every twelve notes, which is how players find their place on the keyboard.
keyNumbers: 36 black keys
About 12 to 13 mm wide on top
Raised roughly 12 mm above the white keys
details.madeOf: Traditionally ebony, a dense black hardwood, but today usually black plastic such as phenolic resin on a wooden key stick. Plastic is cheaper, consistent and more hard-wearing.

parts.name: Black keys

parts.description: Wooden frame the keys pivot on, with guide pins that keep each key moving straight.

details.didYouKnow: Piano technicians slide out the whole keyboard and action, often in a minute or two, to regulate, clean or retrieve coins and pencils dropped between the keys.
details.howItWorks: The key frame has three rails: a back rail, a balance rail where each key pivots on a pin, and a front rail with a pin that keeps each key from wobbling sideways. Felt-lined holes in the keys slide on these pins quietly. In a grand the keys, frame and action form one unit that slides in and out of the case like a drawer, and the soft pedal moves this whole unit sideways.
keyNumbers: 88 balance pins and 88 front pins
Slides out as one unit with the action
Keys level to within about a millimetre
details.madeOf: Hardwood rails such as beech or maple, with steel guide pins and felt bushings and punchings. The wood must stay flat and stable so all 88 keys stay level.

parts.name: Key frame

parts.description: Rows of small levers, one set per key, that throw the hammer and let it escape just before it hits the string.

details.didYouKnow: The double-escapement action patented by Sébastien Érard in 1821 is the basis of almost every grand action today, and made fast repeated notes possible.
details.howItWorks: When the key lifts the wippen, a jack pushes the hammer towards the string. Just before contact, the jack trips out of the way, called escapement, so the hammer flies freely, strikes and rebounds instead of jamming against the string. A repetition lever catches the hammer on the way back, letting the note be replayed before the key has fully risen.
keyNumbers: About 50 or more parts per key
Hammer released roughly 1 to 3 mm from the string
Hammer travels about 45 mm to the string
details.madeOf: Wooden levers of hornbeam or maple with felt and leather cushions, brass or wooden flanges, steel springs and pins, mounted on cast metal brackets and rails. Many modern actions use some composite parts for consistency.

parts.name: Action (wippens & levers)

parts.description: 88 wooden hammers with tightly packed wool-felt heads, shaped and voiced to strike the strings.

details.didYouKnow: Technicians voice hammers by pricking the felt with fine needles to soften it, or hardening it with a solution, to make the tone even across the keyboard.
details.howItWorks: The hammer is flung at the strings, touches them for only a few thousandths of a second and bounces off. The firmness of its felt shapes the tone: softer felt gives a warm sound when played gently, while harder layers beneath produce brilliance when played loudly. Each hammer strikes at roughly one-seventh to one-ninth of the string's length, which weakens some harsh-sounding overtones.
keyNumbers: 88 hammers
Heads roughly 5 to 12 g, light in the treble
Contact with the string of a few milliseconds
details.madeOf: A wooden core, called a moulding, often of hornbeam, maple or mahogany, wrapped in wool felt pressed under great force. Hammers get smaller and lighter towards the treble.

parts.name: Hammers

parts.description: Wooden rail in front of the keys and blocks at each end of the keyboard.

details.didYouKnow: A key slip set slightly too close to the keys can rub against the key fronts and make them sluggish, which is a surprisingly common cause of a sticking key.
details.howItWorks: The key slip runs along the front of the keyboard, below the key fronts, and the cheeks close off each end beside the lowest and highest keys. Together with the key blocks they frame the keyboard and stop the keys being knocked sideways. On many grands the key blocks also hold the action in place in the case.
keyNumbers: Key slip about 1.25 m long
Two cheeks, one at each end
Removed in minutes for servicing
details.madeOf: Solid hardwood or veneered wood finished to match the case. They are often screwed in place so they can be removed to slide out the action.

parts.name: Key slip & cheeks

parts.description: Tapered wooden leg on a castor, bolted to the case bottom.

details.didYouKnow: To move a grand, movers usually stand it on its straight side on a padded board and take all three legs off.
details.howItWorks: This leg stands under the front left corner of the case, at the bass end of the keyboard, near the heavy end of the plate and the long bass strings. Together with the other front leg, it sets the height of the keyboard. It is fixed into a socket or plate on the case bottom, so it can be removed for moving.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 100 kg
Keys sit about 70 to 75 cm above the floor
Castor wheel typically 5 to 7 cm across
details.madeOf: Hardwood, often built from glued layers, finished to match the case, with a castor of brass or steel and a rubber or nylon wheel. Laminated wood resists splitting under a heavy load.

parts.name: Leg (front, bass side)

parts.description: Tapered wooden leg on a castor, bolted to the case bottom.

details.didYouKnow: Castors are made for occasional nudges, not regular rolling; pushing a grand around on its castors can strain the legs, so movers use a dolly or board.
details.howItWorks: The treble leg stands under the front right of the case, where the curve of the rim begins. With the bass leg, it forms the front pair that takes the weight of the keyboard, action, pinblock and front of the plate. Since a pianist sits between these legs, they are spaced to leave room for knees and the pedal lyre.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 100 kg
Typically 55 to 65 cm tall
Usually swivelling castor
details.madeOf: Laminated or solid hardwood with a castor at its foot. A leg plate or dovetail fitting spreads the load into the case bottom beams.

parts.name: Leg (front, treble side)

parts.description: Tapered wooden leg on a castor, bolted to the case bottom.

details.didYouKnow: Some piano owners fit castor cups under the legs, shallow dishes that spread the load and stop the wheels denting wooden floors.
details.howItWorks: The tail leg supports the narrow back end of the case, under the far end of the strings and soundboard. With only three legs, the piano always sits steadily on an uneven floor, just like a three-legged stool. It carries a smaller share of the weight than the front pair because most of the heavy parts are towards the keyboard end.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 80 to 100 kg
About 1.5 to 1.7 m behind the front legs
Same height as the front legs
details.madeOf: Hardwood matching the other two legs, with a castor. It is bolted to a beam near the tail so the load goes straight into the case structure.

parts.name: Leg (tail)

parts.description: Frame under the keyboard that holds the pedals and the rods running up to the action.

details.didYouKnow: The pedal assembly takes its name from the shape of early versions, which looked like the lyre, the ancient Greek stringed instrument.
details.howItWorks: The lyre hangs under the keyboard and holds the three pedals on pivots near the floor. Each pedal pushes a wooden or metal rod straight up into the case, where levers, called trapwork, turn that push into lifting the dampers or shifting the action. Slanting braces run from the back of the lyre to the case bottom so the player's foot pressure does not push it forwards.
keyNumbers: Holds 3 pedals
Usually 1 or 2 back braces
Rods typically 30 to 50 cm long
details.madeOf: Hardwood with a decorative shape, metal brackets and springs, and felt or leather cushions to keep the pedal action quiet.

parts.name: Pedal lyre

parts.description: Left pedal: shifts the whole action sideways so each hammer hits fewer strings, for a softer, veiled tone.

details.didYouKnow: Una corda means 'one string', because some early pianos could shift so far that each hammer struck only one string; composers write tre corde to release it.
details.howItWorks: Pressing this pedal slides the keyboard and action a few millimetres to the right. Treble hammers then strike two of their three strings, and every hammer meets the strings with a softer, less-worn part of its felt, giving a softer, more veiled sound. The unstruck string still vibrates sympathetically, adding a hazy colour.
keyNumbers: Shift of only a few millimetres
Hammers hit 2 of 3 strings in the treble
Leftmost of 3 pedals
details.madeOf: Brass or brass-plated cast metal, polished, on a lever pivot in the lyre. Brass is durable and does not rust where shoes rub it.

parts.name: Soft pedal (una corda)

parts.description: Middle pedal: sustains only the notes already held down when it's pressed.

details.didYouKnow: The sostenuto was shown by a French maker in 1844 but only became common after an American patent in 1874; it is the least used of the three pedals.
details.howItWorks: When pressed, it catches and holds up only the dampers that are already raised by keys being held. Those notes keep ringing, while everything played afterwards is damped normally. This lets a pianist hold a low bass note while playing crisp, separated notes above it.
keyNumbers: Middle of 3 pedals
Controls dampers on roughly 65 to 70 notes
Standard on grands since the late 19th century
details.madeOf: Brass or brass-plated metal like the other pedals, linked to a long rod running under the dampers with a catching edge.

parts.name: Sostenuto pedal

parts.description: Right pedal: lifts every damper at once so all notes keep ringing; the most used pedal.

details.didYouKnow: It is often called the loud pedal, but it does not make notes louder; it only lets them ring longer and adds sympathetic resonance.
details.howItWorks: This pedal raises every damper together so notes keep sounding after the keys are let go, letting a pianist join chords smoothly. With all dampers up, other strings also vibrate in sympathy, giving the sound a richer halo. Skilled players use partial or half pedalling, letting the dampers just brush the strings to thin the sound without fully cutting it.
keyNumbers: Rightmost of 3 pedals
Lifts roughly 65 to 70 dampers at once
Raises each damper only a few millimetres
details.madeOf: Brass or brass-plated metal with a textured or polished top, connected to the damper lift tray through the lyre rod and trapwork.

summary: A 2.1 m grand piano with 88 keys: each key throws a felt hammer at steel strings stretched across a cast-iron frame, and a big wooden soundboard turns their vibration into sound.
